items.title: Aethos London Shoreditch designed using an "East meets East" approach
items.summary:
Boutique hotel brand Aethos has opened its first London outpost with interiors designed by Astet Studio in a Ron Arad Associates building that was formerly home to Nobu Hotel Shoreditch. Created by Astet Studio, the interiors of Aethos London Shoreditch were designed to blend the industrial design language of the original building with a softer Japanese-inspired […] 
 The post  Aethos London Shoreditch designed using an "East meets East" approach  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Clara Finnigan 27 August 2026 Boutique hotel brand Aethos has opened its first London outpost with interiors designed by Astet Studio in a Ron Arad Associates building that was formerly home to Nobu Hotel Shoreditch. Created by Astet Studio , the interiors of Aethos London Shoreditch were designed to blend the industrial design language of the original building with a softer Japanese-inspired material palette. Astet Studio used earthy tones to introduced warmth into the industrial setting “When we first approached the project, we saw an opportunity to explore what we call East meets East,” Astet Studio co-founder Oscar Engroba told Dezeen. “Rather than recreating Shoreditch’s industrial past, we wanted to bring its existing character into conversation with the precision and craftsmanship of Japanese design traditions.” Textured fabrics were used to absorb rather than reflect light in the breakfast room The Barcelona -based interiors studio was inspired by the Japanese concept of Utsuroi for the project, explaining to Dezeen that its employment meant “the architecture stays constant while the experience quietly evolves”. Astet Studio used the Japanese concept of Utsuroi to evolve the hotel’s lobby, bar, gym, members’ lounge and Mitsu restaurant . The 164-room hotel, originally built in 2017, is defined by its striking industrial facade, featuring cantilevered balconies framed in glass, steel, and concrete. Aethos London Shoreditch is housed in a building designed by Ron Arad Associates Guests enter through this layered concrete facade into an open lobby characterised by earthy browns and muted natural tones, which was designed to introduce warmth into the industrial setting. “We wanted guests to feel welcome and connected to the rhythm of Shoreditch, while still offering moments of calm,” said Engroba. “The colour palette draws from the Japanese Shin-Bijutsukai movement, using natural materials, planting and filtered light to soften the architecture without diminishing its character.” Aethos London Shoreditch fuses East London’s industrial design language with “the craftsmanship of Japanese design traditions” Contemporary, low-height seating was used throughout the space, while a series of large, textured rugs zone the space to create areas of relaxation. Vintage decorative pieces and furniture were used intentionally throughout the lobby alongside works by local artists and designers to connect the interior to its east London roots. Astet Studio brings warmth and tactility to the industrial spaces by using bespoke wood panelling across the lobby area, breakfast rooms and bedrooms. The timber detailing across the interiors of Aethos draws inspiration from traditional Japanese carpentry “The palette combines hand-finished timber, textured ceramics, woven fabrics and predominantly matte finishes,” Engroba explained. “By favouring materials that absorb rather than reflect light, the interiors develop subtle changes throughout the day, giving the spaces a quieter, more tactile quality.” Astet Studio designed the bedrooms to have a more refined and pared-back colour palette In the bedrooms, the studio shifted the material palette to be simpler and more refined, featuring muted tones of grey, burnt orange, and blackened wood. “In the bedrooms, the focus moves towards comfort, tactility and a quieter sensory experience,” said Engroba. “Materials become softer, lighting more controlled and the overall atmosphere more intimate, creating a retreat within the city.” Aethos London Shoreditch features 164 hotel rooms plus a restaurant and private members bar Other Japanese-style interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Mitsu restaurant in London and Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio in Tokyo . The photography is Pion Studio . Read more Interiors Highlights

items.title: Shigeru Ban unveils coastal wellness retreat on Awaji Island
items.summary:
Pritzker Prize-winning architect Shigeru Ban has completed a wellness hotel on Awaji Island, Japan. Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat, the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as "pre-illness". The hotel is the […] 
 The post  Shigeru Ban unveils coastal wellness retreat on Awaji Island  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Tom Ravenscroft Editor-in-chief 24 August 2026 Pritzker Prize-winning architect Shigeru Ban has completed a wellness hotel on Awaji Island, Japan . Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat , the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as “pre-illness”. The hotel is the third project designed by Ban for Japanese company Pasona Group on the island. It follows a thatch-topped restaurant and a wooden meditation retreat . Shigeru Ban designed the Pasona Natureverse Retreat According to Ban, the hotel’s D-shaped form was designed to take advantage of its location between the coast and a forest. “To express the characteristics of a site defined by these two completely contrasting landscapes, distinct facades were designed for the east and west sides,” said Ban. “Two linear structures with individual qualities are integrated into a single D-shaped plan, flanking a light-filled atrium.” The hotel stands on the seafront The five-storey hotel was designed primarily for long-term, 30-day-plus retreats, as well as offering shorter stays. Its 57 rooms are arranged around a large, skylit central atrium with half overlooking the sea and half facing the forest. While the landward facade is adorned with stylised timber columns, the seaward side was designed to express horizontally, with balconies running the full width on all levels. The seafront facade was designed to express horizontally “On the seaside, using the seawall as a podium, the facade is highly transparent, featuring four levels of emphasised horizontal slabs that create a seamless continuity between the interior, exterior, and the surrounding scenery,” said Ban. “In contrast to the horizontal emphasis of the seaside, the mountain-side facade features a rhythmic arrangement of timber-clad columns that emphasize a symbolic, somewhat classical vertical structure,” he continued. “At the center, a massive timber canopy and a grand staircase welcome visitors.” Rooms were arranged around a central atrium Stays at the hotel are focused on preventive wellness treatments, with all guests receiving a personalised wellness program that may include thalassotherapy, hammam meditation, yoga, sound therapy and aromatherapy. Every room in the hotel contains a private onsen – a natural hot spring bath – and several rooms have sensor-operated beds that monitor nighttime body movement and adjust automatically to encourage the best sleep. Along with a wellness clinic and treatment room, the hotel includes a dedicated room for aerial yoga with suspended fabric hammocks and a gym. An indoor swimming pool is fed with salt water from the Seto Inland Sea. Rooms either have views over the sea or forest Alongside the wellness facilities, the hotel contains five restaurants, several run by Michelin-starred chefs, as well as several cafes. On the third floor, an event hall was designed for live musical performances and contains 500 window panes covered in artworks. An event hall was decorated with 500 glass artworks One of the world’s most respected architects, Ban won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2014 and was recently awarded the 2026 AIA Gold Medal . He is known for his innovative architecture that often uses cardboard and natural materials, with the Cardboard Cathedral in Christchurch one of his most influential buildings. The photography is by Hiroyuki Hirai. Read more Architecture Highlights

items.title: Yarlington Lodge at The Newt in Somerset blends "little snippets of history with life today"
items.summary:
British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England, restoring their interiors to nod to the site's past. Named Yarlington Lodge, the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset, a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located […] 
 The post  Yarlington Lodge at The Newt in Somerset blends "little snippets of history with life today"  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 24 August 2026 British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England , restoring their interiors to nod to the site’s past. Named Yarlington Lodge , the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset , a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located just outside of Bruton. Yarlington Lodge is a three-building holiday home at The Newt in Somerset Conceived by Richard Parr Associates as a 32-guest holiday home, the project comprises the main lodge, the Coach House and the Cottage in the Wall – three buildings that historically served as a rectory, its coach house and the gardener’s cottage, respectively. “They were once a functioning trio and we wanted them to become so again,” studio founder Richard Parr told Dezeen. Patterns and bright colours reference the Napoleonic era in the main lodge The architect worked with The Newt in Somerset’s founders, Koos Bekker and Karen Roos, to restore each property. For the 1831 lodge, striking patterns and bright colours were selected to reference the high drama of the Napoleonic era . The Coach House was renovated to reflect its equestrian history Bedroom ceilings were clad with swooping textiles that give the impression of military tents, while classical paintings embellish the green-hued library. Despite these statement design features, Parr explained that interventions to the bones of each building were intentionally subtle. This included carefully restoring the lodge’s old fireplaces, elm floorboards and stonework. “Deliberately pared-back” changes were made to the facades “Houses need to retain the spirit of their entire life and should reflect their many owners, hence the references to previous occupants through portraiture and furniture,” said the architect. “The renovation is a mix of little snippets of history with life today,” he added. A swimming pool also features within the grounds The Coach House was also adapted to reflect its equestrian history. Blackened steel and raw timber characterise the interior spaces, including the brick-clad living room with a low-slung, beam-lined ceiling. By contrast, Parr and his team renovated the Cottage in the Wall with sandy-hued walls and wooden accents, which complement the building’s lofty ceilings. “Deliberately pared-back” changes were also made to the facade of each building, Parr said, using local Hadspen stone as well as brick, slate, tile and lead. “Internally, these same materials were subtly reinterpreted to different levels of sophistication in the form of timber floors, local blue limestone, and a range of pastel colours lifted out of late Regency England,” explained Parr. A greenhouse sits opposite the pool Alongside the three buildings, the Yarlington Lodge site is home to a rectilinear, tile-clad swimming pool opposite a lush plant-filled greenhouse . When revitalising the 19th-century properties, Parr described the main hurdle as subtly incorporating air conditioning into the rooms – something he said felt necessary in 2026. “As the summers get hotter, the need to air-condition all of the bedrooms was introduced into the project,” he said. “Devising a way of discreetly housing ducts and grilles into a listed building was extremely challenging.” The Newt in Somerset’s sprawling grounds also include a lakeside apiary for honey bees and a rammed earth yoga studio , both designed by Invisible Studio. The photography is by Ollie Tomlinson . Read more Interiors

items.title: KTGY revamps interiors of Fairmont Hotel in Chicago
items.summary:
US architecture studio KTGY has revamped the interiors of the HOK-designed Fairmont Hotel off of Chicago's Millennium Park. KTGY's Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as […] 
 The post  KTGY revamps interiors of Fairmont Hotel in Chicago  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 23 August 2026 US architecture studio KTGY has revamped the interiors of the HOK -designed Fairmont Hotel off of Chicago ‘s Millennium Park. KTGY ‘s Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level. KTGY has revamped the Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park hotel Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago’s Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it’s crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels. However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the “postmodern” descriptions of the building. The scope included lounges and premium rooms The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper’s facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale. “KTGY’s interiors team reflected the building’s postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale,” said the team. This included the uncovering of previously concealed architectural details, such as in the Rouge meeting room, where KTGY revealed windows and raised a sunken floor. Here and throughout, the team integrated a visual palette that is modern while retaining some of the decadent detailing – such as an abstract chandelier and a textural sideboard, flanked by roped-LED sconces. The finishes and interior architecture were updated to lighten up the spaces In the 15th-floor lounge, the studio completely redid the finishes and flooring and placed a library area to make the space feel more homey. On the second-floor terrace, patterned wood flooring meets fluted wall details painted a matte green. KTGY wanted to reference the architecture of the 1980s postmodern skyscraper The rooms themselves were given lighter colours and bronze accents. Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park is among the dozens of architectural landmarks in central Chicago. Nearby is Edward Durell Stone’s AON Tower and Studio Gang’s Aqua . The photography is by Mike Schwartz. Read more Interiors
designers: bringing that prominence down to a human scale

items.title: Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books
items.summary:
The vintage bookstores of Mexico City's Roma neighbourhood influenced the interiors of this basement bar, designed by local outfit Em-Estudio. 
 The post  Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 31 October 2026 Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) The vintage bookstores of Mexico City ‘s Roma neighbourhood influenced the interiors of this basement bar , designed by local outfit Em-Estudio. Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Photography Close “It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio . Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond. “The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio. Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere. The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room. Cove lighting illuminates the books, creating a dramatic contrast with the otherwise shadowy bar, while banquettes below are accompanied by circular marble tables for placing drinks. “The pages of thousands of books resting on bookshelves that reach the ceiling shed their literal meaning, becoming a tapestry in shades of white that only time can give, bathed in a gradient of warm light,” Em-Estudio said. Other areas such as the DJ booth, the bar and the bathrooms are highlighted with gold leaf and brass to draw the eye. A further hidden lounge space is disguised by another bookshelf, decorated with cans and objects that “evoke a grocery-store bar”. This room swaps burgundy for green, applied in gloss across the ceiling and appearing in a long marble table that runs through the centre. Dark wood Van Beuren chairs with yellow upholstery are lined up along each side, parallel to more walls of books that are uplit along each shelf. A mirror that covers the back wall visually doubles the space, extending the table and the bookshelves in the reflection. Em-Estudio was co-founded by architect Ivan Esqueda and interior designer Gala Sánchez-Renero – a husband and wife who also operate individual practices. Their previous collaborations include a holiday home on a steep hillside in Oaxaca, Mexico, built from coloured concrete chosen to blend into the rocky mountainside. Project credits: Architecture and interior design: Taller Ivan Esqueda and Gala Sánchez-Renero Estudio Design team: Berenice Galindo, Sergio Peláez, Fabián Cedillo Construction and installations: Miguel Ángel Márquez Carpentry: Leonardo Cabrera Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw
items.summary:
Echo is a listening bar in Rotterdam featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis. 
 The post  Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 30 October 2026 Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam , featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis . Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music. Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud . Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam. “We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen. The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach. Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek , a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport. Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline. “We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet. “We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.” The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis , who is Cournet’s partner. Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar. Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl. Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency . Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year. These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar. “There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet. “When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.” ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam. The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering. It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests. Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme. “Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet. “It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.” Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Read more Interiors

items.title: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
items.summary:
Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna's iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan's Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos's famous bar, an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. "The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct […] 
 The post  NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 19 October 2026 Photography by Piercarlo Quecchia (unless stated otherwise) Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna’s iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan’s Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Photo by T-Space The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. “By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club,” said Zorzi. “The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions.” At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Photo by T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a “raw” interior for Milan’s Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it’s like to be a contemporary designer in Italy’s design capital. Restaurateur Josh Greenspan and furniture company USM have created VV's Cocktail Room in Manhattan, a small space wrapped almost entirely in Steel Blue USM Haller modular shelving and informed by Greenspan's visits to Japan and Hong Kong. Named after Greenspan's daughter Vivienne, VV's Cocktail Room (VV's) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats […] 
 The post  Josh Greenspan creates New York cocktail lounge almost entirely with USM modules  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ellen Eberhardt US reporter 8 October 2026 Restaurateur Josh Greenspan and furniture company USM have created VV’s Cocktail Room in Manhattan, a small space wrapped almost entirely in Steel Blue USM Haller modular shelving and informed by Greenspan’s visits to Japan and Hong Kong . Named after Greenspan ‘s daughter Vivienne, VV’s Cocktail Room (VV’s) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. Josh Greenspan and USM have completed Manhattan cocktail bar VV’s Cocktail Room The project stems from Greenspan’s ongoing conversations with USM, which frequently collaborates with designers to outfit spaces and create installations from the flexible panelling system. “I started imagining something a little wild – a space built entirely from the USM system, pushing its modularity in unexpected ways,” Greenspan told Dezeen. “I’m thrilled that the USM team embraced the idea and came along for the ride.” The space is wrapped in a dark blue USM Haller System Visitors to the bar pass a glass block wall partition to enter the space. Inside, navy blue USM panels form the walls that surround the space and wrap behind the bar, where they jut out into shelving. A dark walnut wood was used for the bar top and tables, which is offset by bar seats upholstered in a burgundy fabric and banquette seating built by Greenspan’s father, Michael Greenspan, covered in a similar hue. Other details include a wavy pendant light by New York lighting studio Studio Kawabi that spans the length of the bar and a painting by Japanese artist Keita Morimoto affixed to the back wall. The space was informed by the “visual language” of Tokyo and Hong Kong, according to the team, and aims for the futuristic aesthetic between the 1960s and 1990s of the two metropolises. The panels expand into shelves behind the bar Greenspan worked with USM’s director of architectural development, Ian Mutschelkanus, to create an interior where the USM Haller System serves as “the architectural framework of the space” rather than simply being inserted. “Rather than furnishing the interiors, USM defines them,” said the team. “Each composition of the modular system demonstrates its remarkable versatility beyond furniture and into the realm of spatial design.” It was informed by the “futuristic aesthetic” of Tokyo and Hong Kong between the 1960s and 1990s Greenspan partnered with James Beard Award-winning bartender Neal Bodenheimer and longtime friend Vincent Favela for the omakase cocktail program, while his mother, five-time James Beard Award winner Dorie Greenspan , created a bar snack menu. Past spaces that used USM panels for walls include retail space for Coperni in Paris . Other recently completed bars in New York include Odd Ball by House Under Magic and a second Brooklyn location for concept shop and wine bar Million Goods designed by Gjergji Shkurti . items.title: Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn
items.summary:
Architect Gjergji Shkurti has collaborated with concept shop Million Goods for its second Brooklyn location, using marble, custom millwork and curated furniture to create a transition from hospitality to retail. A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became […] 
 The post  Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 25 September 2026 Architect Gjergji Shkurti has collaborated with concept shop Million Goods for its second Brooklyn location, using marble, custom millwork and curated furniture to create a transition from hospitality to retail. A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became the Million Goods ‘s second shop after co-founder Matt Reyer, who lives nearby, spotting it when it was inhabited by a design studio. Gjergji Shkurti designed the Fort Greene outpost for Million Goods Reyer and fellow co-founder Drew Kaufmann brought on local architect Gjergji Shkurti, founder of Figure Ground , to convert the space. Whereas the original Million Goods in Greenpoint is condensed into a single level, the Fort Greene location gave the team more room to work with, with two levels and an expansive courtyard. The studio revamped a two-level space “I think this was more regal, whereas Greenpoint was a little bit more fun,” Shkurti told Dezeen, referring to the expansive Breccia Pernice stone countertop that forms the wine bar portion on the first level. Stripping the interiors back to their essentials, Shkurti organised the space to provide social areas and retail, integrating them stylistically but separating them physically, with the social spaces on the bottom floor and the retail above. Shkurti designed the space and fabricated the millwork The first-level bar and social space combines multiple different design languages into a contemporary New York style. Behind the bar, metallic speaker boxes were integrated into the custom casework, which was rendered in sapele wood finished in a peca tone. Bridge Street Sound did the sound system, integrating a large speaker directly into the face of the marble bar. Emeco bar stools by Philippe Starck line the bar, and these chairs were used with the wooden banquet seating that hems the space. A backyard takes cues from Brazilian brutalism The ceiling has a distinctly Japanese appearance, with fabric draped between wooden slats. This fabric and an additional layer of insulation were included for sound, but also, with an interesting effect, dampen the lighting from the fixtures above the fabric. A relatively large backyard space was given a central planter for a mature tree. The circular planter doubles as a bench and seating was integrated into the washed concrete walls around the space. Upstairs, a space was included for retail Shkurti said the backyard was designed to evoke Brazilian brutalism. A Louis Poulsen Flindt Plaza post is the centrepiece of the backyard space, rising from the custom pavers. The lighting company sponsored the store and its lamps and fixtures can be found throughout. The refinished facade of the historic low-rise building was refinished with the blessing of the local preservation boards, and the backyard-facing trim was given a red that aligns with the staircase in the front. In the front, the facade was kept black. The spiral staircase at the front of the shop was original, but given siding and painted a bright red by local fabricator Wood Steel Stone . Wood Steel Stone also completed an impressive central display table on the upper floor that folds aluminium and wood into ply layers with aluminium on top. Upstairs, the original wood from the floors was refinished and used. The team knocked voids in a partition wall to place speakers Shkurti’s custom millwork appears again as casing for the clothing and goods on display, which Reyer described as contemporary and accessible. Through a portal door, a metal stand, also created by Wood Steel Stone was designed to function as both a point-of-sale location and a DJ booth for events. To the sides of the portal door, voids were cleared out to put additional speakers that face into the primary retail space. Above the custom display table is a Louis Poulsen pendant lamp designed to have a vintage look. An upstairs changing area doubles as a point-of-sale station and DJ booth From the upstairs, shoppers can see kids playing basketball on courts across the street, anchoring the location in the neighbourhood. Other recent stand-out interiors include Federico Stevanovich’s studio designed with Nama Studio in Mexico City . Litening bars are increasingly a site of interesting design. Check out seven listening bars from across the globe . The photography is by Joe Thomas . Read more Interiors

items.title: Joyce Wang draws on "colonial country manors" for Hong Kong hotel interior
items.summary:
Designer Joyce Wang has completed an interior renovation at the Mandarin Oriental The Landmark hotel in Hong Kong, designed to evoke the feel of living in a colonial mansion. Located on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation […] 
 The post  Joyce Wang draws on "colonial country manors" for Hong Kong hotel interior  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Christina Yao 4 August 2026 Designer Joyce Wang has completed an interior renovation at the Mandarin Oriental The Landmark hotel in Hong Kong, designed to evoke the feel of living in a colonial mansion. Located on Queen’s Road in Hong Kong’s Central district, the hotel was first established a decade ago. It recently reopened after the completion of interior renovation by Joyce Wang Studio and a new facade design by Neri&Hu . Terracotta tones in the lobby nod to Hong Kong’s colonial architecture Joyce Wang Studio referenced Hong Kong’s historic architecture and skyline when designing the hotel, whose interior was informed by the city’s colonial country manors. “We took inspiration from the colonial country manors frequented by the Tai Pans of a bygone era to celebrate the beauty of these historic homes that still fascinate today,” Wang, principal of her eponymous studio, told Dezeen. “Our vision this time has a greater focus on local relevance and the heritage of the building.” The studio also aimed to fuse art into the hotel . “We also used art as an integral part of our philosophy for the space, with a commitment to adding local flavour. The artwork program is rigorous in that there is a story behind each piece,” Wang added. Undulating staircase extends around a large-scale contemporary artwork The hotel lobby features a mix of materials including stone, timber and textured wallcoverings. Custom eglomisé glass was added as detailing to create a contemporary atmosphere. Terracotta tones within the space nod to Hong Kong’s colonial architecture and were combined with a touch of green and orange in response to the city’s lush green parks. The interiors of the hotel aim to reimagine the feel of a historical mansion Throughout the hotel, a collection of artworks was carefully curated to create an authentic lived-in residence. Artwork, objects and accessories scattered around an undulating staircase , artwork bays and sculptural plinths invite guests to pause and interact with them while venturing into the space. The bar features a backdrop of patinated brass, verdigris and bronze panels Custom artworks capturing Hong Kong’s signature skyline were created by the studio and integrated into carpet designs, tapestries and the églomise glass located at the lobby, as well as lifts and guestroom corridors. According to the Hong Kong-based studio, the artistic intervention aims to celebrate the hotel’s prominent location in the city, while presenting a series of treasured objects as if collected over time for one’s own home. Artworks informed by Hong Kong’s signature skyline were integrated into carpet designs Joyce Wang Studio aimed to create an intimate and residential feel in Mandarin Oriental The Landmark’s 109 rooms and suites. Details include bespoke wallcoverings by wallpaper brand Fromental , featuring hand-painted and silk elements, and cracked gesso wall finishes. Custom rugs on top of timber floors reference Hong Kong’s historic brickwork. A new communal bar was reimagined as a contemporary family gathering space. Here, the design is defined by a backdrop featuring patinated brass, verdigris, and bronze panels, allowing the space to adapt seamlessly between day and night service. The green and yellow hues reference Hong Kong’s parks Ceiling lamps in matching patinated finishes pay homage to the domestic lighting found in the historic mansions of Yuen Long, a town in the western north of Hong Kong’s New Territories, where several notable historic mansions and grand residences are located. Fluted jade-toned tiles wrap the bar front, recreating the roofline silhouettes of traditional housing. Tangerine and cherry-toned bar chairs contrast with the bar table. Their backs are adorned with a crest-like motif that symbolises a contemporary family emblem inherited through generations. The studio curated a collection of artworks throughout the hotel “For this latest renovation, we were inspired by the identity of our hotel as a pied-à-terre for our guests to feel the pulse of Hong Kong, intimately. The curation of pieces are windows into expressions of our city through lenses of both local and international, emerging and established artists,” said Wang. “As you journey through the hotel, we hope these storied perspectives fill you with curiosity and contemplation, at the ready to strike up conversations,” she continued. For the hotel spa , Joyce Wang Studio added design details informed by breathwork and calligraphy to create a sense of calm. Custom flooring patterns were designed to mimic the natural rhythm of inhalation and exhalation, allowing guests to connect with the space as if it is breathing with them. Hand-painted and silk elements feature on the walls of guest rooms Two distinct wood veneers were paired together within the gym, yoga, and pilates studios, creating a balanced, organic environment that encourages a sense of focused calm. The sinuous and fluid lines on the ceiling and decorative screens aim to recreate the brush strokes of Chinese calligraphy. The hotel renovation was completed recently and includes a new facade design by Neri&Hu The hotel has officially reopened since June, while the spa will fully reopen later this year. Established in 2011, Joyce Wang Studio is known for luxury hospitality and residential design, with offices in London and Hong Kong. Elsewhere in Hong Kong, Studio Paolo Ferrari designed a “timeless futurism” cocktail bar , while the Dragon-i nightclub renovated by local interior designer Pirajean Lees captured the romantic atmosphere of director Wong Kar Wai’s films . The photography is by Common Studio. Read more Interiors

items.title: Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar
items.summary:
Cantilever chairs, wood panelling and mirror-clad surfaces meet in Lève Office Bar, a Space Age-informed bar in Turin by Italian architect Fabio Fantolino. The venue is located in the centre of the Italian city and nods to the aesthetics and culture of workplaces built in post-war America. The original building dates from the 1920s and […] 
 The post  Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Alice Laycock Showroom editor 29 June 2026 Cantilever chairs , wood panelling and mirror -clad surfaces meet in Lève Office Bar, a Space Age-informed bar in Turin by Italian architect Fabio Fantolino . The venue is located in the centre of the Italian city and nods to the aesthetics and culture of workplaces built in post-war America. A stainless steel bar sets the tone upon entry The original building dates from the 1920s and before the intervention, it was divided into two distinct units: one contained a cafe, while the other housed a bookshop. It now functions as one cohesive interior subdivided into three spaces, all of which reference retro workplaces. Herringbone bricks give way to green resin flooring beyond The space aims to serve professionals working in the city centre over the course of a typical working day; hence the architect’s decision to theme it around retro offices. “The 1960s were chosen as the reference period because they marked a time when offices were regarded as prestigious and carefully designed workplaces – the ‘office bar’ concept, on the other hand, reflects the way we work today,” Fantolino told Dezeen. “It is conceived as a space that supports the everyday rhythm of contemporary office life, whether for breakfast, lunch, coffee breaks, or aperitivos, while also acknowledging that work can naturally extend into hospitality spaces.” All the fittings and fixtures were selected according to 1960s aesthetics “The three areas reinterpret the concept of an open-plan office, each through a distinct design language,” Fantolino continued. A monolithic stainless-steel bar dominates the initial interior upon entry. Its strong presence is bolstered by a red enamel wall panel mounted behind it. The ceiling beneath the mezzanine presents a mirrored alternative to conventional grid ceilings The effect is softened by a herringbone floor made up of sandy-coloured bricks, which gives way to a green resin floor at the threshold of the second space. Banquette seating upholstered in fawn-coloured leather runs along the far wall, accompanied by red-topped cafe tables and brown-and-chrome cantilever chairs. Seating for bar-goers sits within the double-height space, with more tucked beneath the mezzanine, where a lower ceiling clad in mirrored panels puts a chic spin on dropped ceilings common in offices. The upstairs mezzanine is where the office spaces are most closely mimicked, with cubicle-like segments created by high-backed, boucle-upholstered sofas placed back-to-back. The mezzanine was a preexisting architectural feature Partitions up here create intimacy for guests, rather than privacy for focused work, with the area making use of the preexisting mezzanine to create a cosy bolt-hole. “The mezzanine introduces office-style partition elements to create a more intimate and structured atmosphere,” said Fantolino. Upstairs, high-backed sofas create segmented private zones The pendant lights on the mezzanine, as well as the sconces attached to the walls beneath and the illuminated panels integrated into the dropped ceiling, reinforce the 1960s aesthetic. The overall neutral colour palette is made more interesting by pops of green, red and mustard, as well as material contrast between flat enamel, shiny chrome and tactile leather. The overall warmth of the material and colour palette is contrasted by metallic elements “The intention was to evoke the feeling of stepping back into the 1960s, creating an immersive atmosphere that feels almost like entering a time machine while remaining fresh and contemporary,” Fantolino concluded. Other distinctive bars published on Dezeen include a bar in Rome decorated with disembodied plaster limbs and a Hong Kong bar featuring a lime green interior studded with tiny lights . The photography is by Luca Argenton. Read more Interiors

items.title: "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona cocktail bar
items.summary:
Spanish designer Isern Serra has completed a speakeasy bar in Barcelona featuring multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton's retro-futuristic 1960s installations. Focacha is the latest venue from hospitality specialist Grupo La Confitería, which tasked Serra's studio with creating a space that pays tribute to an important period in the history of Barcelona's nightlife. The […] 
 The post  "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona cocktail bar  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Alyn Griffiths 28 June 2026 Spanish designer Isern Serra has completed a speakeasy bar in Barcelona featuring multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton ‘s retro-futuristic 1960s installations. Focacha is the latest venue from hospitality specialist Grupo La Confitería, which tasked Serra ‘s studio with creating a space that pays tribute to an important period in the history of Barcelona’s nightlife. Isern Serra has designed a Barcelona bar with multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton pieces The 1960s and early 1970s coincided with the heyday of Tuset Street where the bar is located, which became a hub for a group of young liberal professionals known in Barcelona art the “gauche divine”. The cocktail bar was designed to evoke the futuristic styling that characterised this time and immerse guests in a multi-sensory environment defined by design, light and music. The bar is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria “I wanted visitors to feel enveloped by an environment with a strong artistic and emotional presence, capable of sparking curiosity and creating a sense of wonder from the very first moment,” Serra told Dezeen. “More than designing a cocktail bar, the intention was to create a setting that evokes emotions, encourages contemplation and leaves a lasting impression on those who experience it, turning their visit into something truly memorable.” Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop The speakeasy-style venue is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria that has been serving Italian bread for 50 years. Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop, which adds a sense of theatricality to the experience. The venue was divided into two spaces, the first of which is a bar that pays homage to Danish designer Panton’s iconic Visiona installations. A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space, forming intimate niches for small groups along one side. On the other side of the space, a stainless-steel bar with rounded edges subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room. The fully carpeted ceiling and walls extend behind the bar, where rounded openings accommodate shelves displaying bottles. A stainless-steel bar subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room “We were inspired by Panton because his creative language perfectly reflects the optimistic, experimental and progressive spirit of the late 1960s and early 1970s,” Serra pointed out. “The goal was not to recreate a retro aesthetic, but to capture the sense of freedom, creativity and innovation that defined that era.” The DJ room was lined with curved banquettes A circular opening at the end of the bar leads into a DJ room designed to merge 1960s nostalgia with a dystopian vision of the future, resulting in a surreal, technology-led aesthetic. The room is lined with curved banquettes that evoke the era’s psychedelic and modular interiors, while the domed ceiling and walls incorporate openings that allow dynamic lighting effects to transform the atmosphere within the space. Mirrored walls create the illusion of more space, while lighting fixtures including the Panton-designed Flowerpot VP2 and Panthella lamps contribute to a carefully curated atmosphere. According to Serra, the interior’s complex curves demanded a sculptural construction approach that meant elements were not fully defined from the outset and evolved as different solutions were tested using mock-ups and full-scale prototypes. Isern Serra said that the interior’s complex curves demanded a sculptural construction “Rather than building conventional architectural elements,” he said, “we were shaping volumes and forms to create a fluid and immersive spatial experience, where every curve contributed to reinforcing the overall atmosphere of the project.” Serra’s studio is based in the Poblenou neighbourhood of Barcelona, in a space he designed to embody the practice’s values and provide an inspirational working environment. The architect is known for combining contemporary, vibrant and essential forms with Mediterranean influences. Previous projects include a gallery-like apartment renovation and a bakery featuring cave-like walls . Read more Interiors Highlights

items.title: Wild Form designs with "no straight lines" for bar next to New York's Stonewall Inn
items.summary:
New York-based Wild Form Design Studio has crafted a sculptural interior for a bar called Love Thy Neighbor, which "celebrates the queer community" next to The Stonewall Inn in the West Village. Opened ahead of this weekend’s Pride celebrations in New York, Love Thy Neighbor sits next to the landmark where a series of protests […] 
 The post  Wild Form designs with "no straight lines" for bar next to New York's Stonewall Inn  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 27 June 2026 New York-based Wild Form Design Studio has crafted a sculptural interior for a bar called Love Thy Neighbor, which “celebrates the queer community” next to The Stonewall Inn in the West Village . Opened ahead of this weekend’s Pride celebrations in New York, Love Thy Neighbor sits next to the landmark where a series of protests in 1969 became a pivotal moment in mobilising the Gay Rights Movement. The bar features free-form shapes that nod to queerness and individuality Founders Shigefumi Kabashima and Elias Popa, along with Wild Form Design Studio , wanted the bar and dining concept to pay homage to the history of this location, both through design and their approach to hospitality. “Guided by the ethos of no straight lines, Love Thy Neighbor celebrates the queer community, chosen family, and the joys of gathering and belonging,” said the team. Shelves behind the bar follow the “no straight lines” rule set out by the owners Just over the below-grade threshold, a concrete floor panel is gilded with a quote from Marsha P Johnson – a transgender woman who was a key figure in the Stonewall Uprising protests for LGBTQ+ rights, and who continued to fight for queer rights and representation throughout her life. It reads “No pride for some of us without liberation for all of us” in gold letters and includes her signature below. A series of banquettes is divided by sculptural partitions A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche at the end of the bar, representing those thrown at the police who raided the bar on 28 June 1969 during the uprisings. “These elements serve as understated reminders of the past, while reinforcing a bright future ahead,” said the team. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche Elsewhere, the curvaceous walls and partitions form an intimate, cavern-like space for 40 guests, and nod to queerness and individuality. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” said Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries.” Spotlights illuminate the bar counter and tables The sculpted surfaces carry warm beige tones across banquettes on the left-hand side, and the bar along the right. A curated selection of liquor bottles and glassware is displayed behind the bar on back-lit shelves, which slant and dip to continue the free-form visual language. The cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision Spotlights illuminate the rounded bar counter and dining tables, directing focus to the food and drinks, while cove lighting traces the fluid edges around the space. In the rear bathroom, a recessed mirror appears to be carved from the thick plaster walls, the vanity has an equally textured edge and features a long, contoured basin, and bronze-hued faucets are suspended from the ceiling. Love Thy Neighbor’s highly inventive cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision, and uses techniques like clarification, infusion and carbonation to create innovative ingredients like wasabi gin and homemade cola. Drinks are presented in delicate glassware, while Asian-influenced bar snacks and shareable plates are served on hand-crafted ceramics. The rear bathroom features a recessed mirror and a rough-edged vanity “We wanted Love Thy Neighbor to be a space where people from different walks of life can share a delicious meal, connect, and feel like they belong under one roof, at any time of day,” said Papa. “We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others,” added Kabashima. The basin is contoured and faucets hang from the ceiling Many queer spaces are under threat from a variety of social, urban and economic issues, and continued support is needed to protect venues used by the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ+) community. The transgender community is particularly being targeted in the US and UK. The architecture profession “must engage” in ensuring safety for trans people, the founder of Queerscapes told Dezeen in an interview last year. The photography is by Aichan Mama. Read more Interiors

items.title: Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar in London
items.summary:
Design studio Golem has completed a subterranean cocktail bar in central London featuring a glossy counter and tactile booths entirely covered in soft red velvet. Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. "Dive's experience is an ongoing negotiation […] 
 The post  Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar in London  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Alyn Griffiths 18 June 2026 Design studio Golem has completed a subterranean cocktail bar in central London featuring a glossy counter and tactile booths entirely covered in soft red velvet. Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive “Dive’s experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests,” explained Golem founder Ariel André. “The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills.” “Wear and tear is part of the architecture,” he added. “Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies.” The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive’s owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains “the imprint of bodies” “The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus,” André explained. A dark corridor leads to the steps that descend into the richer, more tactile lounge space. This area was designed to facilitate moments of interaction between guests, while also offering cosy corners for private conversations. Structural arches supporting the street above contain flexible seating areas that can be configured to suit various social scenarios. Built-in benches lining the niches are covered with loose cushions that can be repositioned as required. “The upholstery is conceived to be appropriated by guests,” André pointed out. “Bodies shape the furniture, not the other way around.” “When unoccupied, the seating still carries the imprint of previous guests, holding the evening in a suspended time and space.” Golem aimed to create cosy corners for private conversations One of the arches known as the “fun room” is covered from floor to ceiling in lush carpet, allowing its U-shaped layout to be used for anything from lounging to dancing. Golem created quart-de-lune tables specially for the project, which can be used individually by couples sitting side by side, or combined in sets of two or four to comfortably seat up to eight guests. The main bar features contrasting smooth, glossy finishes The lounge also functions as a listening room, with the choice of absorbent and reflective surfaces helping to create a tailored acoustic environment. A dedicated DJ booth is positioned next to bespoke shelves housing the owner’s extensive vinyl collection. The mixing desk is height adjustable to allow for seated or standing performance. A one-way mirror conceals the bathroom At the centre of the bar, the non-gendered bathrooms are arranged around a banquette where guests can sit and chat. A one-way mirror conceals this space from the outside while providing a glimpse back into the lounge. André founded his Paris-based studio in 2021, working across the worlds of architecture, art and design. Previous Golem projects include a modular furniture system made of hundreds of squishy balls , which was used to create a conversation pit in a Brussels apartment. Read more Interiors

items.text: Amy Peacock Architecture reporter 15 June 2026 UK practices Heatherwick Studio and SPPARC have revealed a faceted glass canopy that shelters new outdoor spaces, as part of the transformation of the Olympia events centre in London . Opening to the public today, the rooftop bars , restaurants and landscaped terraces mark the completion of the first phase of Heatherwick Studio and SPPARC ‘s renovation of Olympia, which was originally built in 1886. Heatherwick Studio and SPPARC have completed the first phase of their transformation at Olympia. Top photo by Heatherwick Studio Designed to attract more activity to the site, a public staircase and escalators lead visitors from ground level to the public space above, which was built between Olympia’s barrel-vaulted roofs. A pleated canopy, made up of 520 glass panels supported by five 22-metre-wide steel arches, shelters the outdoor space. A glass canopy was built between two Victorian barrel-vaulted roofs The shape of the canopy fans out at the entrance points, designed to draw people in, and its faceted surfaces draw from the arched glass facade of Olympia’s Grand Hall. Elsewhere at the Olympia site, office towers with faceted glazed facades are also taking shape as part of the transformation project. A staircase and escalators lead visitors to the rooftop space. Photo by Hufton + Crow Heatherwick Studio and SPPARC wanted to diversify the site, which has functioned as an events space and exhibition hall for 140 years, and make it more accessible to visitors. Once complete, Olympia will contain a 3,800-capacity entertainment venue, a 1,575-seat theatre, shops, offices and two hotels. “Olympia has held a strange place in the hearts of Londoners, sitting at the centre of our city, hosting so many unusual events, yet simultaneously closed off to most of us,” said Heatherwick Studio founder Thomas Heatherwick. “It certainly wasn’t a place to take your family or go on a date.” “Our work over the last nine years has been about opening it up so anyone can enjoy it, whether they’re going to a play, a music concert, an exhibition, or simply wandering around.” The canopy is supported by five steel arches. Photo by Heatherwick Studio “What was once a lifeless perimeter is now a place where you can feel the city’s energy,” Heatherwick continued. “The new Olympia reflects a quiet confidence, showing that we can take extraordinary British heritage and adapt it with care, imagination and purpose for the future.” Landscaped roof terraces give views across London. Photo by Hufton + Crow Also in London, Heatherwick Studio is nearing completion on Google’s upcoming landscraper office in King’s Cross , which was designed with BIG. Elsewhere in the UK, Heatherwick Studio revealed its design for a 62,000-seat stadium encircled by brick chimneys for Birmingham City Football Club . Other projects by SPPARC include a brick-lined shopping area in London and a renovated Georgian townhouse with a honeycomb-shaped roof . The photography is by Raquel Diniz unless stated. items.title: New York's art deco icons inform revamped restaurant at The Edge
items.summary:
Design studio Journey and Tao Hospitality Group have refreshed the interiors of dining venues at The Edge, the triangular observation deck at New York's Hudson Yards. The team has completely redesigned Peak with Priceless, the restaurant located on the 101th floor of the KPF-designed 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper. The overhaul also includes the addition of […] 
 The post  New York's art deco icons inform revamped restaurant at The Edge  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 11 June 2026 Design studio Journey and Tao Hospitality Group have refreshed the interiors of dining venues at The Edge , the triangular observation deck at New York’s Hudson Yards . The team has completely redesigned Peak with Priceless , the restaurant located on the 101th floor of the KPF-designed 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper. The interiors of Peak by Priceless have been redesigned so every seat has an uninterrupted skyline view The overhaul also includes the addition of Avenue Sky Lounge – a revival of the popular Avenue nightclub in Chelsea, which shuttered in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and never reopened. Susan Nugraha, Tao Group Hospitality ‘s SVP of design and development, worked closely on the project with experiential design group Journey . Custom tiered lighting nods to art deco skyscrapers such as the Empire State Building Both hospitality concepts draw design influences from the Manhattan skyline visible through the wraparound, floor-to-ceiling windows. “The inspiration behind Peak and Avenue was always New York itself, its energy, glamour and unmistakable sense of occasion,” said Journey managing director David Taglione. “Suspended above the city with the skyline as its stage, we wanted to create a hospitality experience that feels both elevated and deeply connected to the rhythm of New York.” Soft blue and warm brown suede covers the booth seating References to art deco structures such as the Empire State Building and Rockefeller Center can be spied in tall, tiered lamps, customised to softly illuminate both Peak and Avenue spaces. “Every design decision, from the rich materiality to the layered seating and subtle Art Deco references, was shaped to frame the view while creating a space with its own distinct sense of presence,” said Taglione. At Peak, stepped booths are oriented towards the views, while smaller tables run along the windows – ensuring every seat has an unbroken sightline. Soft blue and warm brown suede upholster the curved seat backs, with wavy patterns echoed in partitions that run along the back of the dining space Avenue Sky Lounge (also main image) continues the same colour palette A similar colour palette appears across Avenue Sky Lounge , which can be divided into more intimate spaces by coffee-hued curtains that follow arched ceiling features. Lacquered wood panelling surrounds the bar, where more geometric shapes in the stone counters and liquor display cases again nod to art deco. “Our vision was a design that is both timeless and of the moment, seamlessly adapting to any time of day or occasion,” said Nugraha. Lacquered wood panelling and geometric details around the bar again nod to the city’s art deco icons The revamp at The Edge will also see the return of Marquee Skydeck , a series of events that include DJ sets and performances on the platform that at 1,100 feet (335 metres) above street level is currently the highest observation deck in the western hemisphere. Other sky-high hospitality venues in New York City include Manhatta , a Woods Bagot-designed restaurant atop 28 Liberty in the Financial District. The photography is courtesy of Tao Group Hospitality. items.title: 4Space draws on cultural significance of Arabian horses for UAE restaurant
items.summary:
Design studio 4Space “explored the physical and kinetic qualities” of horses for the fluid, organic design of Falwa, an Abu Dhabi restaurant celebrating modern Emirati cuisine.  Located in the Abu Dhabi Royal Equestrian Art (ADREA) academy, the contemporary restaurant is led by Michelin-starred Emirati chef Faisal Alharmoodi. To showcase the importance of the Arabian mare […] 
 The post  4Space draws on cultural significance of Arabian horses for UAE restaurant  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dezeen staff 6 November 2026 Partnership content In partnership with: 4Space Design studio 4Space “explored the physical and kinetic qualities” of horses for the fluid, organic design of Falwa, an Abu Dhabi restaurant celebrating modern Emirati cuisine. Located in the Abu Dhabi Royal Equestrian Art (ADREA) academy, the contemporary restaurant is led by Michelin-starred Emirati chef Faisal Alharmoodi. The restaurant has a fluid, organic design To showcase the importance of the Arabian mare as a cultural icon in this equestrian space, 4Space designed the restaurant to represent abstract depictions of horses and their anatomy. “The design team explored the physical and kinetic qualities of the animal itself, specifically its skeletal structure, muscular tension, and fluid movement,” 4Space said. The Vibia Plusminus lighting system by Stefan Diez was used throughout the space It aimed to convey the animal’s cultural and historical importance through architecture, using an organic design language throughout the restaurant, which fittingly opened in 2026 – the Year of the Horse. Named Falwa after the Arabic term for a young female mare in her first year of life, the eatery has a fluid interior with stretched, curved walls designed to evoke horses in motion. 4Space created custom-made dining chairs with decorative leather straps, visible stitching and metal hardware The restaurant interior also references a specific horse named Rabdan, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan’s, which inspired the custom-made dusty white mineral plaster that wraps its walls and adds a tactile feel. “This earthier, softer alternative to pure white acts as a passive canvas for the shifting daylight, allowing natural and artificial light to paint dynamic shadows across the curved walls, evoking the powerful presence and coat of the horse,” 4Space explained. The restaurant has stretched and curved walls Rabdan’s coat also influenced Falwa’s overall colour palette, which features warm reddish, tan and brown hues against the white walls. “By utilising rich crimson tones and warm, tactile materials, the design team evokes the powerful presence and coat of this legendary steed,” 4Space explained. The space is designed to celebrate the Arabian mare as a cultural icon of the equestrian industry Falwa’s tactile, organic feel of the walls is contrasted by the polished, glossy flooring, which was made from Breccia Aurora marble. Its beige and brown veining matches the restaurant’s earthy brown leather and wood tones. While the restaurant mostly features abstract references to Arabian horses, 4Space also added more specific equestrian details to the interior. The eatery has polished, glossy flooring 4Space created custom-made dining chairs with decorative leather straps, visible stitching and metal hardware in a nod to horse saddles and tack. Above the central tables at the restaurant, a tactile sculpture with a skeletal, undulating design once again evokes movement and anatomy. The space is located within the Abu Dhabi Royal Equestrian Art (ADREA) academy 4Space also used the Vibia Plusminus lighting system by designer Stefan Diez for Falwa. Its signature textile straps, from which glass globes are suspended, match the equestrian leather straps on the chairs and add a playful effect to the interior. Overall, 4Space aimed to tie Falwa’s food and interior together, with both aspects of the restaurant functioning as contemporary expressions of Emirati culture and heritage. “The design demonstrates how a deep cultural relationship can be expressed as a living, modern architectural language,” the studio concluded. To learn more about 4Space, visit its website . Gallery Close Read more Promotions

items.title: "Direct and unrefined" materials create tactile interior at Jeju restaurant by &Daughters
items.summary:
Canadian studio &Daughters used basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood to design Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver that features traditional touches in a contemporary interior. 
 The post  "Direct and unrefined" materials create tactile interior at Jeju restaurant by &Daughters  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Cajsa Carlson Editor 4 November 2026 Canadian studio &Daughters used basalt, cork , concrete, thatch and wood to design Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver that features traditional touches in a contemporary interior. The architect’s starting point for the design was the restaurant’s menu, which includes modern dishes developed by chef Dylan Kim, traditional dishes created by his mother, chef Myungseok “Julie” Suh and dishes that they created together. Jeju’s interior is a mix of different tactile materials “The restaurant exists in the space where these two narratives meet,” &Daughters principal Emma Sims told Dezeen. “We began to think of tradition and reinterpretation as the foundation for the design, translating this relationship into a physical space through a specific set of people, places, materials and traditions.” While Jeju’s exterior has a modern steel-mesh facade, the interior juxtaposes wood and concrete for a warmer, more tactile feel. A version of a traditional thatched house is at the heart of the restaurant At the heart of the 44-seat restaurant is a reinterpretation of a traditional thatched house from Jeju Island, South Korea, called a chogajip. This was constructed using lumber and hand-thatched grass, and creates an artisanal focal point for the space. Other materials, including basalt, were chosen by &Daughters for Jeju to ensure a natural feel. Basalt was used for the bar, chef’s table and host stand, while cork cladding helps create a soft feel while adding acoustic dampening. &Daughters kept and polished an existing concrete floor The studio kept the existing concrete floor but polished it to reveal variations in its colour. “The palette is quite simple – basalt, cork, raw concrete masonry units, polished concrete, wood and thatch,” Sims said. “Basalt is one of the most recognisable materials of Jeju Island,” she continued. “Formed through volcanic activity, it is found throughout the island’s landscape, architecture and traditional stone walls. Beyond that, we were interested in materials that felt direct and unrefined, allowing them to retain their natural character.” A traditional three-pole gate evokes Jeju Island Wood and cork create a warm atmosphere The studio wanted to “introduce elements of tradition, ritual and memory into the interior,” Sims said. As well as the thatched house, another traditional architectural feature from Jeju, a jeongnang three-pole gate, was also introduced to the interior. “Historically used as a means of communicating whether a household was home, away or nearby, it offered an alternative to a conventional locked entrance, rooted in trust and shared understanding,” Sims said. “At Jeju, we incorporated our interpretation into the glazing beside the entrance, where staff lower two poles each day to signal that the restaurant is open and guests are welcome, raising them again at the end of service,” she continued. “In this way, a traditional architectural element becomes an active part of the restaurant’s daily life.” Other restaurants recently featured on Dezeen include a brick-clad eatery in London’s Soho area and a bistro in Montreal influenced by Japanese metabolism .
