items.title: A Hotel in a 6th-Century Monastery, an Office Channeling 90s New York, and More
items.summary: Plus: The butter plate of your dreams.
items.text: 07.30.26 The Weekly A Hotel in a 6th-Century Monastery, an Office Channeling 90s New York, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up. Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . Art and Architecture Find a Perfect Dialogue Inside a Modernist Connecticut Landmark Artworks made from paper layered on top of linen canvases by Kim Bartelt, on view through tomorrow at the 1960 John Landis–designed Gores Pavilion in Connecticut. One downside of taking an annual summer break from our newsletter: We sometimes miss the window for exhibitions and other time-sensitive projects. This site-specific exhibition of new work by Berlin artist Kim Bartelt is only on view until the end of the day tomorrow, but assuming most of you aren’t anywhere near New Canaan, Connecticut, anyway, we figured we might as well enable you to enjoy it from afar. For “Exhibit No. 2,” presented by Arden + White Gallery , Bartelt installed 8 of her understated-yet-colorful paper-and-linen compositions inside the Gores Pavilion , a landmarked home designed by modernist architect — and Philip Johnson collaborator — Landis Gores in 1960. The artworks resonate with both the colors and the geometries found in the home, but they weren’t so much inspired by the architecture as chosen to complement it; if you know Bartelt’s work, you know this has been her visual language for years. As the gallery puts it: “This exhibition is not about illustrating architecture, nor about placing contemporary art within an iconic building. Rather, it reveals a shared architectural sensibility, one rooted in proportion, restraint, and the thoughtful orchestration of material, light, and space.” Walker Street Market Is Turning the Berkshires Into a Contemporary Design Destination At Walker Street Market in Lenox, Mass., the craft-forward fare includes a custom counter by Brian Persico and painting by David Silverstein (top), a side table by Simone Bodmer Turner and lamp by Ashley Joseph Martin (above left), and a teapot by Akira Satake (above right), among many others. Photos: Chris Mottalini Out of all the reasons to visit the Berkshires — a woodsy region of western Massachusetts that many New Yorkers escape to in the summer — I never really considered design to be one of them, unless we’re talking about MASS MoCA or modernist architecture, I suppose. So it’s honestly a little bit wild that something has popped up in the area like Walker Street Market , a sprawling design showroom full of commissioned work from a roster of talents that could rival The Future Perfect’s. Opened in mid-July inside a 3,000-sqft early-1900s former department store building, by fashion-designer-turned-interiors-guru Matthew Ames, the project is pretty much exactly how you might imagine a Berkshires version of The Future Perfect that’s lovingly attuned to its own context: lots of gallery-level studio crafts, with a contemporary edge, culled from the best new talents who still work with their hands and venerate, as Ames does, the beauty of pieces that make that fact obvious. Since Ames is working with over 70 makers on the store’s wares — which also span flowers, jewelry, beauty products, and kitchen supplies — it’s impossible to give the full scope, but some favorite pieces when I visited a few weeks ago included a wall of multi-colored ceramic tiles by Shane Gabier, beautiful paintings by David Silverstein and Dan Bruinooge, ruffle-shade lamps by Studio Ford, textile still-lifes by Andrew Pierce Scott, glass vases by Dana Arbib, andirons and chairs by Simone Bodmer Turner, and some absolutely epic wooden floor and pendant lights carved intro trompe l’oeil frills by Ashley Joseph Martin , a name that was new to me. Obviously anyone who recognizes some of the other aforementioned names might note that not all of Walker Street Market’s designers are local to the Berkshires/upstate New York area, but highlights in that department include delicate floral lamps by Jake Coan and several monumental shelves, benches, and tables by woodworker Lily Thorne and her father Peter, some of them topped with ceramics by Natalie Weinberger. The project is so ambitious, and the work it contains so meticulously crafted, that one can only hope that if and when the good people of Massachusetts descend upon it, Ames can keep the shelves stocked. A Sixth-Century Priory Becomes Burgundy’s Most Atmospheric New Hotel (Extremely) old meets new at Les Sources de Vougeot, a hotel in Burgundy, France. Photos: Jules Focone It’s certainly true that, given the tragic outbreak of wildfires there right now, it’s a strange time to be talking about vacationing in France, in this case to a new hotel called Les Sources de Vougeot , with interiors by the Paris firm A.S.L . But at the same time, France will forever be a prime holiday destination, and for what it’s worth, this latest Les Sources — the third in a growing boutique chain, all three in different French wine countries — just so happens to be in Gilly-lès-Cîteaux, Burgundy, and thus far from the worst blazes. Anyway, whether you make plans to go or just want to join us in admiring the design, it is a very nice one; the building was constructed as a priory in the 6th century before being transformed into a country house in the 1600s, and then into Les Sources earlier this year. Because it’s a landmarked property, the hotel team had to tread carefully with their renovation, hiring historic specialists Chevalier & Guillemot to preserve original details in the process, like the indoor pool room’s stunning vaulted ceilings and a pair of fireplaces in the lobby, which used to be the priory kitchen. A.S.L accordingly focused on classical details like antique paintings, tap
designers: Jake Coan and several monumental shelves

items.title: Sketch’s new cocktail book shakes up mixology – try these recipes
items.text: (Image credit: Courtesy of Sketch) Jump to category: The Glade Cocktail Book 2 breakfast martini recipes Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter We are fast approaching the season to be merry, and Sketch , the Mayfair restaurant, is preparing for the festivities by launching its new cocktail book. The publication is an anticipatory nod to the restaurant’s 25th anniversary in 2027. The Glade Cocktail Book Jon Croft Editions Sketch - the Glade Cocktail Book Sketch is known for its history of bold design , from its dining spaces to its pod loos. The Glade is the building’s forest-themed bar and has often undergone transformations and artistic interventions, whether reimagined as the Hundred Acre Wood to celebrate 100 years of Winnie-the-Pooh , or used to host a Jane Austen-inspired floral display. Singapore Sling and Tropical Mai Tai (Image credit: Courtesy of Sketch) Now, the cocktails that define the dining area are now charted in The Glade Cocktail Book . Striving to be more than a recipe book (although it’s that too), it explains the journey and philosophy behind cocktail creations. In total, it features 106 cocktails, from classics to reinterpretations and alcohol-free suggestions. Golden Cadillac (Image credit: Courtesy of Sketch) The monograph is divided into themes: Roots, Alchemy, and Essence. At the front of the book, readers will find drinks in their traditional form before flipping forward to the bar’s signature concoctions. With illustrations decorating each page, the book also offers advice on presentation, from garnishing to glassware, noting that every detail matters when crafting delicious moments. Rhum Punch (Image credit: Courtesy of Sketch) The book is authored by Sketch founder and restaurateur Mourad Mazouz , who reflects on the establishment’s 25 years: ‘I never imagined writing a book. As someone who is dyslexic, it felt impossible. But Sketch has always been about proving that impossible things can become reality. This book isn’t simply a catalogue of cocktails; it’s the story of 25 years of creativity, distilled into a journey of ideas, experimentation and imagination. I hope it inspires people to create their own stories, celebrate both successes and failures, and most importantly, enjoy the process.’ sketch.london Shake things up with Sketch’s breakfast martinis Left to right, Essence, Alchemy, Roots (Image credit: Courtesy of sketch) Roots 50ml Gin D’Azur Mediterranean gin 1 barspoon fine-cut orange marmalade 15ml triple sec 15ml freshly squeezed lemon juice Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Glass: Coupette Ice: None Garnish: Orange peel, or none Pour the gin into a mixing glass and stir in the marmalade until fully dissolved. Fill a shaker with ice and add the marmalade-gin mixture and the remaining ingredients. Shake vigorously, then fine-strain into a coupette glass. Garnish with an orange coin or peel, or serve ungarnished. Essence (alcohol-free) 50ml Tanqueray Alcohol-free 0.0 gin 1 barspoon fine-cut bitter orange marmalade 15ml Lyre’s Italian Orange 15ml freshly squeezed lemon juice Glass: Martini Ice: None Garnish: Orange coin or peel, or none Pour the alcohol-free gin into a mixing glass and stir in the marmalade until fully dissolved. Fill a shaker with ice and add the marmalade-gin mixture and the remaining ingredients. Shake vigorously, then fine-strain into a Martini glass. Garnish with an orange coin or peel, or serve ungarnished. TOPICS Tianna Williams Staff Writer Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.
designers: Sketch founder and restaurateur Mourad Mazouz

items.title: It’s a family affair: PriestmanGoode’s private jet concept offers up a multi-generational interior
items.text: The main bedroom in the Ways of Seeing private jet concept (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Chinese ultra-luxury is having a moment. Mindful of the buying power, cultural sensitivities and tastes of a new generation of wealthy Chinese family and elite corporate buyers, London -based design studio PriestmanGoode has created a private jet concept to explore new facets of aviation design. Ways of Seeing / 观 Guān is the name of this new cabin concept, one that has grown organically out of local research and needs, instead of just being ‘a generic template with local dressing applied’. Shown here in renders based on the Boeing 737’s narrow-bodied long-range jet platform, the studio reckons the design language could also be adopted for a locally made jet such as the Comac C919. The bedroom concept (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) One of the principal shifts is the idea of an aircraft that goes beyond a mere business tool to represent a shared family environment, ‘a space where three generations; grandparents, parents, children, can travel and spend time together’. The layout includes a private retreat space at the rear of the cabin, complete with a bedroom, en-suite bathroom and study area. The last can also be used as an office or even a meditation suite or wellbeing space, alongside a second bedroom. The design of the main bathroom (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The main space is a shared lounge and dining area, with a multifunctional table for dining, gaming or just socialising, alongside a woven metal screen. ‘We didn’t want to design a Chinese-inflected version of an existing template,’ says Ben Rowan, creative director at PriestmanGoode. ‘We wanted to start from an honest, well-researched picture of how a specific person actually lives and travels and let the cabin follow from that. It’s why the input from our cultural consultant sits at the centre of the brief rather than layered on at the end, and why we didn’t default to a house style: the design has to be driven by the people it’s for.’ Another view of the main bedroom (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) It was this work with a cultural consultant, along with crafted collaborations, that determined the way the limited space aboard would be used, especially in the way it rejects the ‘single principal’s use’ strategy that results in so many jet interiors resembling boardrooms or mancaves in the sky. As PriestmanGoode notes, the consultant’s ‘insight pointed to a clear shift towards multi-generational travel among Chinese entrepreneurs and their families, with a personal style blending natural cues and a contemporary aesthetic of clean, understated lines and natural materials’. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The main space features a reconfigurable table setup (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The main space features a reconfigurable table setup Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original Throughout the cabin, technology has been designed to keep out of sight; screens and speakers are hidden unless required. Craft is used to highlight key areas of the design, soften the lines and bring in human warmth and interest. Tai Ping was responsible for the bedroom carpet, a bespoke design that uses traditional geometric motifs from Chinese culture, while the shared areas feature an organic patterned carpet by Andre Fu. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The living area, day (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The living area at night Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original The lacquer artwork onboard was supplied by The Gallery by SOIL in Hong Kong . It includes works by National Master of Crafts Erke Gan, featuring a marbled ‘rhinoceros hide’ texture on the table surfaces, alongside some of his standalone vases. In the bedroom, you can find lacquer artwork by Shi Yuguang. Jade-toned stone veneer is found in the bathroom alongside patterned fabric in the bedroom. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The living area by day (Image credit: PriestmanGoode) The living area at night Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original ‘These collaborations … are proof that the cultural authenticity PriestmanGoode set out to achieve rests on genuine craft authority, not surface styling,’ the designers note. ‘Our research found that this business traveller seeks to combine business and family time… Modularity runs through the cabin: the dining table becomes a place for family games and tea, the study transforms into a workspace, and the sofa converts for rest, allowing both cabin, and family within it, to move fluidly between both purposes over the course of a shared journey.’ PriestmanGoode.com , @PriestmanGoode TOPICS Jonathan Bell Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design , 21st Century House , and The New Modern House , and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.
designers: National Master of Crafts Erke Gan

items.title: A Ukrainian midcentury house finds new life as an artist-designed guesthouse
items.text: (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A 1960s rural Ukrainian midcentury house near Kyiv has been transformed into a rich tapestry of found materials, antiques and creative interventions. Hata Yarova, which stands out in the village of Derev’yana thanks to a mural on its facade inspired by Ukrainian modernism and Suprematism by Levchenya, is the first of three neighbouring Soviet architecture -era homes that Ukrainian artist Oksana Levchenya (Konstantinovska) is remodelling as guesthouses, turning an ordinary, anonymous typology into something distinctive and woven with narrative. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Inside Oksana Levchenya's Ukrainian midcentury house project The idea for the guest houses emerged during the pandemic, but the project has taken on new meaning since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. 'Continuing to build during the war is, in a way, an act of defiance against the death and destruction that Russia has brought to us,' Levchenya tells me via video call from Kyiv, her background darkened by a power cut. She relies on a small group of builders, led by a man approaching his seventies, and the goal of renting the houses is largely about covering costs and sustaining the teams’ livelihoods. 'These houses serve as places of calm and restoration for those who have remained in Ukraine. We are all working enough for three people now, and all of us need rest and comfort.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Levchenya’s own childhood was another spur. After her parents’ divorce, she stayed with her grandmother and later her aunt while her mother pursued a career as a surgeon. At the age of nine, she went to live with her mother in one of the meagre apartments allotted to physicians during the Soviet era in low-cost blocks, called Khrushchyovka . 'Throughout my early childhood, I was always staying in other people’s homes, dreaming of a place of my own,' she explains. 'The Hata Yarova project was born from a desire to create a space in which time is somehow suspended – a place that does not belong to any particular period.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) She calls her approach 'intuitive additive architecture': an organic method of adaptation, in which the final form emerges through a slow process of interventions and additions, rather than from a fixed blueprint. Replacing the roof gave her a chance to add an attic level housing guest rooms. The original porch was dismantled, its timber planks reused as the staircase. In its place, Levchenya added an extension housing the kitchen and bathroom. Salvage is a defining feature of the project: oversized arched windows rescued from the renovation of a private residence have been cut up to suit the scale of the house and reassembled in a new composition, while an old timber platform from the former Kosmos factory was refashioned as outdoor decking. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) In the bathroom, reuse becomes even more expressive, with unglazed tiles from the 1960s and 70s mixed with rare, hand-painted pieces from Kharkiv, and contemporary Spanish ceramics. The interiors are kitted with vintage finds and pieces collected from friends, such as a stove from a restaurant. An antique wooden chest from the 1930s purchased from a fair is a poignant nod to her family history, made during the time of Soviet collectivisation, when privately owned farms were consolidated into state-controlled collective farms. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) ‘My family has lost its inheritance and material possessions several times: first in the aftermath of the October Revolution of 1917, and again during the upheavals of the 1930s,' she explains. 'Today history has cruelly repeated itself; the elders of my family - my mother, her sister, and her brother – have once again lost their homes in Krasnopillia, a rural settlement in Sumy Oblast.' Rebuilding from these ruptures has shaped a particular understanding of value within the family: that the most enduring forms of inheritance are not material, but intellectual - one’s knowledge, skills and capacities. The chest becomes a metaphor for the limits of what can be carried through history: only what is essential, portable, and internalised. It is more than symbolic, however. 'It is an authentic domestic object, originally used to store textiles and rugs, and therefore carries a direct connection to the material culture of the home,' she adds. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Textiles have always had a particular emotional resonance for Levchenya, who describes them as a 'matriarchal medium' that connects women across generations. Thanks to her mother’s medical supplies, Levchenya’s favourite plaything as a child was gauze, which she used to create toys. Later, she was drawn to them again through her research into traditional Ukrainian craft heritage, but also a frustration with painting , 'which began to feel too confined and controlled,' she says. 'I wanted to have more freedom to experiment and make mistakes.' Today she creates textile sculptures and woven wall-hangings that draw from local traditions, spliced with Ukrainian modernism and contemporary imagery. 'I find a particular magic in combining opposing textures and creating structures that contain a certain paradox within themselves,' she explains. 'This can happen through visual imagery - for example, Pac-Man combined with traditional Ukrainian ornament - or through the contrast of materials.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Her own work is present in the

items.title: How Isamu Noguchi's Akari lanterns became interior design’s favourite fixtures
items.text: (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Isamu Noguchi ’s glowing washi lanterns and light sculptures have nearly become as universal as light itself. The paper lanterns glow far and wide, bringing a supremely soft warmth to homes, offices, hotels, restaurants and film and TV sets. The pioneering American artist and designer (1904–1988) created the first designs for his Akari light sculptures 75 years ago, a milestone that's now being celebrated with a new exhibition, now on view at his namesake museum in New York. From then on, Noguchi relentlessly formed new iterations. Despite spawning a legion of copycats and dupes, Noguchi’s original Akari shows no signs of dimming in appeal. Here's what to know about the Akari lantern's history and influence. Isamu Noguchi photographed among Akari fixtures. (Image credit: Photo: Louise Dahl-Wolfe. © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) When did Isamu Noguchi create the Akari lantern? Noguchi’s Akari light sculptures were born in 1951 during a visit to Gifu, Japan , where he encountered illuminated paper lanterns called chochin . The handcrafted lanterns made of mulberry bark paper were mostly used as decorations or advertisements, as Noguchi observed. Eventually, Noguchi was introduced to the city’s mayor, who requested that the artist revive Gifu’s lantern industry as it had become diluted by inferior replicas. Noguchi swiftly developed two ideas for lanterns with an eye toward the future:x he replaced the customary candle with an incandescent lightbulb. Early Akari lantern designs in the 1950s. (Image credit: Photo: Stephen Michael. © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) What is an Akari lantern made of? Under the term Akari, a Japanese word meaning ‘light’ that’s also associated with weightlessness, Noguchi established paper lanterns as sculptures that blend traditional craftsmanship with modern living. He fashioned Akari from high-quality materials used in Gifu: strips of mulberry bark washi paper structured with bamboo ribbing. The washi paper’s durability with impressive plasticity allowed Noguchi to play with shapes while maintaining the practicality of their collapsible construction. With the ability to flatten and expand, the lanterns proved easy to ship and towed the line between material and immaterial. Isamu Noguchi’s studio in Kita Kamakura, Japan, 1952. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) A decades-long dedication to developing new designs In Noguchi’s lifetime, he created more than 200 Akari models. ‘Noguchi spoke of developing new designs as a way to ‘foil [his] many imitators, through innovation, to reach a point where they could no longer follow,’ ‘ says Kate Wiener, curator for The Noguchi Museum in New York , which has recently opened an exhibition dedicated to the influential lanterns. ‘Certainly, this was one motivation, but he also described his continued efforts as something more deeply felt: "[It] became like a cause with me—a new shape, merely, was not enough; it obviously had to be fitted into today's new ways and uses."' Noguchi working on a paper template for an Akari design. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) Noguchi fiercely believed in the modern relevance of Akari. ‘They embodied his lifelong vision of a hybrid, accessible form of sculpture that could transcend the boundaries between art and design and become an integral part of everyday experience,’ Wiener adds. ‘I think this is ultimately what kept him returning to Akari. He saw in them seemingly endless possibilities and was continually inspired to explore just how far he could take them.’ The earliest versions of Akari are a table lamp identified as 9A and floor lamp labeled 14A , says Evan Scott, the museum’s director of retail and merchandising. Set on three-legged metal frames, both styles feature wooden collars and evenly spaced bamboo ribbing. Other Akari models range from globe-shaped ceiling lights to column-shaped shades with minimal bamboo ribbing. While they predominantly come in an off-white hue, some models feature colourful screen-printed designs on the neutral background. Noguchi designing Akari with Japanese architect Kenzo Tange and Michio Noguchi in 1952. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) The enduring allure of Akari light sculptures Akari light sculptures still enthrall the contemporary era. ‘There is an obvious beauty to the way light suffuses and filters through the mulberry bark paper used for Akari that probably accounts for a good bit of their lasting appeal,’ says Matthew Kirsch, curator and director of research for The Noguchi Museum. ‘There is a warmth in the way light is transmitted through the paper of an Akari that is missing from its many imitators.’ Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Akari lanterns also possess a fine handmade quality, partly apparent in the shades’ natural wrinkles. ‘The method of construction for most models, based on the chochin lantern's spiral bamboo ribbing, is relatively unchanged from how they were made when Noguchi began working with the Ozeki family in Gifu in the 1950s and, obviously, for many decades before that,’ Kirsch explains. Noguchi among colourful Akari light sculptures in 1954. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) How to buy an Akari lantern of your own Over the years, design lovers seeking ‘elegant people’s art,’ as Noguchi

items.title: Wallpaper* checks into The Webster hotel, a design-led gem for your next London stay
items.text: (Image credit: Adam Firman) Jump to category: What's on your doorstep? Who is behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The verdict Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter ‘Morning,’ said the businessman next to me as we waited for the lift to take us from the ninth floor to reception at The Webster Hotel in Covent Garden. There was something reassuringly un- London about his greeting. In the spirit of lift small talk, I asked if he was checking out and how he'd enjoyed his stay. His face lit up. ‘I’ve come down from Harrogate, and I always struggle to find a hotel in London that I actually like,’ he said, as he smoothed down his trench coat. ‘Here I feel like I’ve stepped into a countryside manor. I’ve been here for two weeks and eaten dinner at the restaurant almost every night and loved every minute. It's a hotel that feels inviting. It's been wonderful.’ To that, I agreed. It's a surprisingly hard balance to strike. The appeal of The Webster is its domestic scale. While many London hotels favour grand entrances and expansive public spaces, here the reception is intimate, the interiors inviting and the atmosphere closer to that of a country house than a conventional city hotel. There's a sense of British manor-house character, without the period flourishes. What's on your doorstep? (Image credit: Adam Firman) The Webster in Covent Garden is a new hotel brand, designed to reconnect guests with analogue pleasures. Though new, it is already thinking ahead with a second outpost set to open in Times Square, New York , in 2028. The Webster is a two-minute walk from Holborn station, ten minutes from Tottenham Court Road, and, of course, Covent Garden. The hotel sits opposite Lincoln's Inn Fields, which was also the moody backdrop for Charles Dickens’ novel Bleak House. Who is behind the design? (Image credit: Adam Firman) Behind the design is London-based architecture firm, Red Deer, which they describe as ‘magical realism’. ‘This felt like a natural expression of the playfulness we wanted for The Webster: something familiar and welcoming, with moments that gently interrupt your expectations,’ says Lucas Che Tizard, co-founder, lead architect and designer of the firm. ‘There’s a freedom to hotel design because people arrive ready to step outside their everyday lives. We wanted to encourage that curiosity.’ (Image credit: Adam Firman) They captured this through a dialogue of materials and colour: bespoke terrazzo, hand-painted murals and tactile fabrics. Says Che Tizard, ‘For me, the magic is in discovering something slightly unexpected within a space you already feel at home in.’ Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Adam Firman) The hotel’s architecture itself feels cosy. Gone are the intimidating entryways and unused lounge areas. The check-in desk is bijou, evoking nostalgia for small boutique hotels of the 1970s. The architect explains: 'We approached The Webster through its own story and surroundings. The relationship with Lincoln’s Inn Fields, the energy of Holborn and the idea of a hotel as a creative meeting place all helped shape its character. That comes through at every scale, from the terrace connecting the hotel to the square to the mohair headboards in the guestrooms.' The room to book (Image credit: Adam Firman) Considering its quaint feel, there are 167 keys. There are three room options: the King Deluxe with a park view really showing off what the hotel has to offer. The room has beautiful bespoke joinery to hang and store clothes for longer stays. There is also a design-led mini bar offering Torres crisps, Form protein bars, ‘healthy’ sweets, and to enjoy with tea, coffee, or something stronger. The bathroom is generous, with contemporary tiling and Malin + Goetz products. Staying for drinks and dinner? (Image credit: Adam Firman) Carmelina's has all the character of a restaurant with a life of its own. Tucked down a set of hidden steps to the right of The Webster entrance, it feels more New York than London: a moody, intimate space of low ceilings, wood-clad walls and an open kitchen, with velvety green booths, a nostalgic black-and-white tiled floor and petal-shaped chandeliers. (Image credit: Adam Firman) Carmelina's avoids the familiar Italian restaurant shorthand. Its contemporary interiors provide a backdrop for a menu rooted in Italian cooking, overseen by head chef Simone Serafini and restaurant manager Francesco Patti. (Image credit: Adam Firman) Towards the back of the restaurant is a secret cloaked bar, Carla’s. Helmed by bar manager Peppe Corallo, the space has a 90s energy that encourages you to spark up a conversation with a stranger. The menu is something special. Peppe has expertly crafted each cocktail, each nodding to traditions found when dining with family, from the woody scents of the cabinet that holds special-occasion drinkware to the idea of having a remedy concoction to help ease a cold, or perhaps a bad day. But at the heart of his menu is La Conserva, a stunning take on a martini that feels fragrant and refreshing, with strong basil notes; it is an ode to a late-summer Italian ritual where families jar and preserve fresh tomatoes. It is worth visiting Carla’s just for that. Where to switch off (Image credit: Adam Firman) The lounge area just off the reception feels comfortable and sociable, as Che Tizard also notes, ‘with enough intimacy to make yourself a little corner of it.’ It is the character shift throughout that day which charms the designer, as he continues, ‘In the morning, there’s something quite studious about it – somewhere to read, work or simply sit with a coffee. By evening, it becomes more animated, with conversation and people gathering. The fu

items.title: Amansara: a revived royal guesthouse in Siem Reap
items.text: (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Jump to category: What’s on your doorstep? Who's behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The Verdict Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The former Villa Princière, a royal guesthouse commissioned by Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihanouk, lives largely behind a long white wall in Siem Reap. To most, Amansara flies subtly under the radar, unnoticed by almost anyone unaware of what lies beyond its discreet gate – and all the better for it. Siem Reap may beep and honk like most Southeast Asian cities, but this corner of Cambodia moves in a softer lane, in line with its ancient sites and therefore slower, more spiritual pace. The temples are a big reason guests come here; the other is the chance to retreat afterwards to the gentle hug of Aman’s beyond-exceptional service and fragrant cold towels. Fresh from a thoughtful renovation, the 24-suite hotel feels like stepping right back into the 1960s, where, if you squint hard enough, Jackie O might just be sunbathing beside the cool curving pool. What’s on your doorstep? Angkor Wat (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Amansara sits on the main road towards Angkor, a remarkable fact that a site as striking and transcendent as the UNESCO-listed temples is just ten minutes from the hotel, and perhaps part of the reason Amansara feels so relaxed is its proximity to all that ancient history. Villa Princière was built with privacy in mind, set along the French Quarter, among the royal parks and leafy streets around Charles de Gaulle Boulevard and the Siem Reap River. The obvious excitement is its nearness to Angkor Wat, but tying in a few other surrounding temples into a ‘petit circuit’ makes the most of an early rise: Bayon, with its big-block carvings of smiling faces, and Ta Prohm, where a web of enormous tree roots winds through mossy ruins. Amanbala boat trips (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Downtown Siem Reap is walkable or a speedy remorque ride away, with the bright lights of its night market stirring up street food and cold bottles of beer, while the Made in Cambodia Market and Kandal Village are good for daytime pottering – the latter has a run of smarter shops selling lacquered homeware, silk scarves, and silverware. While Aman’s knack for detail and serious service make it all too easy to stay put, its experiences take on something totally different. The Amanbala boats, for instance, head out to the floating village of Chong Kneas on Tonlé Sap, garnering an up-close look at life on the country’s largest freshwater lake. Who's behind the design? (Image credit: Amansara, courtesy of Aman) It’s worth remembering the many iterations of a residence like this, too. French architect Laurent Mondet was commissioned to design Villa Princière in 1962, one of two state guesthouses built for Prince Sihanouk. The single-storey white cement buildings feature stone accents, while two uniquely shaped pools sit at the centre of the grounds and a grand circular dining room occupies one corner of the property. It was a subtle, modern design for its time, with long columned corridors and areas that made the most of the Cambodian climate. (Image credit: Aman) After changing hands and names over the years, the property eventually fell into disrepair before Aman took it on in 2002. Kerry Hill Architects handled the latest round of work and took care not to disrupt the long-standing formula. The building’s minimalist shapes and time-worn charm are a near-perfect example of 1960s New Khmer architecture, a shift in Cambodian design that moved away from French colonial nostalgia in favour of expressive curvilinear forms, layered concrete, and plenty of open-air spaces. The bones have been left largely unchanged, with a few modern amendments: armchairs have given way to sweeping banquettes in the restaurant, and the palette remains an earthy mix of dusty browns, stark whites, and bold blacks. The room to book (Image credit: Amansara) All 24 suites follow a familiar monochrome scheme, with a hint of orange here and there, nodding to the saffron-coloured kasaya robes worn by Buddhist monks. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Amansara, courtesy of Aman) The latest update has been artful: all suites have been spruced up, and five additional guest suites have been upgraded to include private swimming pools, expanding Amansara’s collection of Pool Suites. Two new categories have also been added: a Junior Pool Suite and a Two-Bedroom Family Pool Suite for young families who’d prefer to stick together. The look is pared back and modernly spiffed, with enough warmth (and natural light) to keep it from feeling too two-toned. Staying for drinks and dinner? Dining at Amansara (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) The food is reliable, flavourful and intentionally familiar, mixing international dishes with local staples that are intriguing to try. Breakfast comes on an A3 printout of traditional Khmer dishes alongside the usual spreads, including avocado toast, colourful fruits, chia pudding and eggs any style. Try something traditional: Bor Bor Bangkear is a rice-style porridge with bean sprouts, spring onion, and stir-fried prawns. When th

items.title: 8 Best Hotel Mattress Picks for a Five-Star Staycation (2026)
items.summary: Bring home the beds behind some of the world's most high-end stays—no reservations required
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The hotel mattress probably isn't on your vacation itinerary, but it can make or break the trip. A lumpy, unsupportive bed can derail even the most carefully planned getaway . A really good one, though, might become an unexpected highlight—the kind that has you looking forward to bedtime and quietly checking the mattress label before checkout. Recreating that experience at home doesn't require another plane ticket. Some of our favorite properties, including design-forward waterfront retreats and charming bed-and-breakfasts, put just as much thought into their mattresses as they do their interiors. Many turn to brands like Saatva , Ostermoor, and Casper to outfit their guest rooms; others, like the W Hotels , have signature mattresses you can purchase directly. We've rounded up our favorites, such as options with plush pillow tops, supportive coils, and pressure-relieving foam, to help you bring home the best part of your stay. The room service, unfortunately, is still up to you. items.title: Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises
items.summary: From Bauhaus to his house, we’re gobbling up all the decor ideas on display at Ditto
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story “I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.” At Ditto —the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron —the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test. The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas. Photo: Adrian Gaut For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock , is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.” It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be . But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus , de Stijl , and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says. The Bauhaus-inspired counter at Ditto. Photo: Adrian Gaut They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman . Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says. Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window. Photo: Adrian Gaut The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil. Flaky Biscuits will be a signature dish. Photo Credit: Adrian Gaut The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani. Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors. But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas —was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles. Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says. White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric. The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam , and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative , which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It , which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms— Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo . “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says. Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

items.title: 12 Best Bar Carts to Elevate Your Entertaining Game (2026)
items.summary: Happy hour is best served on wheels
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Bar carts are not just for someone who likes to host a cocktail soirée. In fact, the predecessor of the bar cart was once a Victorian-era tea trolley. Only when the Prohibition hit did these side tables on wheels find their true calling. Many, many iterations later—think: Alvar Aalto’s iconic tea trolley, which has inspired many picks on this list, and USM ’s blessedly minimalist spin on the genre—the beauty of this booze trolley remains that it can completely transform a room or give a useless nook some purpose. Though they’ve fallen out of favor in many modern homes, these rolling wonders make an elegant—and functional—home base for all your mixology essentials, from stemware and decanters to liquor bottles and mixers. They also don’t have to be used to haul booze at all, instead doubling as portable storage for crafts, books, beauty or bathroom supplies, and houseplants. Employed outside, a stylish bar cart can give a dinner party some polish or emulate a poolside butler. Load it up with a pitcher of lemonade and a basket of sunscreen on top, and extra towels on the bottom and you’ll never have to leave your lounge. items.title: In This Midcentury Nashville Home a Mosaic Rainbow-Hued Window Brings Color to the Earthy Interiors
items.summary: Founders of Eneby Home combined one-of-a-kind pieces with a natural palette to create their memorable family home
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Here’s one you may not have heard before: What do Serge Mouille sconces, a Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant, and Borge Mogensen dining chairs have in common? Hint, hint: They all live in the Nashville home of Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of antiques and vintage furniture store Eneby Home . One might reasonably presume the home of antiques purveyors to be chock-full of one-of-a-kind finds from far-flung locales, and while that is certainly the case here, the husband-and-wife duo’s house otherwise expertly subverts expectations. Built in 1970, the uber-quiet four-acre property sits at the top of a hill overlooking seemingly endless rolling valleys. It’s surrounded by native honeysuckle bushes and Tennessee Fieldstone, and the sun sets on the front side of the home at 6:37 p.m., says Doug, who dreamed of building what he describes as an “art gallery” for their furniture. The Jenkinses kept the wall of original Tennessee Fieldstone—and the original copper fireplace—but added their own flair with vintage furnishings, like a La Mura sofa, Gianfranco Frattini for Cassina leather lounge chairs, a Charles Dudouyt credenza, and a 1960s marble fossil coffee table from Italy. “It’s super unique,” says Doug. “It doesn’t have a name behind it.” Save to wishlist Save to wishlist CB2 Leather Square Brown Pouf $229 CB2 Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Slow Roads Tabac & Noir Hand Towel $45 Shop $45 Slow Roads Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of Eneby Home, with their daughters. They kept the original Tennessee Fieldstone on the wall and paired it with an antique marble dining table that’s “huge and heavy,” says Doug. “The guys hated bringing stuff to our house.” Even though the Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant is often seen in copper, the Jenkins were able to source one with a green finish, seen here. The chairs are Borge Mogensen; the 1960s geometric painting is from France. Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Louis Poulsen PH Artichoke Lamp $17,490 Shop $17,490 Design Within Reach Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Louis Poulsen PH 3/2 Table Lamp $2,250 Shop $2,250 Design Within Reach A well-lit workspace features a vintage 1950s desk, an Italian cocoon lamp, and a Hans Wegner chair from Denmark. Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Gatto Table Lamp by Achille Castiglioni $830 Shop $830 Lumens Save to wishlist Save to wishlist IKEA ULLERSLEV Sheepskin $60 IKEA “There’s not a lot of this type of house in Nashville,” says Greg Dutton, the founder and architect behind Columbus, Ohio-based and AD PRO Directory design firm Dutton Studio . “But we had to look past what was there—a mixed bag with a new era in each room—to create a backdrop for the work they do.” Cue the blank slate. The couple bought the house as-is—black toilets, mustard-hued siding, and early 2000s kitchen included—and embarked on a “bigger than expected” renovation, says Doug, that translated to moving walls, updating floor plans, a new roof and flooring, and overall furnishings, of course. With the resulting minimalist white walls and clean lines, how does one amass the amount of character evident here? “When you build in materials that have inherent imperfection, that naturally bakes in a lot of warmth,” says Dutton. Think locally sourced, character-grade white oak flooring throughout; imported reclaimed European bluestone that’s well over 100 years old in the primary bath; and an original copper fireplace in the living room. “The mosaic supposedly came from a building in Bologna,” says Doug. “The morning sun comes up on this side” and ignites a fire of filtered light within the home. “The island has a commercial look to it,” says Doug of the Vipp system. “It hit every box. It’s sick.” Dutton helped reconfigure the space’s floor plan to open the room to the dining area. The oven is by Miele. A Guillerme et Chambron cabinet, sourced from Eneby Home, houses curiosities. The 1960s pendant light is Stilnovo. The guest bathroom originally had a black toilet and smoked glass. Now it features vintage Serge Mouille sconces, of which Doug has “never seen another pair,” a 250-year-old antique Italian mirror from the 1800s, and a Josef Hoffman bench. “Flaws make the house feel better, not worse,” says Dutton. “But creating something that looks effortless actually takes a lot of coordination. We wanted it to feel like it had just happened that way, and installing materials that feel like they’ve been there forever automatically gives the house permanence and ensures it’ll age gracefully over time.” The push-and-pull between old and new, simple and full of character, clean and distressed is one the Jenkins family is familiar with. The balancing act makes the house interesting, says Doug, and the same inclination to lean on historic materials translates just as well to furnishings. “Some of this stuff we’d been saving in hopes we’d one day be able to use it for our own house,” says Doug. One such example is a 1940s or ’50s-era, rainbow-hued mosaic window the couple bought five years ago and stored in a crate ever since. “We asked Greg to change the layout of the wall to make it work,” says Doug. The stone sculpture on display in front of the window is another; it’s 2,000 years old, from Rome. An earthy palette in the primary bedroom lets the landscape through the windows do the talking. The sconces are by Biny; the oversized 1880 landscape painting is from France; the chairs are Borge Mogensen; the side table is Charles Dudouyt, and the floor lamp is La Borne. “The fireplace is original, and we ran with it,” says Doug. “It’s New Mexico style and is super cool.” It’s paired with an abstract geometric art piece and a collection of vases from Denmark. items.title: Everybody Wants to Do Shabbat Dinner at Erin Foster and Simon Tikhman’s Cozy, Playful LA Home
items.summary: The creator of Netflix’s Nobody Wants This and music executive worked with JDP Interiors to bring in color, pattern, and an AI assistant to their historic home
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The recently dropped third season of the hit Netflix rom-com Nobody Wants This begins with a picture of domestic bliss: Kristen Bell and Adam Brody’s characters cheerfully lugging boxes and eating pizza sans dishes—living together at last. The fictional romance between the witty podcaster and “hot rabbi” is inspired by that of series creator Erin Foster and her husband Simon Tikhman, albeit loosely. Like Bell’s Joanne, Foster converted to Judaism before their wedding in 2019; unlike Brody’s Noah, Tikhman is a music executive, not a rabbi—but art is still intermingling with life. As their onscreen alter egos feather their nest, Foster, Tikhman, and their two-year-old daughter Noa are starring in a new season of their own, moving into a 1920s Los Angeles home that mixes undefinable colors and bold pattern play with the “European flavor” of an old-world estate, per Tikhman. Researching the house’s roots, Foster found Spanish, Mediterranean revival, and English influences, and the couple felt free to embrace all three. “I don’t tend to like following a set of rules,” Foster says, “whether it be in fashion or in television writing or in design.” To create more of a grand entrance, the entry foyer was opened up on the second floor and “guests often mistake the entry tile as original,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. The stair runner is by Stark and the vintage mirror is from Nickey Kehoe . The walls are painted in Benjamin Moore’s Soft Chamois . Tikhman, Foster, and Noa seated on the custom living room sofas upholstered in a Schumacher fabric. “I had girls over for drinks and we sat in the room together,” Foster says. “It’s kind of like the gossip room.” The sofas flank a custom coffee table in the living room. The vintage chair is from 1stDibs , the ottoman is upholstered in a fabric by Scalamandré, and the vintage floor lamp is from PRB Collection. The sconces are from Aqua Gallery and the curtain fabric is by Rose Tarlow Melrose House . The chandelier is by Cox London. “They handmake each metal leaf,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. The artwork is by Danielle Orchard from Perrotin Gallery. The multihyphenate cohost of The World’s First Podcast and cofounder of cool-girl fashion line Favorite Daughter acknowledges that she runs in a “circle of really fashion-forward women who have been featured in AD and have elevated taste in art and in design, and it’s very intimidating,” including when it came to selecting a designer. “There starts to be this culture of, ‘Well, you have to use this person,’” Foster says. Instead, she discovered her own on Instagram. Foster cold-messaged Joyce Pickens Dinwiddy, founder of LA’s JDP Interiors (and later the brains behind Favorite Daughter’s Beverly Hills boutique) about masterminding the new-old home’s four-year renovation and redesign. “They’re a cool couple and they don’t want this stuffy, old-school, fully British-feeling home,” Pickens Dinwiddy says, but Foster and Tikhman still craved classicism their way—something “cozy, young, and playful but sophisticated at the same time.” “I’ve realized I’m obsessed with the color green,” Foster says. “The color feels a little shocking sometimes to people, but it’s also inviting and it’s also kind of earthy and cozy.” The kitchen is painted in Denali Green from Dunn-Edwards and the cabinets are backed in a Rose Tarlow Melrose House fabric. Tikhman requested and received a dedicated drinks fridge in the kitchen, filled with clean sodas and seltzers. “Simon was like, ‘I want a Kardashian fridge,’” Foster says. The kitchen backsplash includes custom hand-painted tiles by Lascaux Tile and the hood is copper. The range is by Lacanche, the fridge is Sub-Zero , and the sink fittings are by Waterstone . The pendants are custom. The result is a warm, hip house where Pickens Dinwiddy, who’s married to a Brit, introduced charming flourishes familiar to UK country homes . She softened cabinetry in the not-quite olive green kitchen with floral chintz fabric by Rose Tarlow Melrose House and added a skirt beneath the sink in the scullery, a hybrid mud room/potting room traditionally used to water herb pots from the garden. The glass-ceilinged breakfast nook—an “architectural feat,” according to Pickens Dinwiddy, that was lowered into the home via crane and which Foster says “probably added a year to the project”—has been crowned the solarium. With sun drenching its slate blue walls and sculpted medallion details, “it’s a really special place for us to have early dinner with our daughter,” Foster says, and also where she pops open her laptop, morning coffee in hand. “Erin likes to wake up, have her coffee, pull up her computer, and sit in a room,” Tikhman says. “And her dream was that’s what the solarium was going to be.” The custom banquette is upholstered in a fabric from Perennials Fabrics and topped with pillows covered in Robert Kime fabric . The chairs by Casamidy are upholstered in a Perennials by Rose Tarlow fabric . The pendant is by Vaughan . ART: Avital Burg “I wanted to do wall-to-wall paneling somewhere,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. “This felt like the place for it so that there wasn’t a wall treatment competing with this beautiful tile floor.” The floor tile is by Ann Sacks. The mudroom bench is upholstered in a fabric by Décors Barbares. The custom dining room table is surrounded by custom chairs covered in a Jasper fabric . The 1950s chandelier is from Fargo Design and the vintage Swedish sconces are from 1stDibs . The 1970s Danish sideboard is from Chairish and the mirror is custom. I revel in the regal room names, but the couple is decidedly unfussy about their solarium and scullery—“words that Erin and I never used before building this house,” Tikhman says. “We actually only speak with English accents when we’re at home,” she cracks. In fact, Foster applauds Tikhman for gently voicing concerns when, in the throes of the project, her old-world sensibilities started to feel a bit too
credits: Michael Clifford Styled by Lisa Rowe November 5

items.title: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027
items.summary: The National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 forecast has arrived.
items.text: 2 min read Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah. Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report . Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways. Defined Layouts Gieves Anderson In a David Netto-designed apartment , linen curtains with Samuel & Sons trim divide the space between the kitchen and dining area. NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers. Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen plans. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow. Hidden Appliances and Enclosed Storage Appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage. Pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report. Martin Morrell An English Victorian manor designed by Linda Boronkay features an enclosed pantry with bespoke oak joinery. Wood Cabinets and Neutral Colors Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes. Layers of Lighting The lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent. Ventilation, Water Filtration, and Leak Protection NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration. Julia Cancilla Social Media & News Editor Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more. items.title: 7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors
items.summary: In honor of   The Gilded Age  ’s fourth season, here are the period mansions-turned-hotels you can stay in right now.
items.text: Erin McGinn Above, Castle Hill Inn in Newport, Rhode Island. Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences. Notable families like the Vanderbilts, Carnegies, and Astors once had houses dotted across New York City and throughout fashionable summer retreats like Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these elaborate structures have since fallen to the ravages of time, with the staggering costs of upkeep rendering their use as private residences all but obsolete. Yet, though some of these private homes have disappeared, our curiosity about them has only increased. Since HBO’s hit show The Gilded Age debuted, interest in visiting the era’s architectural marvels has surged, and in Newport, which is home to one of the country’s largest concentrations of Gilded Age mansions, there’s been a steady rise in visitors touring the town’s mansions specifically because of the show. Visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age ’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night? Up and down the East Coast, a handful of Gilded Age mansions are preserved not as museums, but as hotels—inviting curious travelers to do more than just visit and admire the history, but to sleep within the jewel boxes of their walls. Courtesy of Castle Hill Inn Castle Hill Inn Newport, Rhode Island Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding. The home’s original owner, Alexander Agassiz, was a Harvard professor of natural sciences who made his fortune in copper mining. With his newfound wealth, Agassiz built his summer home—Castle Hill—on a relatively isolated parcel of forty acres, a fifteen minute drive away from the pomp and pageantry of the Vanderbilt’s side of town. He used the home as a summer research lab, hosting students in its many rooms and running the lab in what is today the parlor, while also entertaining a who’s who of literary luminaries, including Edith Wharton and Mark Twain. Today, Castle Hill Inn is one of the most famous places to stay in Newport, not only for its luxurious rooms, afternoon tea, and award-winning restaurant, but also for its sweeping ocean-front lawn and seaside views. Thorton Wilder lived in the turret suite—Agassiz’s former observatory and today the hotel’s most beautiful room—while writing his last book, and Grace Kelly lived in one of the beach cottages during the 1955 filming of “High Society.” Stopping by Castle Hill Inn for a drink and taking a short walk to its still in-use lighthouse remains a summer essential in Newport, but there is nothing quite like staying the night. Courtesy The Chanler at Cliff Walk Hotel Chanler Newport, Rhode Island Hotel Chanler is, unlike Castle Hill, right in the thick of Newport’s Gilded Age neighborhood, and it’s clear from its location that it was built (to use a period expression) to keep up with the Joneses. The opulent mansion was constructed in 1873 as the summer “cottage” of New York Congressman John Winthrop Chanler and his wife Margaret Astor Ward. Chanler hosted an elaborate range of guests at his summer home, including President Theodore Roosevelt and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The home, which Chanler called “Cliff Lawn,” was the very first mansion to be built on the Cliff Walk, now a public walkway with views of these historic homes. Over the years, the mansion went from being a private residence to a museum and later a girl’s school. It wasn’t until 2003 that it opened as the twenty-room Chanler Hotel. Today, it’s ornately decorated in various period-specific styles such as Regency, Louis XVI, Renaissance, and English Tudor. Last spring, The Chanler opened a more pared down restaurant, Remy’s Loose. Remy’s feels fit for Mr. Chanler and his guests, who we can imagine sprawling out across the chenille, fringed edged slipper chairs, and enjoying the just fussy-enough French menu. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Courtesy of The Fifth Avenue Hotel The Fifth Avenue Hotel New York, New York The Fifth Avenue Hotel, which opened its doors in late 2023, has a multi-layered history rooted in the Gilded Age. In 1856, legendary hostess and doyenne of New York society, Charlotte Goodridge, commissioned the construction of a lavish private home and carriage house at the coveted corner of Fifth Avenue and 28th Street. Goodridge filled her mansion with treasures from around the globe and entertained lavishly. But following her death, Goodridge’s home met the same fate as much of the neighborhood and was torn down. However, rather than being replaced by a skyscraper like much of the surrounding area, Goodridge’s mansion was reborn in 1907 as a striking five story neo-Renaissance palazzo design by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind many of the New York’s most famous early 20th century buildings including The Morgan Library and Museum, the Bowery Savings Bank, and the Metropolitan Club. More recently, a decades-long renovation overseen by Flâneur Hospitality, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and architect Perkins Eastman transformed the building into a 153-room hotel, with a restored limestone and brick façade, an added-in glass tower, a ballroom fit for a Goodridge party, and a European inspired restaurant, Café Carmellini. The hotel now has a Gilded Age-inspired look, complete with polished marble floors, grand arched windows, rich color palettes, and art and curiosities from around the world. Michael Worthington Hotel Bardo Savannah, Georgia Hotel Bardo may have opened in 2024, but its history extends much further back. It was built in 1888 as a private home for Lewis Kayton, a businessman from Baltimore who settled in Savannah. items.title: Next-Gen Mineral Surfaces for Your Kitchen, Bath, and More
items.summary: Éclos by Cosentino merges natural beauty and breakthrough technology.
items.text: Courtesy of House Beautiful 3 min read As a homeowner, the two things you tend to expect most from your ideal kitchen countertop are all too often in conflict: You want it to be truly beautiful, to evoke elemental, one-of-a-kind natural stone. But you also want all the resilience, innovation, and eco-friendliness that 21st-century technology can provide. Renowned sustainable-surfaces brand Cosentino has made its reputation bridging those desires, and its Éclos line is both good-looking and good for the planet, simultaneously timeless in appeal and tech-forward in performance. That’s exactly what made it a surface of choice for many of the rooms in the House Beautiful Whole Home in Charleston, South Carolina, an effort of our sister publication. Here’s what makes Éclos the next generation of surfaces: Technology Courtesy of House Beautiful The Whole Home kitchen (also shown at top) is clad in Éclos Legnd. Unlike traditional stone that is cut from a quarry and installed in discrete slabs, Éclos is manufactured from a combination of minerals fused together with a proprietary technology the company calls Inlayr—the name of which gives rise to this new category of high-tech materials: inlayered mineral surfaces. Advanced robotics allow the surfaces to be imbued with sophisticated, three-dimensional veins and patterns that echo those of precious materials pulled from the earth. The result is the unique appearance of prized stone like marble or granite, with a strength that natural stone could never achieve on its own. Durability Courtesy of House Beautiful The powder room countertop was fabricated with Éclos Wonder. So what does that mean once you actually install Éclos in your kitchen or bathroom? For one thing, far less maintenance than might be required of natural materials. Éclos is nonporous, so it never needs to be sealed, much less resealed every six months to a year as, say, you might need to do with a marble counter. And it’s as solid as a rock—wait, more solid than rock: In the kitchen, it can withstand temperatures up to 428°F without showing signs of damage such as stains or cracks. In the bathroom, a knocked-over bottle of nail polish remover is no big deal. Dings, scratches, stains... things of the past. Sustainability Courtesy of House Beautiful A guest bathroom’s double-sink countertop features Éclos Landr. One of Cosentino’s core values as a company is sustainability—the brand devotes a large portion of its research and development resources to discovering new and better ways to employ recycled materials and reduce its overall carbon footprint. In the case of Éclos, Cosentino says the development of the surface involved nearly 30,000 hours of research and testing. The result is its most advanced product yet; Éclos uses zero crystalline silica and a minimum of 50 percent recycled materials (in some products in the new line, that goes up to almost 90 percent). That’s welcome news for designers and homeowners who are committed to incorporating sustainable, socially and environmentally responsible materials and practices into their renovations and new builds. Aesthetics Courtesy of House Beautiful Éclos Wondr gracefully tops a counter in another Whole Home bathroom. Of course, when it comes to creating a space you love and will be happy living with for years, state-of-the-artness only goes so far—style and sophistication are the other half of the equation. It’s a principle Cosentino, which also created designer-beloved modern surfaces like Silestone and Dekton , has doubled down on. The Éclos line is characterized by a carefully curated selection of quietly luxurious colors and textures, each crafted to mirror the richness and tactile appeal of quarry-cut stone. The surfaces have a visual depth and luster that almost make you forget how hardworking they are. For kitchens and bathrooms—anywhere you can envision the sophistication of stone— Éclos can be key to crafting a space that is high-end but never high-maintenance. It's the future of surfaces, delivered right now. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

items.title: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality
items.summary:
Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology […]
