items.text: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality 10 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology with refined design. Together, the two companies are set to bring a new olfactory dimension to the hotel guest experience through an intuitive and refined approach to personalised scent. Through this partnership, Groupe GM will make Compoz Paris’ technology available to its international hospitality network across more than 80 countries, extending access to a distinctive in-room fragrance experience that moves beyond the traditional hotel signature scent and allows each guest to choose an atmosphere that suits their mood or moment. As travellers increasingly look for stays that feel more personal, immersive and attuned to their wellbeing, hotels are embracing new ways to further personalise and enrich the guest experience. By allowing guests to choose the scent atmosphere around them, Compoz Paris adds a more sensory dimension to the stay, creating moments of comfort, relaxation and escape that can be tailored to each individual. Founded by fragrance and innovation enthusiasts Aymeric Wuidart, David Lopez Bonet and Xavier Pourcines, Compoz Paris was launched in response to five years of research and development around how fragrance can be created, personalised and experienced. The brand developed patented technology enabling the real-time blending and diffusion of fragrance composition in one click, bringing together olfactory expertise, digital innovation and intuitive use. Inspired by the natural movement of scent through the air, Compoz Paris technology releases fragrance molecules without heat, water, alcohol or combustion, creating a clean and refined olfactory experience with no lingering scent once diffusion has stopped. Compoz Paris built its original olfactory repertoire around natural-origin essential oils sourced from renowned producing regions around the world, including ylang-ylang from the Comoros, jasmine from Egypt, patchouli from Indonesia, lavender from Provence or bergamot from Calabria. The brand’s collaboration with Groupe GM centres around Le Compositeur, Compoz Paris’ connected fragrance diffuser powered by patented real-time blending technology. The system works with a curated set of five fragrance capsules: Verbena & Musk, Fig & Sandalwood, Jasmine & Neroli, Incense & Spices and Amber & Chai. The experience is designed to be effortless for both guests and hotel teams. Once the set of five capsules is inserted, Le Compositeur is ready to use. Guests simply browse the available scent experiences on the integrated touchscreen and select the atmosphere they prefer. The system automatically blends the capsules to recreate and diffuse one of ten distinctive scent ambiances, from the fresh and uplifting Mist of Sun to the woody warmth and comfort of By the Fireplace or the aromatic escape of Nature Detox. Unlike conventional room fragrance systems that can leave a lingering scent in the air, Le Compositeur is designed for fragrance diffusion without remanence. Guests can enjoy the atmosphere they choose during their stay without imposing the same fragrance on the next guest, making scent a more personal and flexible part of the experience. Its plug-and-play format requires no complex set-up, making it straightforward for hotel teams to introduce into the guest room and intuitive for guests to use throughout their stay. Le Compositeur has been conceived not only as a fragrance diffusion device, but also as an interior object. Elegant, sculptural and carefully designed, it blends naturally into refined hotel interiors rather than appearing as a technical device. Designed by Alnoor Mitha de Bharat, it is available in lacquered, natural wood and leather finishes to complement different interior styles, with bespoke finishes also available for more customised projects. Le Compositeur can be used across hotel rooms and suites, spas, and meeting rooms, with optimal fragrance diffusion indicated for enclosed spaces from approximately 5 m² to 70 m². The exclusive partnership also brings together Groupe GM and Compoz Paris’ shared consideration for product design, sourcing and resource use. Groupe GM’s long-standing commitment to responsible hospitality through its Care About Earth programme aligns closely with Compoz’s sustainability-focused approach. The brand exclusively uses essential oils of natural origin and supports responsible sourcing practices designed to protect both communities and ecosystems. In addition, used Compoz capsules are recovered and processed through the company’s Natucare programme, allowing approximately 80% of materials to be reused in manufacturing while ensuring the remainder is fully recycled. “Our partnership with Compoz Paris opens a new olfactory dimension within the hotel guest experience,” says Laurent Marchand, President of Groupe GM. “By combining Compoz’s patented fragrance technology and refined French design with Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international network, we can offer hotels a genuinely distinctive way to personalise the in-room experience. Guests can choose the scent atmosphere that suits their mood or moment, while hotels benefit from a solution designed to integrate naturally into their guest offering.” Aymeric Wuidart, CEO of Compoz Paris, adds: “When we created Compoz Paris, our ambition was to provide each client with the scents they love, in a fully personalised and natural way. We soon understood that hospitality specialists were looking into enhancing the guest experience and wellness. Today, Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international reach gives us a unique opportunity to bring that vision to life providing all hotels around the world with a scent solution that is intuitive for both guests and hotel teams.” www.groupegm.com bespoke scent compoz pari

items.text: Following its acquisition of Casa Collective, Domes Resorts has announced three new hotel openings in Greece for 2027. Casa Cook Athos will open in northern Greece in Summer 2027, reviving a 1959 Modernist landmark overlooking a sheltered bay on the lesser-known peninsula near the gateway to Mount Athos. Originally designed by one of Greece’s leading architects, Periklis Sakellarios, and now reimagined by Berlin-based studio Vision Alphabet, the 60-key hotel’s architectural character has been preserved through a sensitive restoration with Casa Cook’s distinctive, understated design, and will open a further 45 rooms its second stage. Scheduled to open in Summer 2027 among the pine-covered hills of Kriopigi on Halkidiki’s western peninsula, the adults-only property resembles a relaxed, private summer house centred around the main pool and pool bar area. Art plays a heightened role with contemporary pieces and large murals displayed throughout the hotel, and a collaboration with Brazilian artist Luciano Cian marks the beginning of a wider series of creative partnerships, from original works and live murals to occasional artist residencies. Rooted in the island’s traditional whitewashed cave houses with striking Caldera views, the adults-only boutique hotel brings the brand’s design philosophy to a more personal scale, through tailored experiences, privacy and the flexibility to discover the island at one’s own pace. “The acquisition of Casa Collective represents an important step in our growth strategy, allowing us to expand our lifestyle ecosystem while building on the distinct identities of Casa Cook and Cook’s Club,” saidsaysDr. George P. Spanos, CEO of Domes Resorts and Chairman of Casa Collective. “These three openings in hotels we own showcase how much we believe in the soul and the character of these brands.” Remo Masala, Founder of Casa Collective and Vision Alphabet, adds: “As Casa Collective grows, we’re building on our deeper understanding of our guests to create meaningful reasons to return, with experiences that respect the individual character of each brand and destination.” casa collective Casa Cook Domes Resorts europe expansion Greece Related Posts 24 January 2025 Casa Cook to launch first mountain retreat 29 March 2023 Domes announces further Greek expansion 6 December 2021 Domes Resorts to expand internationally

items.title: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings
items.summary:
As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow […] 
 The post  Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings 5 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow and bioclimatic design can improve guest comfort while reducing energy consumption. How are changing guest expectations reshaping environmental comfort in hospitality? Rising temperatures and increasingly demanding guest expectations are making thermal comfort a strategic priority for hospitality operators. At the same time, rising energy costs are putting pressure on operating margins. The challenge is to create consistently comfortable environments without allowing energy consumption to escalate. This requires a more intelligent approach to managing temperature, airflow and insulation. What is bioclimatic architecture, and why is it so important for hotels and residences? Bioclimatic architecture considers the relationship between a building, its local climate and the people who use it. In hospitality, this means combining effective insulation, natural or mechanical ventilation and efficient heating and cooling systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning. By designing for climate from the outset, hotels can improve thermal comfort, reduce energy demand and create spaces that feel naturally comfortable while preserving their architectural identity. How can climate and airflow enhance the guest experience? Comfort is not determined by air temperature alone. Air movement influences how the body perceives heat, allowing guests to feel comfortable at higher thermostat settings. By combining air conditioning with well-designed ventilation, hotels can create a more balanced and pleasant indoor climate, while reducing energy consumption. The result is an environment that feels better, operates more efficiently and supports a more enjoyable guest experience. How do your solutions help hotels reduce energy use without compromising comfort? The key is to move beyond the assumption that lower temperatures automatically mean greater comfort. Setting air conditioning to 20°C, for example, can significantly increase energy consumption without necessarily delivering a better guest experience. By combining efficient ceiling fans with air conditioning, hotels can maintain comfort at higher thermostat settings and reduce cooling energy consumption. Based on results reported by our clients, this approach can deliver energy savings of 30–45%, depending on the building, climate and operating conditions. Our objective is to make comfort measurable, efficient and easier to manage. Can you share a hospitality project that demonstrates the impact of your approach? One Ibiza Suites is a good example of how a considered combination of building performance and airflow can transform the guest experience. By improving roof insulation and introducing ceiling fans in the lobby and restaurant, the hotel enhanced thermal comfort in key shared spaces. The combined intervention achieved a reduction in perceived temperature of approximately 4°C, demonstrating that comfort can be improved without relying exclusively on more intensive air conditioning. What’s next for Magnovent? Our next step is to help hospitality operators reduce their reliance on air conditioning, in both summer and winter, with a target of reducing energy consumption by an average of 30%. Through increasingly sophisticated control systems, we aim to manage airflow, heating and cooling as an integrated solution, helping operators maintain their desired level of perceived comfort while optimising energy use. Ultimately, we want to move the industry towards a more intelligent understanding of temperature: one in which buildings are designed and operated around how people actually experience comfort, rather than simply the number displayed on a thermostat. www.magnovent.eu air conditioning bioclimatic design climate change guest comfort magnovent Related Posts 19 September 2023 Inside FOH’s luxury hospitality solutions 22 June 2023 Madera talks timber, bespoke design and hospitality interiors 5 December 2019 Cameron Design House’s Inari chandelier designed for hospitality settings

items.title: Thompson Hotels lands in Rome
items.summary:
Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, […] 
 The post  Thompson Hotels lands in Rome  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, marking the brand’s debut in Italy . Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view – have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. Thompson Rome’s 69 guestrooms and suites take cues from the character of a contemporary Roman residence, pairing warm natural materials with custom furnishings and understated details. With 19 suites, nearly one-third of the hotel’s accommodation offering, guests can choose from Junior Suites, Suites with patios or terraces, and the 104-square-metre Thompson Suite with 80-square-metre private terrace. Designed as a counterpoint to the energy of the city outside, the rooms feel residential and refined, with select accommodations offering views across Rome’s historic rooftops and landmarks. Several rooms feature balconies overlooking Via delle Botteghe Oscure, while select rooms offer private patios facing Rome’s historic buildings. Thompson Rome’s art programme, creates a dialogue between the history of the site and contemporary art. The collection brings together works by artists associated with the Scuola Romana and the Scuola di Piazza del Popolo, alongside contemporary artists whose practices reflect Rome’s longstanding cultural openness and international influences including Francesco Del Drago, Giangaetano Patanè, and Guido Strazza. Presented throughout the hotel’s public spaces and guestrooms, the artworks are an integral part of the guest experience, connecting the memory of the site with the creativity of Rome today. A rotating artist-in-residence programme will further extend Thompson Rome’s connection to the city’s creative community through exhibitions, conversations and other cultural programming. Three distinct food and beverage venues carry Thompson Rome from morning espresso and leisurely lunches through aperitivo, dinner and drinks above the city. At Lyve Restaurant, Executive Chef Fabio Fioravanti brings a contemporary Mediterranean approach to ingredients and traditions from the Italian coast and across the region. Seafood is central to the menu, with Mediterranean fish and shellfish alongside dishes that draw on bouillabaisse, rockfish broths, wild coastal herbs and rouille, reworked with a lighter touch while preserving the depth and character of the originals. The same attention extends to the pastry kitchen, where precise technique and contrasting flavours and textures shape the dessert menu. A native of Ostia, Fioravanti brings more than two decades of international experience, including time with the Alain Ducasse group and at the three-Michelin-starred Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse at the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo. At Lyve, that technical precision carries through a dining experience that is refined yet relaxed, with the quality of the ingredients and clarity of the cooking taking centre stage. Above the hotel, Lyve Rooftop pairs views across Rome with cocktails, Italian aperitivi and a menu designed for sharing. The Lobby Lounge offers the hotel’s most casual gathering place throughout the day, from coffee and light fare to aperitivo and cocktails. The hotel will extend the guest experience through a year-round programme shaped by Rome’s culinary, artistic and creative communities. Experiences will range from culinary workshops and guided tastings to Empire of Light, a photography-led experience from the hotel’s seventh floor that invites guests to discover Rome from above. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” says Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt . “The building, the neighbourhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travellers want to discover and Romans want to come back to.” architecture europe hotel design hyatt interior design italy rome thompson hotels Related Posts 14 June 2023 Thompson Hotels heading to Rome 21 February 2022 Design Hotels welcomes four new members 9 August 2021 Thompson Hotels arrives in Savannah

items.text: Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The 115-key hotel will include a collection of suites with private pools, culminating in a 600m 2 Capella Suite conceived as a residential-style retreat. Set along one of Jumeirah’s most desired shorelines, Capella Dubai will open within the 210-acre waterfront destination by H&H. Conceived as a first-of-its-kind, design-driven destination, the Dubai Peninsula brings together hotel brands and private residences, complemented by dining, retail, a superyacht marina, a kilometre of private beach and over two million square feet of botanical gardens. Developed by H&H and designed by Denniston , the hotel will feature five social venues from the lobby lounge and The Living Room to the signature restaurant. Above it all, the rooftop will be home to a specialty restaurant and destination bar, inviting guests to dine against the Dubai skyline. Stretching nearly 70m across the rooftop, the pool will offer a tranquil retreat above the city, alongside single and double cabanas. A family pool will also feature at beach level. Capella Wellness will offer a holistic approach to wellbeing, encompassing the Auriga Spa, a Fitness Centre and Mind Body Studio, as well as an outdoor fitness area. Inspired by the restorative rhythms of the moon, Auriga Spa will feature male and female treatment rooms, a co-ed suite and VIP suite, alongside a hammam, hydrotherapy circuit pool, two biohacking facilities and grooming services. Dedicated relaxation lounges will offer quiet spaces to pause before and after treatments. For celebrations and gatherings, Capella Dubai will offer a spacious ballroom with a pre-function lounge, complemented by two meeting rooms, a VIP Majlis and an outdoor event lawn. “As Capella grows beyond Asia Pacific into the Middle East and Europe, we are entering an important new chapter for the brand,” says Roland Fasel, President, Capella Hotel Group. “The Middle East shares our appreciation for craftsmanship, culture and exceptional service, making it a natural home for Capella. Capella has always been deliberately selective about where it goes, choosing destinations where we believe we can create something meaningful and distinctive. “At Dubai Peninsula, our partnership with H&H is the foundation for all that we are building. They share our vision for the intimate, highly personalised experience Capella is known for, one that connects guests more deeply with Dubai, its culture and its people. With the opening of Capella Dubai in 2030, we will further establish our presence in one of the region’s most compelling cities, while remaining true to the hospitality that defines Capella.” Shahab Lutfi, Chairman, H&H adds: “Dubai Peninsula is conceived as a destination with a distinct identity, bringing together some of the world’s most renowned hospitality brands, exceptional residences and a unique waterfront setting. Capella brings a different dimension to this vision through its intimate, highly personalised approach to hospitality. We see a strong alignment between Capella’s emphasis on individual experiences and sense of place and our ambition to create a destination that offers more than exceptional design and location. Capella Dubai will introduce a more intimate, service-led hospitality experience to the city’s resort landscape, adding depth and character to the overall offering. “Working alongside Denniston, we are bringing hospitality, architecture and landscape together from the outset, ensuring that each responds to the setting and contributes to a coherent vision. For us, the strength of Dubai Peninsula lies in the way its different elements come together, from its shoreline and central park to its collection of hospitality and residential offerings. Capella’s distinctive character will be an important part of that mix, shaping a destination that feels considered, cohesive and different.” capella capella dubai Denniston dubai dubai peninsula H&H Jumeirah Related Posts 27 August 2025 Mandarin Oriental to open second Dubai outpost 11 October 2024 Ennismore’s Delano lands in Dubai 9 December 2009 Dusit Princess debuts in Dubai

items.title: Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel
items.summary:
The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the […] 
 The post  Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the Milan-based architecture and interior design studio led by Federico Spagnulo, Alessandra Carbone and Andrea Spagnulo. Encompassing the hotel’s 317 guest rooms, public areas and event spaces, the project establishes a contemporary architectural language that draws on the property’s history and its longstanding relationship with the city. The project is guided by a principle of architectural continuity, expressed through a system of geometries, proportions and materials that evolves across the interiors according to their scale and function. The grid emerges as a recurring design element, first appearing in the full-height shelving that structures the public areas before becoming a graphic motif reinterpreted in handwoven rugs and textiles. As it shifts in scale and material, its precise geometry takes on a softer, more tactile expression. In the communal areas, the design creates a sequence of spaces with different degrees of openness and intimacy. Bespoke furnishings define the various areas while maintaining visual continuity, whereas the use of wood introduces a warm, tactile element that balances the rigour of the geometry. The predominantly neutral colour palette is punctuated by carefully chosen colour accents, provided by upholstered furniture and rugs, which help to characterise the spaces and create different atmospheres. The same attention to proportion and the guest experience informs the renovation of the 317 guest rooms, where clean lines, natural finishes and contemporary furnishings create interiors conceived around comfort and functionality. The design responds to the requirements of international hospitality, balancing practical considerations with material quality and a distinctive visual identity. From the organisation of the spaces to the design of the furnishings and the lighting scheme, the project embodies Spagnulo & Partners’ bespoke approach, rooted in the relationship between architecture, materials and the quality of living. The result is a hotel that reinvents its character through a restrained design language, capable of interpreting the demands of contemporary hospitality whilst maintaining a connection with its history. hotel renovation italy Marriott milan renovation Spagnulo & Partners Related Posts 27 September 2023 Marriott International launches new midscale brand 9 May 2023 W Hotels to debut in Milan 27 July 2015 First-ever Marriott Hotel in Makkah

 The post  Hilton opens Europe’s first Outset Collection hotel  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hilton has announced the opening of Casa Verbena Madrid, Outset Collection by Hilton, an intimate 45-room hotel on Calle de Preciados in the heart of the capital. Marking the first Outset Collection hotel in Europe, the hotel features interiors by Madrid-born designer Lorenzo Castillo, complemented by views across the city’s rooftops. Casa Verbena Madrid takes its name from the traditional Spanish verbena: a lively neighbourhood celebration that brings people together through food, music and shared traditions. The hotel also draws on costumbrismo, the Spanish artistic tradition of depicting local customs, characters and daily rituals, looking beyond the capital’s landmarks to the cafés, streets and squares that shape life for Madrileños. The hotel’s interiors reflect a distinctly local perspective on the city. Costumbrismo-inspired artwork, warm materials, fluted glass, brass finishes and layered textures reference Madrid’s architectural and cultural heritage in a contemporary way. Many guestrooms look onto Preciados street and its typical Madrid façades, while Preciados Rooms open onto terraces with views across the city’s rooftops and towards the Royal Palace. “Casa Verbena Madrid offers a fresh perspective on the capital, whether guests are discovering it for the first time or returning to experience it differently,” says Álvaro Mazaheri, Managing Director, Arte Hoteles. “From a breakfast inspired by local favourites to recommendations we would share with friends, we want each stay to reveal more of the Madrid that lies beyond its best-known sights.” Elizabeth Scruggs, Brand Leader, Outset Collection by Hilton, also comments: “Casa Verbena Madrid represents the essence of Outset Collection, offering guests a stay that feels deeply connected to the destination. As our first hotel in Europe, it sets the tone for how we envision the collection growing around the world: through independent hotels with compelling stories, strong local identities and a genuine sense of discovery. With more than 100 hotels under development globally, we are building a collection of individual hotels that invite travellers to experience a destination through a more personal lens, all with the benefits of Hilton.” David Kelly, senior vice president, Continental Europe, Hilton, concludes: “Madrid is a special destination for Hilton, and in recent years we’ve broadened our presence in the city with distinctive brands and properties designed to meet different traveller needs. Casa Verbena Madrid builds on that story as the European debut of Outset Collection by Hilton. Full of character and with a strong sense of place, the hotel reflects the creativity and energy of Madrid. We’re delighted to welcome the hotel to our growing portfolio of collection properties across Europe.” europe hilton lorenzo castillo madrid outset collection spain Related Posts 24 June 2024 Curio Collection by Hilton debuts in Croatia 17 May 2024 NH Collection debuts in Finland 11 May 2021 Hilton debuts Tapestry Collection in mainland China

items.title: First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos
items.summary:
Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, […] 
 The post  First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, the property will mark the first Hyatt hotel in Turks & Caicos and the first Caribbean island resort for the Andaz brand. The 132-key resort is designed by architecture by RAD Architecture with interiors by Modus Operandi in collaboration with Hyatt. Gently curving with the coastline, the west-facing property will offer a sunset perspective at every touchpoint. Set directly on the white sands of Grace Bay and steps from Bight Reef within Princess Alexandra National Park, Andaz Turks & Caicos will comprise 59 hotel rooms and 73 branded residences, also available for stays, with 10 penthouses featuring their very own rooftop plunge pools. The resort will feature three swimming pools, the 7,000ft 2 Runa Spa & Wellness, four dining concepts, a dedicated Kids Club, tennis and pickleball courts, in addition to ample weddings and event space. The structural narrative of Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay will unfold around an arrival sequence that takes cues from the island’s early history, when visitors arrived exclusively by boat. The entrance will recreate this experience, translating the pier into a long, immersive progression toward Grace Bay. Guests will move along a wood-lined corridor whose framing references the skeleton of an overturned boat. Set 15ft above the sea, the vantage point will immediately give the feeling of floating over the water as panoramic ocean views open up. That connection will continue throughout the interiors, where local stone and rich, natural materials add warmth while shifting hues of blues draw the surrounding waters indoors. The guestrooms’ expansive views and indoor-outdoor living will be balanced by a sense of privacy. Teak and hardwoods, richly textured fabrics and streams of natural light filtering into the bathrooms will create a tactile warmth, while artwork by Caribbean artists and pops of colour will bring the island’s character indoors. A traditional Turks & Caicos dress, distinguished by its colourful stripes representing the individual islands, will serve as a cultural touchpoint for the interiors. The striped pattern is reinterpreted in the wooden headboards, translating a recognisable element of local dress into a subtle design detail. In addition to 59 standard guestrooms, the 73 branded residences include studios as well as one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom layouts, with the largest four-bedroom residences spanning up to 8,336ft 2 of indoor and outdoor space. Each residence will offer a balcony or terrace, indoor-outdoor living spaces and a Bosch-equipped kitchen. Natural woods, textured fabrics and contemporary furnishings are paired with handcrafted pieces and Caribbean-inspired graphics, creating a warm, layered interior palette. Ten penthouses will feature private rooftop plunge pools, while select residences offer private pools. Anchoring the resort’s social scene, the lobby bar is inspired by the colourful homes found throughout the Caribbean. Saturated hues, natural materials and an open-air setting will create a relaxed, residential feel, while the bar’s expansive setting will make the landscape part of the backdrop. As one of Grace Bay’s only indoor-outdoor oceanfront restaurants, Tamarà’s interiors will feature deep bottle-green tile to evoke the lushness of a tropical forest, balanced by limestone tiling and natural materials. A fishnet-inspired canopy will shade the expansive outdoor terrace, where a central tree will be framed by cascading lights that echo the movement of leaves overhead. Baie will unfold across two levels beside the pool, with the upper level offering a lounge-like perch above the water. The laidback sanctuary will serve as a casual pool bar by day, shifting into a more refined setting with sunset rituals in the evening. Adjacent to the lobby, Palmette will blur the line between neighbourhood café and marketplace, pairing daytime fare with a considered edit of locally made goods including baskets, clothing, tableware, candles and other provisions. The coastline also informs Runa Spa & Wellness, where the calm of Grace Bay’s reef-protected shallows finds expression across natural woods, neutral tones and sculptural forms punctuated by pops of colour that reflect the bay’s shifting hues of blue. The resort’s fitness centre will complement the spa with Life Fitness equipment throughout. items.title: a giant circle frames NIKO’s timber guesthouse and tiny curved sauna in japan
items.summary:
NIKO design studio's 'marumi house' in japan features a giant circular facade opening, exposed cedar logs, and a tiny sauna. 
 The post  a giant circle frames NIKO’s timber guesthouse and tiny curved sauna in japan  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] marumi house and its sculptural sauna NIKO Design Studio has completed Umino Marumi, a two-story wooden guesthouse on a hillside overlooking the Pacific coast of Chiba, Japan . With its enormous circular facade opening and exposed timber structure, the house makes an unusual addition to the surrounding residential neighborhood. In the garden, a much smaller companion building takes shape as a sauna hut, its curved roof designed to accommodate the trees growing around it. Completed in 2025, Marumi was conceived as a second home where the owners could gather with family and friends, while also creating a welcoming presence within the local community. The architects approached this ambition through an engawa, the traditional Japanese veranda, transforming it into a series of staggered outdoor platforms that climb through the house and connect to the upper floor. image courtesy NIKO Design Studio a giant circular opening frames the stepped veranda The Marumi House’s most recognizable feature is the enormous circular opening cut into its dark facade, revealing a network of timber columns and raised walkways beneath the pitched roof. Around one-third of the covered building is dedicated to the semi-outdoor engawa, where visitors can sit, gather, or move between levels without entering the enclosed rooms. With this layout, the architects at NIKO Design Studio give the house an unusually open relationship with its surroundings. From outside, the veranda offers glimpses of people moving through the timber structure, while its various levels accommodate both intimate gatherings and larger groups. The circular opening brings these activities into view, turning the facade into an inhabited space that faces the neighborhood. timber flooring extends through the open-plan interior and onto the covered terrace thick cedar logs and traditional joinery shape marumi house NIKO Design Studio worked with substantial cedar logs measuring approximately 400 millimeters in diameter, assembling the structural frame using traditional kanuki joinery. Horizontal timber members pass through openings in the round columns, creating a durable structure that retains the natural geometry of the wood. The holes were cut using chainsaws, following an approach suggested by the carpenters and inspired by forestry techniques. The same hands-on approach extends into the landscape. To address the sloping site, a stone retaining wall was assembled during a two-day workshop using nozumi, a traditional stone-stacking technique. The rough stonework sits alongside the large timber structure, which brings a sense of craftsmanship to a building designed for communal use. curved brick steps lead toward the bathroom and its sunken bathtub a tiny sauna hut curves around a neighboring palm tree Beyond the main house, the architects faced a different challenge when designing a freestanding sauna for the garden. The owners initially wanted a cabin for three or four people, but commercially available models appeared surprisingly bulky when placed within a model of the site. Looking more closely at the surrounding landscape, the team noticed a neighboring palm tree extending over the property boundary. Its continued growth became the starting point for the sauna’s unusual curved roof. Working with carpenter Murakami of Murakami Carpentry Workshop, the architects sourced naturally bent timber from trees that had grown along a hillside. These curved members formed the roof structure, allowing its profile to rise and dip around the surrounding vegetation. When the timber arrived thicker and longer than anticipated, the team decided to retain the excess length, leaving the beams projecting beyond the roofline. The unexpected detail gives the small building much of its character. the freestanding sauna hut features a sweeping curved roof and arched wooden doorway five square meters accommodate up to six people Despite its expressive roof, the sauna occupies remarkably little ground. Its foundation measures just two by two meters, with a total floor area of five square meters including the stepped portion. Inside, timber-lined surfaces and a tall ceiling make the small space feel surprisingly generous. Although originally intended for three or four bathers, the completed sauna can accommodate five or six people. The hut combines electric and wood-fired heating, while a skylight brings daylight into the compact interior. It connects with the surrounding terrace and the house’s bathroom, which can be a cold bath during sauna sessions. Marumi and its miniature companion together explore two scales of wooden architecture, with one opening itself toward the neighborhood and the other adjusting its form to the trees already growing in the garden. the sauna’s roof rises and dips around the surrounding vegetation naturally curved timber beams meet beneath a skylight in the sauna’s roof sunlight enters through the skylight, illuminating the sauna’s timber-lined interior and tiered benches thick cedar columns frame the elevated veranda and views of the surrounding neighborhood project info: name: Marumi architect: Niko Design Studio | @niko_designstudio_staff location: Chiba Prefecture, Japan construction: Murakami Carpentry Workshop structural engineering: Osajima Architectural Structural Design Office photography: © Toshihiro Bojima, with snapshots by Takeshi Nishikubo Custom Wall Mural - Dinaric MARTINA BANOZIC TEXTILES croatia from $ 89 18k Gold 'Chubby Babies' Studs Carla Morrison Fine Jewelry US $ 1280 Cauny x Ando Cauny portugal $ 318 Knit necklace, 3D printed statement necklace monocircus japan $ 162 V / envelope and key holder is an elegant bill organizer ChiHong taiwan $ 55 Shelf GRID with doors RADIS FURNITURE estonia from $ 899 Gradient Watch – A Timepiece of Shifting Patterns and Minimal Elegance Lawa Design denmark $ 239 Custom Wall Mural - Ombre MARTINA BANOZIC TEXTILES croatia from $ 89 Magnetic Vase - Unique Table Centerpiece | Set

items.title: balzar arquitectos pairs 19th-century modernist interiors with wabi-sabi materiality in valencia apartment renovation
items.summary:
the restoration of the 1890 residence balances original nolla mosaics, wrought iron, and plaster moldings with lime wash, travertine, and curated contemporary furnishings. 
 The post  balzar arquitectos pairs 19th-century modernist interiors with wabi-sabi materiality in valencia apartment renovation  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] BALZAR ARQUITECTOS RESTORES 1890S RESIDENCE IN HISTORIC VALENCIA Located in the historic center of Valencia, Spain , Ciutat Vella Apartment is an interior renovation by Balzar Arquitectos set within an 1890 residential building. Sited in an urban context characterized by layered historical traces, the project approaches preservation not as a static museum display, but as an active framework for contemporary domestic life. Original architectural elements, including geometric Nolla mosaic tile floors, wrought ironwork, decorative ceiling moldings, solid timber doors, and surviving polychrome wall fragments, were retained and restored to guide the layout and spatial rhythm. all images ©David Zarzoso RESTORED MOSAICS AND LIME PLASTER ANCHOR WABI-SABI MATERIALITY Guided by a wabi-sabi philosophy prioritizing material patina and natural imperfection, the intervention by Balzar Architectural Studio introduces a restrained palette of lime plaster, unfilled travertine, solid wood, linen, and wool. Surface textures take precedence over color, complemented by diffused daylight filtering through historic apertures. The interior blends vintage pieces sourced from Nekonato Gallery with artworks from CLC Arte, custom site-specific joinery by Balzar Arquitectos, and contemporary furnishings, including seating by New Works and luminaires by Venicem, establishing a balanced conversation between 19th-century craft and modern minimalism. items.text: TC 177/78- João Mendes Ribeiro Published on November 10, 2026 This double issue brings together, across 406 pages, twenty-five years of work by the Portuguese architect João Mendes Ribeiro (Coimbra, 1960) through eighteen works built in Portugal and Spain between 2000 and 2026. Trained in Porto and assistant to Fernando Távora in Coimbra during the 1990s, Mendes Ribeiro has developed a singular career in which architecture, theatre set design and the design of objects and interiors feed into one another. The result is an architecture that tends towards the essential, attentive to the truth of materials and to the scale of the body, and that understands construction as a precise and reversible assembly. His work has received, among others, the FAD, BIAU, RIBA International Excellence and Secil Architecture awards. A large part of the selection is devoted to intervention in heritage buildings, a field in which the studio is a point of reference: the Centre for Visual Arts in the former Colégio das Artes in Coimbra, the Casa da Escrita, the cloister of Lorvão Monastery, the São Pedro do Sul Roman Baths, the Palace of the Counts of Ourém and the old Aveiro train station. These are works in which the aim is not to leave a contemporary mark, but to re-inhabit what already exists. Alongside them are single-family houses (Fonte Boa, Chamusca da Beira, the Chestnut House, Arruda dos Vinhos and the house in Vilar de Astrés, Ourense, his only work in Spain), small-scale pieces such as the Tea House at Montemor-o-Velho Castle, and public buildings such as Arquipélago in the Azores and the Torre de Palma Wine Hotel.

items.title: Minimal Maximum / Stempel & Tesar Architekti
items.summary: This minimalist family home is the architect's own house—a personal manifesto in which more than two decades of designing residential architecture for others is condensed into a single, highly concentrated response to a demanding urban plot in  Prague . Every centimetre became a deliberate decision, resulting in a "minimal maximum"—a house without corridors, organised around a central dining space that rises four metres and connects three floors through a staggered half-level system.

items.title: Oshinowo Studio Completes Sierra Leone Carrier Corps Memorial in Freetown
items.summary: The  Commonwealth  War Graves Commission (CWGC) has unveiled a new memorial in Freetown,  Sierra Leone , honoring more than 900 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps who died in the First and Second World Wars. Designed by Lagos-based  Oshinówò Studio , the intervention was unveiled on November 7 and commemorates the Carrier Corps individually by name for the first time.  The design was first revealed in May 2025.
items.text: Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © Oshinówò Studio - Tolu Sanusi Written by Antonia Piñeiro Published on November 10, 2026 The Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) has unveiled a new memorial in Freetown, Sierra Leone , honoring more than 900 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps who died in the First and Second World Wars. Designed by Lagos-based Oshinówò Studio , the intervention was unveiled on November 7 and commemorates the Carrier Corps individually by name for the first time. The design was first revealed in May 2025. + 9 Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © Oshinówò Studio - Tolu Sanusi The original Freetown Memorial , designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, was unveiled in 1931. It serves as Sierra Leone's national memorial for those who died in the World Wars and have no known grave. Its bronze panels record the names of African soldiers from the West African Regiment, the Sierra Leone Battalion of the West African Frontier Force and the Royal Engineers Inland Water Transport. Members of the Carrier Corps, however, were not named individually and were commemorated numerically. Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © Oshinówò Studio - Tolu Sanusi Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © CWGC - Lansana Mansaray The new intervention consists of a prism of structural glass permanently integrated onto the Lutyens memorial. Four structural glass fins, reaching 8.4 meters in height, are etched with the names of the fallen, and the structure incorporates 4,000 kilograms of glass. The edges of the glass are lit, and a laser beacon will emit a pillar of light into the night sky on significant days of commemoration in Sierra Leone , visible within a five-kilometer radius across Freetown. Related Article Structures of Memory: 5 Unbuilt Projects on Heritage from the ArchDaily Community The project was developed with the CWGC over 16 months by engineers, glass designers, laser consultants and construction partners from Nigeria, the Netherlands, Spain, Sierra Leone and the UK. CWGC stonemasons and bronze specialists also restored the original base, uplifting the bronze panels and renewing the stonework. The names are accompanied by an epitaph in Krio and English by poets Nii Ayikwei Parkes and Julianknxx, which reads: "from today you will be carried, you are borne, now and ever." Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © CWGC - Lansana Mansaray Oshinówò Studio also designed four marker memorials in provinces from which carriers were raised. These satellite sites follow the language of the Freetown Memorial and result from a co-design process that determines the places, people and events to be memorialized, a new approach for the CWGC. The project is accompanied by a register of names, museum partnerships and educational programs for schools. The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts. The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens' existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served. There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today. — Tosin Oshinówò Oshinówò Studio's Freetown memorial honouring Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. Image © CWGC - Lansana Mansaray Recent news from Africa includes the completion of the new African Futures Institute (AFI) headquarters in Accra, Ghana , transforming a former tile warehouse into a center for architectural education, research, exhibitions and public programs. The Museum of Modern Art in New York is hosting an exhibition called "Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa" until January 2, 2027, examining African modern architecture in the context of political independence in the region. Studio NEiDA recently revealed its designs for The Falcon Cinema , a community art center dedicated to African film in Berekuso, Ghana.

items.title: Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser
items.summary: For its 25th anniversary, Houston Center for Contemporary Craft partnered with Steinbeisser for an experimental dinner where artist-made tableware challenged the conventions of dining
items.text: Art Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser Each month, TJ Girard explores the intersection of food and design, from what we eat to how it’s made, presented, and experienced, in her Taste column. 11.06.26 | By TJ Girard Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Steinbeisser's Experimental Gastronomy dinner at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft brought together artist-made tableware and plant-based cuisine to celebrate the institution's 25th anniversary. Photography by Kerrisa Treanor; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/11 Photos Ceramic bowls by artist Adam Knoche, crafted from locally foraged Texas clays and finished with richly textured glazes. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 2/11 Photos Guests hold monumental hand-carved spoons by British artist Mark Reddy. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 3/11 Photos Gokkal Cups by South Korean artist Heejoo Kim, with Mark Reddy’s monumental hand-carved wooden Standing Spoons. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 4/11 Photos Utensilia spoons by Italian artist Lisa Marcolongo. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 5/11 Photos A guest uses Lisa Marcolongo’s Utensilia spoon. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 6/11 Photos CLOCKWISE FROM LEFT: A ceramic carafe by Adam Knoche, made from foraged Texas clays and filled with roasted mushroom broth; a carved maple wood ottchil lacquer spoon by Kyungwon Hwang; a ceramic sauce bowl by Knoche, incorporating Galveston seashells into locally foraged clay; and Knoche’s Exploding Plate. Photography by Kerrisa Treanor; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 7/11 Photos Chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm of Nicosi plate the second course. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 8/11 Photos The first course featured nixtamalized squash, Koshihikari rice, kosho, and carrot, served on Sustenance #1 by Jaydan Moore, a sculptural platter assembled from reclaimed antique silver-plated servingware. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 9/11 Photos Guests interact with 'Singing Buoys,' an interactive sonic installation by artist Bohyun Yoon, created for the amuse-bouche at the Steinbeisser dinner. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 10/11 Photos Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s 25th-anniversary experimental dinner in collaboration with Steinbeisser. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. 11/11 Photos Steinbeisser's Experimental Gastronomy dinner at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft brought together artist-made tableware and plant-based cuisine to celebrate the institution's 25th anniversary. Photography by Kerrisa Treanor; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. I’ve covered Steinbeisser in this column before, and the Amsterdam studio’s approach to rethinking objects and how we use them continues to hold my interest. Its latest chapter took place on Oct. 23 at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft (HCCC) , where 50 guests sat together at a single long table in the main gallery, surrounded by the exhibition A Material Inheritance , to celebrate the institution’s 25th anniversary. Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s 25th-anniversary experimental dinner in collaboration with Steinbeisser. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Founded in 2009 by Jouw Wijnsma and Martin Kullik, Steinbeisser launched its Experimental Gastronomy initiative in 2012, pairing chefs and artists for one-of-a-kind dinners worldwide. This was its first in Texas and one of the few held in the U.S. The menu was entirely plant-based and seasonal, with produce from regional farms that use organic and biodynamic growing practices. The cooking came from two Michelin-starred restaurants: Tatemó in Houston and Nicosi in San Antonio. The evening opened with Bohyun Yoon’s Singing Buoys , an interactive work in which guests used handheld remotes to steer blown-glass vessels carrying small bites across a water table. When the vessels collided, they rang like bells. Guests interact with ‘Singing Buoys,’ an interactive sonic installation by artist Bohyun Yoon, created for the amuse-bouche at the Steinbeisser dinner. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. The dinner itself kept the focus on the objects. Tatemó’s first course of nixtamalized squash, rice, kosho, and carrot came on Jaydan Moore’s Sustenance #1, a platter assembled from salvaged antique silver-plated serving pieces. The first course featured nixtamalized squash, Koshihikari rice, kosho, and carrot, served on Sustenance #1 by Jaydan Moore, a sculptural platter assembled from reclaimed antique silver-plated servingware. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Nicosi’s Kudzumochi Tamal, with pumpkin juice, mushroom, masa foam, hoja santa, and gold leaf, was prepared by chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm. Chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm of Nicosi plate the second course. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. The course arrived on Adam Knoche’s Exploding Plate, made from crushed basalt clay pressed and fired at 2,250 degrees Fahrenheit to intentionally fracture, alongside his carafe and sauce bowl made from foraged Texas clay and Galveston shells. items.text: Delano London to open early 2027 • Hotel Designs Delano London to open early 2027 WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 10, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Delano London to open early 2027 Overlooking Kensington Gardens and Hyde Park, among the grand Victorian buildings and embassies of one of London’s most distinguished neighbourhoods, Delano London marks a new chapter for the celebrated hotel brand, opening early 2027… Drawing on a legacy that spans Miami, Dubai and Paris, the 67 room and suite hotel brings Delano’s distinctive sensibility for magnetic nightlife, story-led dining and innovative wellness to the capital. Across five floors, more than half of the rooms will be suites, with 14 offering prime views across Hyde Park. Designed by Archer Humphryes Architects , Delano London brings the spirit of Delano Miami Beach into a distinctly West London setting. Residential interiors and subtly theatrical details create an atmosphere of discovery. Image credit: Delano London / Ennismore At the heart of the hotel’s dining experience is Lana Lusa, designed by Pirajean Lees and brought to London for the first time by internationally acclaimed hospitality group Paris Society. Created by founder Jessica Viveiro Kassim, the concept celebrates the warmth and conviviality of Mediterranean hospitality. Within the hotel sits a cocktail destination Rose Bar which brings Delano’s iconic after-dark spirit to the city, reimagining the glamour of its legendary Miami Beach counterpart. Within the space, the Rose Bar Lounge and the Zodiac Room offer more intimate settings for late-night revelry. The Source by Delano will offer a fresh approach to wellness, centred around restorative and rejuvenating movement and longevity. Contrast therapy, treatment spaces and state-of-the-art facilities will sit alongside a changing roster of leading practitioners, residencies and collaborations with some of the world’s most exciting names in wellness. Image credit: Delano London / Ennismore London-based art consultancy Cramer & Bell have curated an original collection, celebrating British art alongside established international artists. Highlights include South African artist Kimathi Mafafo,and London-based artists Isaac Andrews, Hormazd Narielwalla, and Gergei Erdei. Completing the experience, Delano Members Club brings together a global community of creative, accomplished and curious minds. Members will have access to a programme of experiences, partnerships and privileges extending beyond the hotel, both locally and internationally. ‘Delano Beyond’, a global programme, will provide members with bespoke travel experiences. “Delano has always been about creating a feeling’’ commented Ben Pundole, Chief Brand Officer for Delano Hotels, ‘’Bringing the brand to London feels particularly special because this is my home city with such a rich and varied cultural history. Delano London will be a space for discovery, somewhere you might strike up a conversation at Rose Bar with someone you’d never ordinarily meet, encounter a work by an emerging artist, or simply settle into an atmosphere that transports you beyond the bustle of the city outside. It’s a place for those who look for unique experiences.” Main image credit: Delano London / Ennismore You might also like Ennismore signs Delano Puglia News / 05.10.2026 The Hoxton set to make its Middle East debut in Dubai News / 11.09.2026 Gleneagles unveils its most glamorous residence yet Hotel Design / 07.09.2026 SPACE: the latest issue In video Latest articles Delano London to open early 2027 10.11.2026 Case study: Hamilton brings timeless detail to Parade Hotel Bath 10.11.2026 Rosewood Residences Bangkok to rise above Lumphini Park 10.11.2026 Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets 09.11.2026 Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 09.11.2026 Receive our newsletter here Recommended suppliers Latest from the DESIGN POD Episode 50: Grant Woodrow – into the Wilderness 03.06.2025 Episode 49: Fettle, the transatlantic design studio with Andy Goodwin and Tom Parker 14.03.2025 Episode 48: Redesigning Historic Buildings with Tom Thorogood 10.01.2025 Episode 47: Form and Function with Nick Hickson 20.12.2024 Episode 46: 40 Years in the Making – David Collins Studio with Lewis Taylor 22.11.2024 Recommended suppliers Upcoming events The Brit List Awards 5th November, 2026 Hotel Summit 22nd April, 2027 This website uses cookies to improve your experience. items.text: Case study: Hamilton brings timeless detail to Parade Hotel Bath • Hotel Designs Case study: Hamilton brings timeless detail to Parade Hotel Bath WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 10, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Case study: Hamilton brings timeless detail to Parade Hotel Bath Hamilton supplied its Hartland Satin Brass switches and sockets for the refurbishment of Parade Hotel Bath, complementing the property’s Georgian heritage with refined contemporary detailing… Situated in the heart of Bath, Parade Hotel is a distinctive boutique destination that celebrates the city’s rich architectural character while embracing contemporary luxury. The refurbishment brings together historic Georgian features and sophisticated interiors, creating a welcoming hospitality setting where carefully considered details contribute to the overall guest experience. Hamilton, a British manufacturer of decorative wiring accessories , has contributed to the project with its Hartland Satin Brass switches and sockets, introducing a warm, understated finish that complements the hotel’s elegant surroundings. Image credit: Parade Hotel / Hamilton Litestat Considered details, timeless finishes In hospitality interiors, the smallest details can have a significant impact on the overall design. From material choices to decorative finishes, each element contributes to creating a cohesive environment that feels considered and complete. The Hartland Satin Brass switches and sockets introduce subtle warmth to the interiors, offering a refined metallic finish that works harmoniously alongside the hotel’s blend of traditional character and contemporary styling. With its understated appearance, satin brass provides an elegant alternative to high-shine finishes, adding depth and sophistication without distracting from the wider design scheme. Image credit: Parade Hotel / Hamilton Litestat Switches and sockets are essential functional elements within any interior, yet their visual impact is an important consideration during specification. Selecting finishes that complement surrounding materials and furnishings helps integrate these practical details into the overall aesthetic, ensuring consistency throughout a space. At Parade Hotel Bath, the inclusion of Hartland Satin Brass demonstrates how decorative wiring accessories can contribute to a carefully curated interior, balancing everyday functionality with considered design. Supporting hospitality design The project reflects the importance of thoughtful specification within the hospitality sector, where interiors must balance visual appeal with the practical demands of a guest environment. Hamilton offers a wide range of decorative switches and sockets in a variety of styles and finishes, supporting designers, specifiers and developers working across hospitality, residential and commercial projects. For schemes requiring a more individual approach, its Bespoke Design Service provides opportunities to develop tailored solutions that complement specific interior concepts. Image credit: Parade Hotel / Hamilton Litestat By combining design-led finishes with practical functionality, Hamilton’s collections offer flexibility for projects ranging from boutique hotels to larger developments, helping bring the finer details of an interior scheme together. The Parade Hotel Bath refurbishment is a fitting example of how considered product choices can enhance a design-led hospitality environment. Hamilton is delighted to see its Hartland Satin Brass switches and sockets featured in this distinctive project, contributing to an interior that balances Bath’s historic character with contemporary elegance. Designers and specifiers can visit the Hamilton Showroom at Design Centre, Chelsea Harbour, London, to explore the collections in person and discover finishes for upcoming schemes. To discuss a project or learn more about the Bespoke Design Service, visit the Hamilton website or get in touch with the team. Hamilton Litestat is one of our Recommended Suppliers and regularly features in our Supplier News section of the website. If you are interested in becoming one of our Recommended Suppliers, please email Katy Phillips. Main image credit: Hamilton Litestat . items.text: Rosewood Residences unveils residential development in Bangkok Rosewood Residences Bangkok to rise above Lumphini Park WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 10, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Rosewood Residences Bangkok to rise above Lumphini Park Rosewood has announced its first residential development in Southeast Asia: 85 private residences on a rare freehold site, due for completion in 2030… Rosewood is putting down roots in Bangkok. The hospitality group has announced Rosewood Residences Bangkok , its first residential development in Southeast Asia, a limited collection of 85 private residences overlooking Lumphini Park, the city’s most coveted green space. Developed by SC Asset in partnership with Tokyo Tatemono Thailand, the project occupies a rare freehold site on Rama 4 Road. It brings together SC Asset’s command of Bangkok’s ultra-luxury market, Tokyo Tatemono Group’s 130-year heritage of quality and craftsmanship, and Rosewood’s approach to residential hospitality, grounded in place, connection and belonging. The ambition is a true heirloom address for globally minded UHNWIs seeking privacy, permanence and an exceptional quality of living. Discretion and service go hand in hand. Residents will be supported by a dedicated residential team and welcomed into Rosewood’s global community, with access to personalised service and curated experiences across the brand’s hotels and resorts worldwide. The timing is telling. Thailand’s branded residences sector is now valued at 205.3 billion baht (US$6.4 billion), according to C9 Hotelworks, making it one of the fastest-growing corners of luxury real estate. For Rosewood CEO Sonia Cheng, the project is “an address intended to be valued for generations to come.” Completion is scheduled for 2030. items.title: Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets  
  Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets  
 Jess Miles .
items.text: Weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets WORDS BY Jess Miles November 9, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets Editor of SPACE, Jess Miles, travels to Portadown to see how Ulster Carpets makes bespoke carpets for the world’s most revered hospitality projects, from package dyeing and patented looms to a design studio that weaves a property’s story into every pile… After a long, hot summer, it was a welcome change look out at the verdant landscape of Northern Ireland, just hours after leaving the heat-beaten brown of the Sussex countryside. Admiring nature’s enduring carpet seemed a fitting start to the day, before soon arriving at Ulster Carpets in Portadown to take a first-hand look at the craftsmanship behind the luxury carpets made for some of the most acclaimed hospitality projects in the world. Although it has now grown into a global business with clients and projects of grand scale, Ulster has manufactured on this small-town site since it was founded in 1938, and today keeps all of the process in-house across three UK sites. Dyeing, weaving, inspection, finishing and despatch all take place here in Portadown, where around 95% of Ulster’s carpet is made. The remainder is produced at a second site in Northumberland, while wool is spun first at Ulster Yarns, the company’s mill in Yorkshire. Now a fourth-generation, family-owned company, Ulster remains centred on the people, skills and expertise that have been continually refined over generations of designers, weavers and makers. Image credits: Ulster Carpets Ulster’s commitment to its Northern Irish roots is evident upon arrival, where I’m greeted by the close-knit team who show me around with buckets of passion for the work they do. Among them was Ciara Halligan, Marine Sales Manager, who started out at Ulster as a weaver over 30 years ago. Now she works with clients, drawing on her specialist knowledge to show them the endless possibilities of what Ulster can achieve. But Ciara, it turned out, was no exception. As the tour went on, I realised everyone I met had either spent years at the company or had followed in family members footsteps there. It is a heritage Ulster carries with pride, built on investment in its people and, as I would soon see, its engineering and machinery too. First stop was the Dyehouse and Energy Centre, which has transformed dyeing at Ulster in terms of both time and sustainability. Gone are the old-school hanks of yarn immersed in huge dye baths. Instead, yarn is wound onto perforated tubes, and the dye is circulated through it – a method known as package dyeing. Heat from used water is recovered to warm fresh water drawn from an on-site borehole, and since the centre opened in 2018, water consumption has fallen by 46%. Better still, the dye penetrates the wool more deeply, giving richer colours. Image credit: Ulster Carpets The dyehouse is also home to Ulster’s colour hub, with a bank of over 9,000 colours to draw on. My eyes light up like a magpie to gold when the drawers of tufted colour samples are pulled open, but if none of these are the exact shade needed, a bespoke match can be developed from a client’s material or colour reference. From there, we – and the yarn – head to the looms. There are 40 Axminster looms in all, each running Ulster’s patented PSYLO weaving technology which allows for up to 25 colours within a single design, creating more intricate concepts full of texture, movement and depth. I also got to see a new generation of looms in action, engineered and built in Sunderland by GTM (a company within the Ulster Group), designed to produce more carpet using less energy per square metre. It was quite the experience standing in the room as the factory floor boomed to the beat of the looms – and watching the many cones of coloured yarn being drawn in and woven into the finished design was nothing short of a visual feast. Onward, every inch of every carpet is then visually inspected, with any mending painstakingly done by hand. Before despatch, each order is rolled out side by side to check the pattern lines up across adjoining rolls. Having walked through the end-to-end physical process, I was struck by how meticulous the craft of making carpet is, and I certainly left with a newfound appreciation for it. But what surprisingly captured my attention most was my final stop – the design studio. Image credit: Ulster Carpets There, Senior Designer Sarah Moffatt showed me the concept for Ulster’s stand at an upcoming trade show. Working to the theme “designed to be remembered”, the team looked to their Northern Irish heritage, drawing on the patina of the local landscape. They photographed corroded metal around the factory and the nearby beaten chalk landscape, then zoomed in on the textures and patterns until they became abstract forms. Warm tones of rust and weathering supplied the base colour palette, with different shades used to create tonal depth and dimension. It was an insightful illustration of how Ulster approaches its custom work, which makes up the majority of its hospitality projects. Rather than working from existing collections, the team designs bespoke carpet for each property and the individual areas within it, working closely with the interior designer or client to weave the wider narrative of the project into the carpet itself. Storytelling is always a big part of the brief, and Moffatt explained how the team might research a property’s history, from the cultural background right down to its local plant life. On one heritage project, the leaf veining of native plant species was translated into a carpet through colour and form. Image credit: Ulster Carpets The team’s creative skills also extend to technical problem-solving. One

 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 • Hotel Designs Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 9, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 Fairmont Hotels & Resorts has offically opened Fairmont New Orleans, marking the much-anticipated return of the brand to the Crescent City after two decades – and marking Fairmont’s 100th hotel globally… Developed by Kailas Companies and operated by Fairmont Hotels & Resorts , Fairmont New Orleans occupies 17 stories of the former Bank of New Orleans building, a 31-story landmark originally designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in 1970. Its original sidewalks, entry canopy, lobby floors and concrete walls on the first and second floors have been fully restored and refurbished, alongside the second floor’s decorative bronze paneling and local cypress ceiling. Rather than looking primarily to the French Quarter’s colonial architecture, the property draws inspiration from the glamour and optimism of the 1970s, celebrating an often-overlooked chapter in New Orleans’ architectural evolution. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Omer Acar, CEO, Fairmont Hotels & Resorts, said: “Celebrating Fairmont’s landmark 100th hotel in New Orleans is a moment of perfect alignment. This is a city built on the very poetry of celebration, culture, and hospitality, setting the ultimate stage for such a historic milestone. After two decades away, returning to New Orleans feels like a joyful homecoming. This magnificent property is designed to be a vibrant social epicenter, a sanctuary where the city’s rich heritage meets a sophisticated, contemporary energy. Through meticulous design, spirited gastronomy, and exceptional spaces created for connection, we are not just opening a hotel; we are welcoming the soulful spirit of New Orleans back into the global Fairmont family for our next great chapter.” Interior design by Rockwell Group explores the contrasts that define New Orleans, imagining a city emerging from a verdant landscape and shaped by generations of cultural influences from around the world. Mid-century references nod to the decadence of the 1970s oil boom era, while layered textures, saturated colour, local flora, and globally influenced patterns bring a contemporary interpretation of New Orleans design, balancing old and new, polished and playful, and vibrant and restful. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas The hotel’s lobby serves as its social anchor and a cultural living room designed to welcome both visitors and New Orleanians throughout the day. Guests arrive beneath a mirror-clad monumental stair that reflects a three-story magnolia flower and Spanish moss-inspired chandelier. Custom brass relief panels from Italy frame the check-in and concierge desks, while the Lobby Bar pairs handmade Italian lava-stone tiles with a floor mosaic composed of six marbles in a distinctly 1970s pattern. The Lobby Bar’s cocktail-focused beverage program and live entertainment encourage guests and locals to linger from day into evening. “Today marks an exciting new chapter for Fairmont New Orleans and for our city,” said Eric Overstreet, General Manager, Fairmont New Orleans. “From the moment guests enter our lobby to an evening at Delmonico Steakhouse, the hotel was designed to feel distinctly of New Orleans, while offering the service and experience Fairmont is known for. We’re proud to welcome travelers and our local community into these spaces and look forward to seeing Fairmont New Orleans become part of the city’s next chapter.” Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Fairmont New Orleans’ 250 guest rooms and suites are conceived as personal retreats with residential warmth, eclectic finishes, curated furnishings and layered materials designed to feel collected over time. Three-dimensional entry mosaics reference classical European flooring, while large, panelled artworks evoke the rich flora of Louisiana’s bayous. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame sweeping city views, while custom artwork and details reference the cultural and natural history of New Orleans. In select king rooms, ‘faux balconies’ with café tables offer a playful nod to the city’s beloved porches and terraces. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Delmonico Steakhouse marks the celebrated concept’s debut in New Orleans and its first location outside of Las Vegas, bringing Chef Lagasse’s grand American steakhouse to the city that has long inspired his culinary career. Open for dinner, the restaurant pairs timeless steakhouse traditions with his signature bold New Orleans flavours. Open for breakfast and lunch, The Café by Emeril offers a more relaxed brasserie-style experience, combining French-inspired classics with Creole accents and Southern influences. From chicory-laced coffee to thoughtfully prepared breakfast and lunch favorites, the café flows seamlessly into the lobby, creating an inviting gathering place for hotel guests and locals alike. “I’m thrilled to bring Delmonico Steakhouse to New Orleans alongside The Café by Emeril, creating two distinct dining experiences that reflect what I love about cooking and bringing people together,” said Chef Emeril Lagasse. “We’re proud to be a part of Fairmont’s return to the city and look forward to welcoming both locals and visitors to experience the bold flavors, genuine hospitality, and unmistakable New Orleans spirit that defines everything we do.” Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Forthcoming dining and drinking venues, set to open in early December also, include the property’s rooftop pool and Bleu Perdu, along with Third Measure cocktail bar.
