items.text: Fonda San Miguel Dining Out in Austin The Best Restaurants in Austin for Private Dining, Events, and Parties Everywhere to book for all of your small weddings, celebratory dinners, bridal showers, and more by Darcie Duttweiler Updated Oct 22, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Darcie Duttweiler is an Austin-based freelance writer, who covers food, beverages, travel, and lifestyle. Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. Some are swanky and tucked into Downtown dining landmarks. Others are cozy, or perched on patios with sweeping views. All of them make an outing feel like an event, while also taking the stress out of group dining — meaning, there’s no awkward table shuffling, no shouting over the crowd, and no fighting for the check. The city’s best private dining spaces are more than just a curtain and a prix fixe menu. Many spots go beyond dinner, offering perks like custom cocktails, floral design, built-in audio and video setups, and after-hours buyouts. From iconic institutions like Fonda San Miguel, Matties, and Jeffrey’s to sleek hotspots like Eberly, La Condessa, and Bar Toti, these venues combine atmosphere with standout service and memorable menus. items.title: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques
items.summary:
At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla… 
 The post  Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques — Resy | Right This Way Cotoletta 4.7 · Italian · $ Miami Book Now Published: Nov. 9, 2026 At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla Milanese. No substitutions. No alternatives. Just a golden, pan-fried veal cutlet — and a bet that it’s all you’ll need. Until recently, making a reservation required a phone call, which only deepened the sense that this place operates on its own terms. (The good news: You can now reserve a table on Resy.) The concept debuted in Coconut Grove in the fall of 2024 and comes from 84 Magic Hospitality, a restaurant group known for a growing collection of Miami restaurants with minimalist menus ( San Lorenzo , San Marco , and the lasagna speakeasy, Si Papa 3190 , are the others). Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Still, the story behind the concept stretches back further than its Miami address might suggest. Cotoletta is the creation of partners Ignacio Lopez Mancisidor and Mattia Cicognani, and former co-founder Andrea Fraquelli — who share a background in hospitality and a frustration with how transactional the industry had become. From the start, their goal at Cotoletta has been to make things simple for guests and allow them to focus on what really matters: great food and genuine connection. “Across the globe, many of the best restaurants do one item and they do it to absolute perfection,” co-founder Mattia Cicognani says. “We drew inspiration from the Italian essence of committing to one hero dish and prioritizing ingredients of the highest quality.” “Only serving one dish was a risk,” Cicognani acknowledges, “but the popularity and love for the concept has proven that it really works. Our customers learned that they love what we do and that is why they continue to come back.” Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Head chef Davide Rosselli shared the process that delivers a consistent, classic cotoletta every time. Premium veal is hand-trimmed, gently pounded to its thin-yet-tender texture, coated in fresh egg and breadcrumbs, and fried in clarified butter until it emerges with a crisp, even, golden crust. Each cutlet weighs in at roughly 20 ounces, made to be shared between two people. The result is a traditional veal Milanese that is a signature of Northern Italian craftsmanship. Everything else on the table exists to support that centerpiece. “While the process sounds simple, it’s backed by decades of Italian tradition and time-honored techniques passed down by chefs across generations,” Rosselli says. For $90, two diners share the full prix-fixe experience: two antipasti courses of bruschetta and truffle arancino to start, followed by the veal cutlet, and two sides (the only real choice you have to make here). Dessert (tiramisu or a flourless chocolate cake) can be added on for $14. “Each appetizer sets the tone for a true Italian experience, while the sides are thoughtfully chosen to complement the veal without overpowering it.” Rosselli says. “Lighter elements like crisp salads and simple pasta dishes help balance the richness of the veal, creating a well-rounded meal.” Those side options include pasta al pomodoro, zucchine fritte, insalata di rucola, or patatine fritte. Rosselli’s personal picks: the pasta in just the right portion to leave you wanting more of the main event, and the zucchine fritte offering a warm, light bite that balances out the richness of the veal. (Wondering what happens if you bring a third wheel or want to dine solo? Odd-numbered parties can add on an individual portion of bruschetta, arancino, a smaller veal cutlet, and one side for $55.) Guests return because the menu never changes, and neither does the reason to go back. “They know exactly what they are getting every single time,” Cicognani says. Cotoletta is open weekdays from 5:30 to 10 p.m. and until 10:30 p.m. on Friday. On weekends, it opens at 12:30 p.m. until 10:30 p.m. on Saturday and 9 p.m. on Sunday. Lyssa Goldberg is a Miami-based freelance writer and content strategist. She loves telling stories about food, wellness and travel, and you can find her byline in Parade, American Way, Mashable, Miami New Times, Time Out and more. Follow her on Instagram and Twitter . Follow Resy , too. items.title: The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York
items.summary:
As people who love restaurants, we know that when it comes to picking a spot for dinner, it’s much more… 
 The post  The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 As people who love restaurants, we know that when it comes to picking a spot for dinner, it’s much more than about just the food. The vibe is just as important, and music is a key player in creating it. Sometimes, the best soundtrack is the one you don’t notice, but the places on this list aren’t for those kinds of nights. These playlists are hyper specific, the sound systems are top of the line, and often they have some of the best vinyl collections in the country, and a guest DJs on weekends who comes in to spin them. These are places you go to for the music, but where us restaurant lovers won’t need to suffer because the snacks that can often lead to full meals are far more interesting than a bag of stale potato chips. You’ll be able to listen to some Japanese jazz deep cuts over an omakase, or eclectic world beats over some of the city’s silkiest hummus — with playlists and menus like these, you might not need to make it to your second destination for the night. And if you’re looking for spots with live music, we’ve got you covered here . The chef’s tasting consists of an ever-changing menu of multiple courses for $98 a person, whereas the bar has an à la carte menu that features inventive cocktails and bites like a chef’s take on a filet-o-fish and octopus with saag paneer. He’s invested in top-tier audio equipment and carefully selects the music each evening, which can range from funk to Dizzy Gillespie. items.text: 29 New York Bars and Restaurants with Excellent Zero-Proof Cocktails — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 Somewhere around a decade ago the dreaded term “mocktail” first started to surface on menus, referring to drinks meant to offer the cocktail experience, but none of the “buzz.” At the time, unlike their alcoholic counterparts, most of these drinks were overly sweet mixes of juice and housemade sodas with elaborate garnishes. Now, however, there’s been a shift in drinking culture: Dry January, anyone? In other words, we’re drinking less, or thinking about having that second or third drink more, and beverage directors have taken note. Today’s mocktails are now as considered and thoughtfully developed as those made full-strength. Many of them also feature the new wave of non-alcoholic spirits, like Seedlip, Lyre’s, Little Saints, Amass Riverine, and Ghia. So, whether you’re abstaining from alcohol, are taking a night off, or just want to stay and linger at the bar after your glass has run dry, here are some of the best places in the city to find zero-proof cocktails. Newly added: Bar Americano, Lord’s, Overstory, and The Up & Up. Party Size Remove 2 Add Update Close Date Soft Bar + Cafe map Greenpoint One of the newer additions to the non-alcoholic cocktail scene in our fair city, Soft Bar is so named because all of the drinks on their all-day menu are, well, soft. The Golden Hour , with grape, elderflower, pink peppercorn shrub, and alcohol-free Champagne, or the Pear Pressure with prickly pear, agave, and alcohol-free Tequila, are both good choices. Keep an eye out on the menu for the function of each drink, which ranges from focus to “vibey.” Plus, there’s a celebrity at the helm – fans of Bravo’s Summer House might see a familiar face. Read all about Soft Bar here . Book Now Golden Ratio map Clinton Hill What can’t this team do? Golden Ratio comes from the masterminds behind Cafe Mado and Place des Fêtes , serving up cocktails and mocktails to the Clinton Hill crowd. Nearly all of the cocktails here have a nonalcoholic counterpart, and everything is fiercely flavor-driven and seasonal. Past drinks have included interpretations of purple shiso , apple , and toothache tree , and the team is working towards being zero-waste, so you can have your drink and eat it, too. Book Now Lord's map NoHo This beloved purveyor of British fare may not be the first thing that comes to mind when you think of nonalcoholic beverages, but their list (which they title “Teetotaling”) is one of our favorites. Go for a Blood Orange Spritz , a sour made with Ghia, or a S affron White Negroni — all totally alcohol free, of course. Any of them pairs perfectly with a good lamb Scotch egg, too. Book Now Sofreh map Prospect Heights There’s not a lot we’d say no to at Sofreh. While yes, their list of cocktails is excellent, the real pearl here has to be the selection of sharbats , a Persian cooler that comes in flavors like mint and cucumber, sour cherry, and lemon and saffron. If those aren’t doing it for you, there’s also the Persian black tea and a mint and rose petal yogurt drink. No matter what’s in your glass, make sure an order of herb meatballs and saffron rice are on your table. Book Now The Up & Up map Greenwich Village This subterranean cocktail den and ideal date night spot in Greenwich Village has an extensive list of drinks that also includes five excellent nonalcoholic takes on some of their classics. This includes a zero-proof spin of Hold, Please , a watermelon shrub that draws inspiration from New York’s sliced fruit vendors who often sell servings of watermelon spears topped with Tajín. There’s also an N/A version of Zuzu’s Petals , named for the classic film, “It’s a Wonderful Life,” that’s made with ginger, habanero, rose water, lime juice, and demerara. Book Now Spygold map Hudson Yards Greywind’s (also on this list) sister and downstairs neighbor, the fire-lit Spygold, has an equally lovely list of non-alcoholic options for you to peruse. Past favorites have included the Tomato, Tomahto with nonalcoholic gin and tomato-basil soda, or the Cucumber Highball with alcohol-free Tequila and cucumber soda. Miami offers plenty of chances to spend big bucks on dinner, but the harder question is where to make it… 
 The post  The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in Miami  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Amazonico Miami map Brickell Come dressed for dinner and whatever follows at Amazónico, where live bands play jazz, bossa nova, and Cuban rhythms beneath a canopy of greenery. The menu is as extravagant as the setting: guacamole comes topped with sea urchin, and Maine lobster tail arrives with semolina pasta and coconut bisque. Share ceviche with sweet plantain and duck arroz chaufa before moving on to charcoal-grilled picanha or Australian wagyu ribeye. After dinner, follow the music upstairs, where DJs and tropical cocktails keep the lounge and rooftop going into the wee hours of the night. Photo courtesy of Amazónico Miami Cost: A meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Starters range in price from $13 to $42, nigiri sushi is $45 to $65, sashimi is $60 to $80, seafood entrees are priced from $32 to $110, and grilled meats are $38 to $380 each. Book Now

items.summary: From butler-serviced suites to sommelier-led tastings, these Mexico stays are redefining all-inclusive luxury.
items.text: North America Chevron Mexico Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story I first arrived in Cancún, Mexico , more than 20 years ago. I had big hair, pencil-thin eyebrows, and limited expectations for an all-inclusive vacation : A swim-up bar serving frozen margaritas was about all I needed. Since then, my priorities have shifted, and thankfully, Cancún’s all-inclusive resorts have grown up alongside me. After two decades of return visits made easier by an abundance of nonstop US flights , I’ve become more discerning about what deserves a place in that up-front price. I’ve also discovered that Cancún’s enduring spring break reputation tells an incomplete story about what's on offer. Choose the right resort, and you can have a butler draw your evening bath, a private pool overlooking the Caribbean, and à la carte restaurants you’ll look forward to all afternoon, whether you prefer the Hotel Zone’s long sweep of white sand, the relative quiet of Playa Mujeres, or a boat ride out to Isla Mujeres . The frozen margaritas are still here. But now, there’s much more worth checking in for. Read on for the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún worth planning a vacation around. items.title: 7 Best Hotels in Antigua, the Caribbean Island With a Beach for Every Day of the Year
items.summary: From ultra-luxe five-star resorts to boutique beach hideaways, these are the properties worth booking in Antigua.
items.text: Central America and the Caribbean Chevron Antigua Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story With endless white-sand beaches , acres of rugged rainforest, and plenty of untouched tangle just waiting to be explored, the best hotels in Antigua celebrate its landscape, which remains largely true to how nature intended. Most of the properties on this glorious Caribbean island are a stone’s throw from the crystal-clear waters that lap its powder-soft shores. It’s a beach-lover’s dream, and anyone visiting would be hard-pressed to see every stretch of golden sand—as the saying goes, there’s “a beach for every day of the year” here (yes, an even 365). Visit between June and October , and you might just be lucky enough to watch baby turtles emerging blurry-eyed from their shells before scuttling to the sea. There are optimal times for surfing here, too, but the year-round promise is that the vibe on this island is chill. Days stretch lazily from sunrise swims to rum-fueled sundowners, with the opportunity for a poolside snooze in between. It’s easy to sink into vacation mode here, especially when you’re checking into one of the best hotels in Antigua. We've rounded up the most luxurious options on the island below, from high-end resorts with all the frills to boutique hideaways so good you’ll be booking your return before you’ve even left for home. Thanks to the hotel’s unique perch on a secluded promontory, you’ll be flanked by azure-blue waters on all sides: Guests can lounge at the hotel’s two beaches entirely undisturbed, with only peppy team members coming around intermittently with drinks and ice pops. items.title: 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter
items.summary: Because sometimes all you need is a quick change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing . We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate , or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues. From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England , these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away. Courtesy Auberge Collection Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Auberge Collection Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Auberge Collection Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Auberge Collection Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Mayflower Inn & Spa, Auberge Collection Readers' Choice Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 Hannah Chubb , senior commerce editor Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design. What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails. What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County , a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about. Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city. What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner , of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar. What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley. Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city . The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House . The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious. What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul? items.title: Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal
items.summary: Travel and food writer Luke Pyenson shares where to find the city’s best gluten-free bites, sips, and dining experiences.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal —and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border. But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating. Boulangerie Le Marquis Dedicated bakery scene In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant? Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis , near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé , in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong. Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo , a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row. A sweet galette from Crêperie du Marché Luke Pyenson Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché , a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not? Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella , a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive. Chicken Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options. Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico Luke Pyenson At Rôtisserie Coco Rico , a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor. More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune , from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table. Courtesy Mon Lapin Wine bars and neo-bistros Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent. Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon , whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef , Fred Morin now presides over thos

items.title: Bar Le Trente
items.summary: La entrada  Bar Le Trente  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Bar Le Trente — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Design , Food Bar Le Trente The Wild Child of Pigalle Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Tanguy Sergheraert Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share Following Hotel Massé , siblings Corto and Eole Peyron have opened Le Trente. Located next to the hotel, this bar occupies an iconic former loft in Pigalle, transforming it into a place for encounters with both neighbourhood locals and travellers. Like Massé, it draws on the family motto, “make a friend a day”, though its world is slightly different. “Le Trente is a bit like Hotel Massé’s more unruly younger brother. They belong to the same family, but they don’t quite have the same character”, explains Eole. At Massé, calm and intimacy prevail. Step through the doors of Le Trente, however, and the energy shifts: drinks, food , friends and DJs spinning vinyl from Thursday onwards. Close While touches of velvet, wood and beige give the hotel its soft, inviting aesthetic, Le Trente feels sexier and bolder: leather, mirrors and very low lighting in the evening. Once again, Olivier Guyot and studio Gasparetto Parenti worked with the Peyron family to rethink the space and bring Le Trente to life. Outside, the lettering and green marble frontage mark the entrance to this singular place. Inside, a raw, conceptual universe takes shape: a large vintage wooden bar, red-painted floors, high and low seating, small tables and even an outdoor alcove. Close As at Massé, every object has been sourced second-hand or custom-made. “We really didn’t want everything to feel new or perfectly matched”, Eole notes. “There are things we found, contemporary artworks, pieces made specifically for the space and objects and memories from our family”. This is precisely what creates a space that feels both artistic and homely: the walls are covered with personal photographs featuring familiar faces, many of them tracing the expeditions of their father, Stéphane Peyron. Close “Our father has spent his life travelling and meeting people in some of the most remote parts of the world”, Eole comments. “He taught us that it’s the people you meet who make the journey and the memories”. This philosophy, central to both Corto and Eole, runs through Le Trente and is what prompted them to open a bar alongside the hotel. “At Le Trente, Massé guests mix with neighbours and Parisians. You can come for dinner, have a drink, celebrate a birthday, hold an exhibition or a book signing”. Close This same understanding of connections with people from all walks of life extends to their team. Some were friends before the project was born; others have become friends along the way: “The Massé and Le Trente teams are young and very close-knit. It wasn’t something we planned – it just happened naturally”. Close Gabrielle, a young neighbourhood sommelier who knocked on the door during the renovation, curates a minimalist selection of natural wines from France and beyond. Louis, a neighbour of Le Trente and a music enthusiast, is in charge of the music programme. Discovered at listening sessions, on the radio or in the city’s record shops, Le Trente’s DJs share one passion: vinyl. Ambient, house, jazz, downtempo or electro. Corto and his childhood friend Cyril teamed up with Félix to imagine Le Trente’s menu, built around a simple question: what do we want to eat in a bar? The answers became the menu: simple but really good dishes, designed for sharing. Close The menu changes weekly and follows the seasons, so regulars can keep coming back without tiring of the same dishes. The music rotates in a similar way: “We tend to favour artists from the local scene, whether emerging or already established, and we give them a lot of freedom”. Each artist brings their own records, generating a mood that is personal yet lively. “Le Trente never has exactly the same soundtrack two nights in a row, and that’s exactly how we like it”. Close Upstairs, you walk into a huge glass-roofed room: “You can almost feel as though you’re in a New York loft, until you look outside and see the Haussmann façades – you see Paris”. A contrast that sums up the place perfectly. Family, vintage, modernity and intention coexist naturally at Le Trente. The room has an immediate depth and character, and nothing feels forced: instinctively, you feel at home, whether it’s your first visit or you’re a regular. items.title: Badi Restaurant
items.summary: La entrada  Badi Restaurant  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Badi Restaurant — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design , Food Badi Restaurant A Layered Sense of Taste Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Adrien Maurice & Benjamin Baltus Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share For Victoria Merret and Maxime Bourdigal, Badi embraces everything: their job, their interests, their tastes, their values, and their personality. In other words, Badi embodies the couple’s vision. Every sphere comes together under the same sensibility: a pursuit of balance between beauty, precision, and flavour. At Badi, located in Saint-Gilles (Brussels), design , materials, and cuisine interact seamlessly. Initially, the idea sparked for a cider bar: “We kept saying to ourselves: ‘We’d love to go to a wine bar that serves a hundred different ciders,’ so we decided to create it.” As a product that hits close to home with their Breton roots, it seemed like an effortless path to take. Close Nevertheless, three years after opening, Badi has now established itself as a fully-fledged restaurant. “We rediscovered ourselves through the world of natural wine,” and the evolution came instinctively. A place where raw products and ingredients are at the centre of everything, and that is guided by honesty, quality and craftsmanship. The menu and the space complement each other, sculpting an experience that is both curated yet welcoming. In the kitchen, Maxime, who has worked for Bertrand Larcher in Paris and Japan, as well as Ötap in Brussels, collaborates with Paul-Antoine Bertin (Rebel, Grain, Raki, Ötap…) to develop product-centred menus. For the interior, the couple worked with Nelly Smets. Close “We immediately connected through a shared vision regarding materials and influences, but the challenge was then to make all the elements work together harmoniously,” they comment. Inspired by Nordic and Japanese style, raw elements were non-negotiable. Wood, natural stone, steel, textured walls… They all come together around the protagonist of the show. Close A large central travertine counter dominates the space, defining a cohesive and immersive experience. And that was the intention from the beginning: “The central counter encourages interaction with our guests because everyone is seated at the same height, forming a closeness.” The environment becomes convivial, light, easygoing, and authentic. “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” “The design of the space is much more connected to the food and drinks selection than people might think.” Built by craftsmen with honest materials, this philosophy equally translates to the curation of the menu: “It’s just as we do when selecting our natural ciders, wines, and ingredients for the kitchen.” Constantly adapting to the seasons, every menu balances freshness, indulgence, comfort, and elegance, while keeping everything approachable and never overly complex. Close This same ethos translates to Victoria and Maxime’s home: “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” Separating work and private life, the apartment was also driven by the desire to work with raw resources, with wood playing a very important role, but this time in a more personal way. Close “For the restaurant, we tried to develop the most timeless design possible so it could age beautifully over the years. For the apartment, however, we allowed ourselves to make stronger choices to build something with a more distinctive identity.” Altogether, with the help of Nelly Smets and, for their home, her daughter Iolie Coufo. Close In both spaces, the couple is present in many ways. “We constantly dig into memories, experiences, and travels to shape our inspirations; a mix of different influences and emotions we’ve collected over the years, brought together in a way that feels genuinely ours.” For Victoria and Maxime, interior design is about much more than conceiving beautiful places; it’s about shaping spaces where people come to create meaningful moments. items.title: Jaç HiFI Café
items.summary: La entrada  Jaç HiFI Café  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Jaç HiFI Café — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design Jaç HiFI Café A 21st century temple of sound Photographed by Salva López Written by Openhouse Studio Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share A new café has taken over Avinguda Diagonal 335, in the heart of Barcelona: JAÇ HiFi Café. Designed by Isern Serra Studio , the space opened in July 2025 with not one, but two missions: to invite guests to drink coffee and to listen. In fact, its name carries multiple meanings: a nod to jazz music itself, a reference to Japan’s jazz kissa and in Catalan, the word “jaç,” which means to recline, rest, and let go. But, what were jazz kissa ? Characterized by compact and dimly lit venues, these spaces were intimate listening bars that flourished from the 1950s onwards and were dedicated entirely to the appreciation of recorded jazz. Its complex nature, designed and conceived as temples of sound, found no similarities elsewhere: they were neither bars in the Western sense nor cafés in the European style. Close Instead, in jazz kissa , conversation was minimal, the record player was sacred, and music was played on high-fidelity equipment at volumes that demanded full attention. Originating after the Second World War, kissa provided a haven for serious listeners who could not afford records or audio systems of their own. Over decades, their interiors developed a distinct aesthetic — wood-panelled walls, warm lighting, and seating arranged to face the speakers rather than each other — creating a sense of intimacy and deep focus. Close JAÇ HiFi Café reinterprets that philosophy for a contemporary Mediterranean city. The design is warm yet refined, with an emphasis on tactile materials and an atmosphere that feels as familiar as one’s own living room. The space, covering 95 square metres, unfolds in a series of distinct zones, each offering a different relationship with music, people, and the city outside. Close In the lounge area, iconic pieces such as Akari E lamp by Isamu Noguchi and artwork by artist Chidy Wayne welcome the visitors. Further into the bar, a monolithic piece of walnut wood that doubles as a giant speaker cabinet plays both parts, as a functional counter and audio sculpture. The most dramatic element of JAÇ, however, lies toward the rear: a large walnut-wood installation that curves across walls and ceiling to form a semi-enclosed listening alcove. The effect is immersive — a space that seems to embrace the listener, pulling them into a cocoon of warm wood and resonant sound. Close Overall, JAÇ conveys a special closeness, brought by its design and enhanced by the music and the people that enjoy it. With contrasting but matching materials, the space is given its own unique personality, bridging Japanese precision with Mediterranean ease. All accompanied by lighting, shaping the atmosphere and framing shared moments. JAÇ HiFi Café ultimately reimagines the jazz kissa experience for 21st-century Barcelona. It offers a place to slow down, to sit alone or with friends, to discover a song or hear an old favourite in new detail, and to inhabit a space where design, music, and human presence are in perfect balance. items.text: YESS Restaurant — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Food YESS Restaurant “A little bit of effort” (and a whole lot of fire) Photographed by Austin Leis Written by Forde Visser Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share On the morning I met with Junya Yamasaki, chef and partner of YESS restaurant , he arrived with armloads of wild fennel—stalky and open, a tangled supernova exuberance of yellow flowers. Because I had already made a cursory tour of Junya’s online presence, I was not surprised; I knew this activity was not unusual. Close YESS, an izakaya style “progressive Japanese restaurant” (website) opened in 2024 in the Arts District of Los Angeles. That’s the simple version of a more detoured (but no time wasted) trajectory. Junya, from the Japanese region of Kansai, began to map his career(s) through Tokyo, London, and Paris, studying (respectively) politics, photography and fine arts . In Tokyo he had also worked in film, but in Paris a restaurant kitchen job pointed him towards the culinary world, and eventually a return to London to help develop the wildly popular Koya noodle bar, which significantly diversified London’s Japanese food scene with traditional udon and inventive daily specials. Close In addition to Junya’s commitment to the local and seasonal present, he also holds a reverence for change, which has been mightily exercised since the restaurant’s beginnings. This year, between the LA Fires and the immigration dynamics, Los Angeles has been a special test. YESS took a breath, a short pause to ensure a safe environment for everyone, and exhaled with a new invitation, the addition of a lunch menu. As welcoming as an exuberance of flowers. items.title: Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin
items.summary: The post  Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Kissabō Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan On a sunny tree-lined street in Berlin’s Prenzlauer Berg, plum-coloured noren (暖簾) — traditional Japanese split curtains — float gently in the breeze. They mark the doorway to Kissabō , a 16-seat tea bar that its owners, Marcin and Gosia Chelkowski, describe as a space for attention and curiosity. Two years ago, the couple moved to Berlin from Szczecin in Poland to realise an idea that had been brewing across their lives. As Gosia explains, “there wasn’t a specific moment in time that Marcin and I came to tea, it was very gradual.” Marcin continues, “In Poland, we were exposed to a lot of Japanese culture through videos and gaming when we were growing up. My thoughts when I was young were, well, Japanese games are cool, so everything in Japan must be cool! [Laughs] So as soon as we could afford to visit there, we did.” Gosia adds, “Instantly, we felt very at home.” Their first visit to Japan was twelve years ago, and since that fateful trip, they have returned almost every year. “We thought, well, we like it so much here, maybe we shouldn’t waste time visiting or experiencing other things,” Marcin says, Gosia nodding in agreement. It was on these visits that they were first exposed to a culture of tea: from the crisp bottles lining convenience store shelves, to the formal practice of chanoyu (茶の湯) practiced in tea houses. “In Japan, tea is everywhere,” Marcin notes. “But when we began drinking tea, we weren’t really pursuing it with intention. As we continued, we began to develop an understanding of the culture — a curiosity about the practice and the way it is connected to something more meaningful.” They describe their path to opening a tea bar as something like osmosis: every time they visited Japan, they met more and more people related to the world of tea — farmers, teachers, craftspeople — and their interest grew. Neither comes from a hospitality background, but both had reached a point in their careers where they felt the need for change. “We were talking to a friend who has a tea school in Kyoto, and he said something that really vibed with us. He told us that for him, having tea during a tea gathering — what we in the West call a tea ceremony — is like a visit to an onsen, it’s a form of relaxation. You take time out of your day to get there, and you know that it will bring calm and clarity. We found this really interesting and started thinking about tea in this kind of direction.” In The Book of Tea, Okakura Kakuzō wrote that “Tea is more than an idealisation of the form of drinking; it is a religion of the art of life.” Published in 1906, the tea philosopher’s seminal work introduced Western audiences to an understanding of tea as an expression of Japanese aesthetics and spirituality; a practice of attentiveness shaped by its entanglement with Zen Buddhism and Taoist ideas of simplicity, impermanence, and the beauty of the ordinary. The sixteenth-century tea master and cultural reformer Sen no Rikyū refined the developing wabi-cha (侘び茶) tradition, in which tea ceremonies emphasised humility and restraint. "In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music." With this rich history in mind, Marcin notes that tea culture itself can be very broad. “It can be very casual, it can be very simple: it is special in different ways. There are many places you might be afraid to step into because you feel you don’t possess the experience required. We want to remove that ‘knowledge’ barrier and make it easy for everyone to share in our curiosity.” The result is a space that draws from the rich culture of tea houses and ceremonies, but renders it slightly anew. “Beyond appreciation for the craft, the culture, and everything that surrounds it was really the desire to create an easy-going atmosphere. In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music. We thought this idea was great. Why not present the depth of tea in this way?” "We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention." The kissaten tradition offers a useful lens: where the formal tea ceremony demands studied preparation and ritual knowledge, the kissaten asks only that you sit and attend. Kissabō’s name draws on this lineage. Written 喫茶房, it shares its first two characters with kissaten — 喫茶, tea-drinking — but swaps 店, shop, for 房, chamber. A quieter word for a quieter place; and in Berlin, where inner-city neighbourhoods are crowded with VC-backed coffee chains serving thousands of three-euro flat whites, a completely unique hospitality offering. As are Kissabō’s guidelines: lowered voices, no photography or filming of those present without their consent, and the expectation of queueing quietly outside during busy times. “We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention,” Marcin explains. “And since opening, we’ve observed that people really enjoy this — the calming of the space — even if they didn’t have that intention when they arrived.” "Nobody is in a rush when they see how much attention is being put in." When visiting Kissabō, it is easy to see how it elicits such a response. The earthen-toned interior – replete with a custom oakwood tea bar, a communal table, a tatami area, and Noguchi light sculptures – is warm and atmospheric. “Everything kind of blends in, but has a voice of its own,” says Gosia. Their tea offerings – currently matcha, gyokuro, genmaicha, and hōjicha – are sourced from Japan and served alongside non-alcoholic seasonal cocktails and a range of handmade Japanese sweets. “We are very fortunate that people have trusted us with their work, their traditions, their years of culture. It is very humbling, and we are trying to do our best to share it in a proper way: without fuss, without overexplaining, always with proper care. I think when people see how everything is prepared, they behave in a way

items.title: Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play
items.summary: The post  Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Celeste Asfour Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan In the heart of Berlin, a quiet courtyard sits framed by historic properties that once thrummed with the energy of industry. Here, on the ground floor of a 19th-century building, you’ll find Strom —a café where reverie meets play, conceptualised by Berlin-based architectural multihyphenate Celeste Asfour . Celeste’s early life unfolded in an architectural household. “I grew up completely surrounded by it,” she explains. “As a child, my mum was always dragging me to museums and construction sites.” For a time, such proximity made her hesitant about joining the world of design. “That is, until I realised I was lying to myself,” she laughs. While grounded in architecture, her practice finds form in a range of aesthetic expressions—from interior design to objects and photography. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” She says that this path emerged while studying: “It was at university that I realised I might not want to be an architect in the classical sense, because I had a problem with the scale required. It was always: Building, building, building. New, new, new. And that’s just not how I enjoy working.” Her approach turned to what already exists, to material research, and a combination of old and new. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” In late 2024, she was approached with a proposition that closely aligned with her interests: a to-be-determined café, bar, or bistro set on the ground floor of a historic complex that was once home to Berlin’s earliest and most successful restaurateurs. Today, the 19th-century buildings are populated by a new generation of businesses, start-ups, and studios whose offices overlook a large internal courtyard. “The courtyard is beautiful and so are the buildings,” Celeste notes. “But it is a space that was never really used by the public because it wasn’t activated—you would never walk in and discover it unless you worked there.” "In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal..." This project was determined to change this, and—unusually—Celeste joined at its very inception. “It was quite a different setup,” she recalls, “there was no name, no logo, no website, no branding, no colours.” Working with the founders and Swedish branding and design agency Several, Celeste helped imagine what kind of offering would best serve the location. “In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal,” she adds. “The outcome was really shaped by the process: by the way it began, by the space and its requirements, and by the people that I worked with, and by a desire to have fun with it.” From their early conversations, an idea emerged: a seasonal café for artisanal coffee, small plates, and afternoon drinks. A space that would transform the courtyard from a place of transit to one of gathering and encounter. The courtyard has three entrances through which people stream in and out of each day—this perpetual circulation animates the area and renders it a kind of “safe harbour,” says Celeste. From here came the café’s name: Strom translates from German as “electrical current” or “stream”: a flow of people and energy. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture." The graphic identity embraces these ideas. Playful and minimal, its refined sensibility bounces across the webpage and stacks atop itself in the logo. This concept is given physical form by Celeste’s interior design, which focuses on spatial arrangement and a balance of materials. “In every project, I think you have to create some sort of tension,” she says. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture. You have to balance hard things with soft things. That kind of tension results in balance.” In Strom, this balance emerges through combining traditional techniques and historic elements with contemporary processes and objects. “A lot of thought went into the textures and materials,” Celeste explains. “We spent a long time selecting the marble and the wood, considering how the colours and forms would work together.” The rich darkness of the oiled cherry wood contrasts with the bright weight of the brutalist-edged rose marble counter. The tension between these elements is counterbalanced by the softness of the locally handmade terracotta tiles covering the floor. These organic materials are complemented by a range of modern finishes that lend the space a distinct character. Brushed-steel shelves, produced by Studio Ultimo alongside the wooden panelling, hold magazines and objects that Celeste sourced from local antique markets. One shelf provides a view into the kitchen, giving guests a small insight into the creation of their plates before they arrive at their tables. Another features a mirrored backing that adds further depth to the space. Milky-hued mauve tabletops, made from recycled polycarbonate ‘Karlite’ by Dutch studio Plasticiet, are grounded by wooden chairs from Form&Refine and bench seats upholstered in Kvadrat fabric. The space features concertina windows that open the café to the courtyard during warmer weather. When the sun is high, they bring ample light into the space. During the winter months, the lighting design is used for aesthetic form and atmospheric effect. Hand-textured Murano sconces from Milan-based studio 6 am cast a warm rose-hued glow across the interior. A Noguchi lamp throws papered light from the shelves, and a faceted pendant by Asca Studio draws the line of sight to the coffee bar below it. Though the interior is undoubtedly elevated, it is not without a sense of play. The bathroom has been completed with a bulbous, bubble-gum pink sink, whi

items.title: TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency
items.summary: The post  TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name TRADER HiFi Images Clemens Poloczek Words Anna Dorothea Ker Hamburg’s growing TRADER constellation stems from founder Vincent von Thien’s wish to offer his city more than another café. TRADER Gallery in the Schanze set the first tone, uniting specialty coffee with art and design. The latest outpost, TRADER HiFi in the city’s Ottensen district, brings von Thien’s interest in sound into clearer focus. Drawn from the lineage of Japanese kissas and tuned to contemporary life, the space shifts between daytime sociability and evening sessions that invite attentive listening. A considered acoustic architecture, a custom sound system and collaborations with design studios across Europe give the small space its distinctive presence. What emerges is a third place where listening becomes a shared daily pleasure. Origins Vincent von Thien’s route to TRADER began years earlier during long stints in Australia during his modelling career. Sydney in 2011 introduced him to a style of café culture he hadn’t encountered at home—in his words, “my first real encounter with the specialty coffee scene.” It left a mark, even though the tools to build something similar in Germany were out of reach at the time. He began with a mobile version, launching Coffee Bike Hamburg with a friend and serving espresso at festivals. When modelling lost its appeal, he returned to the idea of a fixed space. A small unit in the harbor city’s Schanze district became TRADER Gallery, combining coffee with art and a selection of vintage design. von Thien wanted to offer something civic, not only commercial. “A small fusion of specialty coffee and art,” as he puts it; “to give Hamburg something more than just another café around the corner. I liked the idea of offering emerging artists a fair platform.” TRADER Gallery laid the groundwork for what would follow. Its second iteration, TRADER HiFi—opened in Ottensen in September 2025—extends that vision into the field of sound. Culture of Listening TRADER HiFi’s framework comes from Japan’s jazz kissas—listening cafés—of the 1970s, where, as von Thien puts it, “people could listen to music in high-quality sound because they didn’t have the equipment at home.” He matched this with the atmosphere of today’s listening bars, then rethought the model for Hamburg. The café works in two modes. Days are social, shaped by DJs whose sets provide a spirited backdrop to conversation. Evenings shift to focused sessions where the room falls still. “The idea is that for those sessions we ask people not to talk,” von Thien shares. “They’re dedicated to music.” Performances range from live sets to curated record journeys routed directly through the custom sound system. An accompanying beverage program keeps the mood clear-minded. “We don’t serve alcohol, as I want full focus on specialty coffee and music.” Programming Eclecticism Though still young, TRADER HiFi has already welcomed a wide sweep of genres. “We’ve already had world music, ambient, jazz, disco house,” von Thien shares. Artists such as Coco Maria, Barış Kadem and Dounia hint at the range that threads through the programme, alongside recurring sets by Panama.x and others. “What matters is high-quality music and talented people,” von Thien says. The format attracts those looking for a change in pace or setting, and requests arrive from both Hamburg and abroad. “We’re getting lots of requests from DJs, including international ones. It shows there’s a real need here in Hamburg.” As the first listening café in the city, TRADER HiFi gives artists a venue to explore ideas outside the club context. “Many DJs want to break out of their usual musical setting or play in a different environment, maybe even try another genre,” von Thien notes. The only condition is that the set suits the space. “It’s not a party. It should fit the concept, and artists should have freedom to shape the evening as they imagine.” Room for Sound The interior in Ottensen had to support both hospitality and audio without asserting either too strongly. von Thien pursued his vision for a room that settled the senses. “I wanted to create a timeless, grounding space that suits the music, an atmosphere that invites you to linger and feel calm,” he explains. Cork became central to the acoustic design. Burnt cork lines the ceiling of the main listening room, and a required structural beam was enlarged, packed with acoustic wool and wrapped in cork, acting as a central sound absorber. The custom concept grew in partnership with Antwerp-based Studio Corkinho , whose practice draws on the Alentejo’s long tradition of harvesting oak bark and reworking reclaimed cork into objects and spatial elements with a highly sensorial presence. For the sound system, von Thien worked closely with H.A.N.D. HiFi in Berlin. They developed the layout of the horns, booth and supporting speakers, ensuring the acoustic performance sits naturally within the space. With 70 square meters to work with, every decision counted. To define its configuration, von Thien spent in the emptied space, studying how people would move and where sound would settle. “I moved ideas around, thought things through,” he shares. The footprint is compact, so circulation and bar flow had to work intuitively. Collaborators contributed meaningfully to the final environment. Lisbon-based THER created furniture pieces that lend the room its stripped-back clarity, including wooden tables informed by Japanese woodworking techniques and produced with Portuguese carpentry studio Nó Marceneiros . Brussels-based porcelain studio Frizbee Ceramics produced the tableware used throughout the café, and Vitra supported the project with Akari lamps that bring a soft, diffused light to the interior. Von Thien emphasizes the long view that guided his collaborations: “The idea wasn’t to create hype, but to build a place that still works ten years from now.” A Growing Menu Specialty coffee anchors the beverage program at TRADER HiFi. items.title: The Artful Life: 6 Things Galerie Editors Love This Week
items.summary:
From a jewel-box bakery in Brooklyn from James Beard Award winner Chad Robertson to the return of Anna Petrus’s pewter lions in a painted garden at Svenskt Tenn 
 The post  The Artful Life: 6 Things <i>Galerie</i> Editors Love This Week  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: “Sequence of Spaces,” an exhibition of pewter works by Anna Petrus and murals by Elvira Solana at Svenskt Tenn’s flagship in Stockholm. Photo: Henrik Lundell 1. At Svenskt Tenn, Anna Petrus’s Pewter Lions Return in a Painted Garden Anna Petrus became one of the Swedish Grace movement’s most prominent figures after her breakthrough at the 1925 Paris World’s Fair, where her work in cast iron earned a coveted gold medal and caught the eye of Estrid Ericson, founder of legacy Stockholm design shop Svenskt Tenn . The first woman in Sweden to work in cast iron for the Näfveqvarn ironworks, Petrus went on to create some of the emporium’s most enduring objects, including a pewter lion that has been cast from the same molds since 1927. A century after their collaboration began, Svenskt Tenn is celebrating Petrus’s artistry with “Sequence of Spaces” at its Stockholm flagship on the city’s waterfront. The exhibition brings together pewter and cast-iron pieces from the emporium’s archive and sculptures on loan from Petrus’s family. Among the reissued works are a pewter lamp base ornamented with female figures and grape clusters in relief. Photo: Henrik Lundell Among the lesser-known early pieces Svenskt Tenn has reissued are an elegant pewter lamp base, its surface ornamented with female figures and grape clusters in relief, and a substantial mirror frame crowned by a reclining lion. Backdropping the pieces are Spanish painter Elvira Solana ’s murals depicting painted courtyards that give way to gardens with dancing figures. — Ryan Waddoups Cover of Louis Vuitton’s Thailand tome. Photo: Courtesy Louis Vuitton Photo: Liu Shuwei Cover of Louis Vuitton’s Thailand tome. Photo: Courtesy Louis Vuitton Photo: George Hoyningen Huene 2. Louis Vuitton Travels to Shanghai and Thailand for New Additions to Fashion Eye Book Series A brand known to recognize how fashion and travel intertwine, leading fashion house Louis Vuitton has now crossed two new destinations off their list as part of their extensive Fashion Eye Photography Collection . On the occasion of Paris Photo running November 12-15, two new tomes spotlighting the city of Shanghai and the country of Thailand will transport readers to these areas through striking photography of both its people and landscapes. Leading fashion photographer George Hoyningen-Huene spearheads the Thailand tome, where his field notes and personal photography taken throughout the country have been compiled to present an authentic representation of architecture, residents, and history. For the Shanghai addition, photographer Liu Shuwei showcases the city not as the bustling hub visitors may know it to be, but captures moments of peace and serenity. Having lived there for a decade, softer elements such as residents’ everyday lives, fallen leaves on the ground, or empty roads are highlighted through Shuwei’s polaroid-esque style of photography. — Shelby Black New Orleans artist Hill Spriggins with “A Night on Earth, The Finale” Macallan Whiskey. Photo: Courtesy of Macallan 3. The Macallen Whiskey Celebrates The Spirit of New Orleans with Local Painter Hill Spriggins’s Craftsmanship The Macallan Whiskey , in collaboration with local artist Hill Spriggins, has unveiled “A Night on Earth, The Finale,” the fifth and final release in its “A Night on Earth” collection, bringing the series to a close with a special edition single malt Scotch whisky. Inspired by the music, community, and vibrant culture of New Orleans, Louisiana, the spirit captures the warmth and optimism of the New Year through exceptional craftsmanship and artistry. “‘A Night on Earth’ has become a cherished collection celebrating New Year traditions from around the world,” Macallan Creative Director Jaume Ferras said. “It is fitting that this final chapter honors New Orleans — a city renowned for its creativity, resilience and extraordinary sense of community.” Matured in a harmonious combination of sherry-seasoned American and European oak casks, the whisky was crafted by The Macallan team to echo the soulful flavors and spirited aromas of the city. Widely regarded as the birthplace of modern cocktail craft, New Orleans’ spirit of flavor invention inspires an expression that is unmistakably The Macallan. Continuing The Macallan’s tradition of artistic collaborations for its end-of-year releases, New Orleans native and painter Spriggins translated her memories of citywide celebrations into three bold, multi-layered artworks, bringing her oil paintings to life. — Rebecca Anderson Installation view, “Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow.” Photo: Joshua White 4. Legendary Restaurateur Michael Chow’s Deep Ties to the Art World Go on View at Gagosian Michael Chow , the visionary behind the iconic Mr. Chow Chinese restaurants, has long been a central figure in the art world as a collector, patron, and practicing visual artist. Now, a two-part exhibition is showcasing highlights from his 60-year collecting history, including pieces by Andy Warhol , Jean-Michel Basquiat , Urs Fischer, and many others. Last week, “ Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow ” debuted at Gagosian’s Beverly Hills location, where it was on view through November 7. Now, the collection is en route to New York, where it will go on view from November 14 through December 22 in conjunction with the fall auction season. “Art and artists have been at the heart of my life,” said Chow. “The privilege of living with these treasures and sharing them with the public has brought me great joy. Every piece carries a story, a seat at the table, and a cherished friendship—and over time, these artists have proven to be the greats of our century. Now, it’s time to see them go out into the world and have my fifteen minutes.” Additional highlights include a half-length portrait by Hockney and a work made from paint and plate fragments, including china from Mr. Chow, by Julian Schnabel.— Alexandria Sillo Photo: Austin Leis Photo: Austin Leis 5

items.title: A 600-Year-Old Istanbul Shipyard Finds New Life as a Luxury Wonderland
items.summary:
Along the Golden Horn, Turkish fashion powerhouse Beymen unveils a dazzling flagship filled with imaginative interiors and contemporary art within centuries-old shipbuilding halls  
 The post  A 600-Year-Old Istanbul Shipyard Finds New Life as a Luxury Wonderland  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen The Golden Horn, an estuary that curves into Istanbul ’ s European shore, owes its evocative name in part to the warm sunlight that gilds its waters at sunset. Branching off the Bosphorus, the sheltered waterway served as a bustling harbor for Byzantine Constantinople and later the Ottoman Empire, its shores once crowded with shipyards and merchant vessels. Today, a different kind of splendor has arrived along its storied waterfront. Within a 60-acre complex of former shipbuilding halls at the historic Ottoman Imperial Arsenal, whose origins date to the 15th century, Beymen —Turkey’s leading luxury fashion retailer, akin to Neiman Marcus in the United States—has unveiled a mind-bending new destination for luxury fashion. Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen Designed in collaboration with OMA and fittingly christened the Galleries of Luxury, the 129,000-square-foot flagship marks Beymen’s largest to date. Inside, nine imaginatively designed galleries contrast dramatically with the building’s timeworn masonry. The original shipbuilding halls, some soaring 44 feet beneath exposed roof beams, run perpendicular to the waterfront and connect through monumental arches. Each gallery houses a different retail category, from menswear and womenswear to beauty, fragrance , and homewares, with shoppers wandering through a phantasmagoria of punchy palettes and sumptuous materials. Think lime green resin panels backdropping Alaïa gowns, men’s shoes perched on movable, shard-like recycled plastic display fixtures that resemble marble, and perforated steel wall panels cold-formed to emulate the shape of an existing stone arch. Knowing the transformation would be more arduous than a standard-fare retail interior, Beymen sought a world-class architect with a lengthy résumé of adaptive reuse. When Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçi first approached OMA , the firm founded by Rem Koolhaas initially demurred. “They didn’t want to do a department store,” she recalls. Once she explained the extraordinary nature of the undertaking and they agreed to visit the site, they accepted her offer. Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen “They found a way to preserve the history of the building and introduce a very contemporary architectural approach,” Çapçi says of OMA’s intervention, which involved adding an extension along the buildings’ rear and inserting a mezzanine level. In the handbag gallery, the firm suspended giant oval, rectangular, and rhomboid structures finished in decorative plaster overhead to carve out surprisingly intimate-feeling settings within the cavernous hall. The menswear gallery’s procession of powder-coated steel screens, inset with smoked glass, gradually widens toward the waterfront, drawing eyes toward the Golden Horn. Another gallery stuns with a gravity-defying installation by Miguel Rodrigues that undulates overhead like calligraphic brushstrokes, its lustrous gold automotive paint paying tribute to the waterway. Collectible furnishings introduce further surprises, from Mario Belini’s generously cushioned armchairs to Korean artist Saerom Yoon’s glimmering furnishings in translucent acrylic. Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen Outside, OMA made room for new plazas, including a secluded garden nestled behind the historic halls. Expansive glazing opens sweeping views across the Golden Horn toward Istanbul’s Old Town, while a waterfront terrace at the in-store café, Bardot Blue, invites shoppers and passersby to settle in over a leisurely alfresco brew. Such interventions give the centuries-old shipyard a marvelous second life—far removed from the days when gargantuan vessels passed through its towering arches. “They didn’t impose anything on the building,” Çapçi says of OMA’s interventions. “They took it as it was and tried to make it relevant again.” As the imaginative architecture may suggest, Beymen operates differently from a traditional department store. “Here, everything is selected and purchased by us,” Çapçi tells Galerie . “Curation is our business, and fashion retail is all about curation.” Her discerning eye becomes evident throughout the galleries, which showcase an exceptional assortment of more than 350 brands, including limited-edition creations from internationally acclaimed houses such as Valentino , Brunello Cucinelli, Maison Margiela, Jil Sander, The Row, and Bottega Veneta. Dedicated pop-up areas introduce an ever-changing roster of coveted labels, from an exclusive selection of Phoebe Philo garments to the sumptuous cashmere of Parisian label Kujten. Beymen Tersane: Galleries of Luxury in Istanbul. Photo: Courtesy of Beymen Further distinguishing Beymen is a dedicated exhibition hall, which inaugurates its programming with “Timeless Treasures: The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” a sweeping survey of the handbag’s evolution and significance as a symbol of identity and craftsmanship. Curated by fashion journalist Laurence Benaïm with scenography by Bureau Betak, the show unites 80 dazzling creations from 55 luxury houses, many inspired by Anatolia’s craft traditions. Handbags adorned with motifs drawn from İznik ceramics and Ottoman embroidery appear alongside archival treasures, including an 1886 Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk originally crafted for Sultan Abdülhamid II. Several fashion houses also created exclusive pieces for the exhibition. “Timeless Treasures: The Eternal Journey of the Bag” at Beymen Tersane, Istanbul. There’s not that much traffic.” He’s blown away. And we went to this restaurant, CHARCUT , get a table, and he’s like, “Did you make a reservation?” I’m like, “Nah, man, I just assume we get a table.” He’s like, “You just walked into a restaurant at 7:00 and got a table at this nice of a place?” I’m like, “Yeah, man.” He’s mind blown Nora Richie: Ah, the Calgary life. No traffic, no reservations, no problem. I’m Nora Ritchie, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side. This month, we’re talking with Canadian writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, I’m talking with Andrew Phung. Andrew is a comedian and actor best known for playing Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience , and he’s the creator and star of Run the Burbs . But for this conversation, what matters most is that Andrew is a superfan of Calgary, the medium-sized city where he grew up. This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast : a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and all major podcast apps. To Andrew Phung, Calgary is simultaneously a big city and a small town—in all the right ways. Travel Alberta / Sameer Ahmed Calgary is in southern Alberta, where the prairies meet the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. And to be honest, it’s not exactly considered the poster child for Alberta tourism. That honor usually goes to places like Banff and Lake Louise, with their turquoise lakes and mountain views. But Andrew thinks his hometown deserves a little more love. Andrew: I would describe Calgary as a really big city that has all the amenities but feels a bit like a small town at times in regards to its friendliness. The mountains are right behind you. There’s really fresh air, and it is so bright. I think there’s some wild statistic, like Calgary gets the most sunshine in, like, all of the world during the winter or something like that. Nora: I wanna hear about the street you grew up on, your neighborhood. Andrew: I will talk about Northeast Calgary until I die. The northeast of Calgary is a quadrant of the city. It is the most culturally diverse. I grew up in Whitehorn, Temple, Falconridge, Coral Springs. I’ll name the neighborhoods, but Coral Springs was where we ended up last. And what I loved about it was, Coral Springs is full of dreamers. It’s people who this was the first new house they bought. And it was really affordable to new immigrants, families starting out fresh. So literally everyone on my street had kids, and so we were always playing. Like, every day after school, we’d come home, we would get on our bikes, we would go to someone’s house, get the baseball equipment, get the hockey equipment, carry the net, you know, all that stuff. Every day at 5:00, you know, people would come home from work, and then we’d have to go inside and have dinner and do homework. That was our street. It felt a little bit like Pleasantville. Nora: It does sound like Pleasantville. So your parents are Chinese and Vietnamese. How did they end up in Calgary? Andrew: So most people assume your parents come to Canada together. My parents met in Canada. They had different immigration stories. My mom immigrated to Airdrie, Alberta, which is a suburb of Calgary. My dad ended up in Saskatchewan. A church there had sponsored a bunch of Vietnamese refugees into Canada. And then my dad tracked down a friend living in Calgary, and he went to take the bus to Calgary and waited for him at the bus station, and the guy didn’t show up. And then my dad saw another person delivering Chinese food, went and talked to that guy, and that guy took my dad home, and my dad lived with him for two years. The Asian community in Calgary in the ’70s and ’80s was so tight-knit. Like, if they saw one of their own, they would take you in. It was so supportive. And I remember years later, my dad saw an old friend. I’m like, “Yo, who was that guy?” My dad’s like, “Oh, I used to live with him.” And I’m like, “You need to give me the full backstory on that.” But my mom and dad met in Airdrie at a card game. My uncle introduced my mom and dad, and I was born and raised in Calgary. That’s our immigration story, and I really always reflect on how welcoming Canada was in the ’70s and ’80s. Really welcoming in refugees and immigrants to build a better life. And my parents always say, “Andrew, we’re living the Canadian dream. Everything we do is the Canadian dream.” Nora: Related to your work in comedy and growing up, was there a time in your childhood that you were sort of like, “Wait a minute, I’m pretty funny.
